The daughter comes through eating something out of her hand. The mother's eyes go straight to the wet hair. Her chin comes up and she gives her a flat unimpressed look. She makes a small circling motion at her own head, then points down at the floorboards where water is dripping. The daughter looks at her, looks at the floor, and shrugs one shoulder. The mother's eyes go up to the ceiling for half a beat and come back down. She puts the towel back on her daughter's shoulders properly, briskly, both hands. The daughter lets her, dead-faced, then walks off pulling it straight back off. The mother watches her go and lets out one breath through her nose. HARD CUT.

SHOT 3 · 6–9s · THE SKIRT · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 130 cm in the daughter's bedroom doorway, pushing in forty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the empty windowsill with its pale ring. Frame CENTRE: the daughter in the grey hoodie and a short black skirt, backpack half on. Frame RIGHT: the mother in the doorway with a longer garment on a hanger.
She holds the hanger up beside her daughter, level with her hip, comparing lengths without touching her. Her eyebrows go up. She gives the hanger a small shake. The daughter looks at it, looks at her, takes the hanger and hangs it on the door handle beside her, pointedly, then walks past her mother in exactly what she was already wearing. The mother turns and watches her go with a small five-degree head shake. HARD CUT.

SHOT 4 · 9–12s · THE PHONE AND THE FIRST DOOR · 50 degrees [35mm], camera at 115 cm in the living space, arcing right sixty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the two couches and the coffee table. Frame CENTRE: the daughter on a couch, feet up on the cushions, phone in both hands. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT: the mother crossing. Frame RIGHT: the console with its two standing picture frames and the calligraphy above it.
The mother comes past and taps the daughter's shins twice with the back of her hand — feet off. The daughter takes her feet off slowly, one at a time, without looking up. The mother stops, turns back and holds out one open palm for the phone. The daughter looks at the palm, looks at her mother, and puts the phone face down against her own chest. A beat. Then she gets up and goes toward the stairs, and THE BEDROOM DOOR GOES upstairs off frame — firm, the latch cracking home, the floorboards carrying a light shock. In frame the calligraphy shifts about two degrees on its hook and settles. ONE of the two small picture frames on the console tips onto its face with a flat knock. Nothing else moves and nothing is damaged. The mother stands with her palm still out, looks at the ceiling for a beat, drops the hand, crosses to the console and stands the frame back up without ceremony. HARD CUT.

SHOT 5 · 12–15s · THE REPORT CARD · 30 degrees [65mm], camera at 125 cm in the living space, drifting right thirty-five centimetres. Frame LEFT: the mother holding a folded printed sheet, seen from behind so nothing on it is legible. Frame CENTRE: the daughter facing her across the coffee table. Frame RIGHT: the couches and the console.
The mother holds the sheet up between them and taps it twice with two fingers, hard, in the same spot. She turns it toward her daughter and raises her eyebrows. The daughter's eyes go down to it for half a beat and back up. She shrugs — the same one-shoulder shrug from shot two, deliberately the same. The mother's hand comes down. She folds the sheet in half, then in half again, and sets it squarely on the coffee table between them. The daughter looks at it lying there, steps around the table without picking it up, and goes. The mother looks at the folded sheet and puts one hand up and down. HARD CUT.

SHOT 6 · 15–18s · THE DESK LAMP · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 100 cm in the daughter's bedroom, arcing right forty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the empty windowsill with its pale ring. Late. The daughter is at the desk under the lamp, headphones on, drawing — plants, wild and overgrown, sprawling off the edges of the page. The mother appears in the doorway. She taps the door frame twice with two knuckles. No response. She reaches in and switches the lamp off at the wall. The daughter turns, slow, pulls one headphone cup off her ear, holds it there, and looks at her with absolutely nothing in her face. A beat. The mother taps her own wrist twice and gives her a flat look. The daughter switches the lamp back on without breaking eye contact and turns back to the desk. The mother stands there a beat, exhales through her nose, and goes. HARD CUT.

The plate goes down on the corner of the desk — food on it, and steam, because it has been reheated. The mother's fingers stay on the rim. She waits. Half a beat, then a full one. The daughter does not look up, does not turn her head, does not acknowledge the plate or the hand that put it there. Her pencil does not stop. The mother's fingers lift off the rim, hover, and come back down. Then she picks the plate back up and takes it out with her. Hold on the empty corner of the desk. HARD CUT.

Frame CENTRE: the daughter and the mother facing each other across two metres of floorboards. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT and RIGHT: the console with its frames and the calligraphy above it.
The mother is holding a loose sheet of paper — one of the drawings, wild sprawling overgrown plants. She holds it up. Her other hand makes a small flat gesture at it and then a wider one toward the ceiling, toward the room upstairs. The daughter's jaw sets. She steps forward and takes the sheet out of her mother's hand — not snatching, but taking — folds it once against her own chest, and turns and goes. THE BEDROOM DOOR GOES again upstairs off frame, a little firmer than the first. The calligraphy shifts a couple of degrees and settles. The same picture frame tips over again with a flat knock. Frame RIGHT: the bedroom door standing open, and the mother arriving in it.
The mother stops in the doorway and watches for a beat before her daughter clocks her in the mirror. Their eyes meet in the glass — not directly, only in the reflection — and both hold it. The mother lifts one hand and makes a small wiping gesture across her own cheek, unimpressed. The daughter's jaw shifts. She turns her back to the mirror and to her mother at the same time, reaches out and pushes the bedroom door closed in her mother's face — not slammed, just shut, deliberately and quietly, the latch clicking. On the other side of it the mother stands looking at the timber, raises both eyebrows, and walks away. HARD CUT.

The daughter comes through fast in the grey hoodie and jeans with her backpack on one shoulder, heading for the front door. The mother comes into frame at frame LEFT and puts a hand out — not to stop her, just raised. The daughter does not slow down, does not look at her, and goes out. THE FRONT DOOR GOES, firmer than either of the bedroom ones, the latch cracking and the floorboards carrying it. The calligraphy shifts and settles. The picture frame tips onto its face one last time. The mother lowers her hand. She does not go to the door and she does not go to the frame. She stands there in the middle of the room, looks at the ceiling, lets out one long breath through her nose, and puts one hand flat on the back of the nearest couch. LAST FRAME: the mother alone at frame LEFT-OF-CENTRE with her hand on the couch back, the fallen picture frame lying face down on the console beside her, the front door shut in the entry beyond, and the withering ivy up on its shelf at frame RIGHT, exactly as it has been all sequence, unlooked-at.

PHYSICS: a firmly closed door cracks its latch home, flexes its frame slightly and sends a light shock through the floorboards that reaches objects resting on surfaces in the room — a framed artwork on a hook shifts a degree or two and settles, and a small standing picture frame with a shallow foot tips onto its face with a flat knock and slides a centimetre. Nothing breaks, nothing cracks, no glass leaves any frame and no plaster is damaged. A door pushed quietly closed clicks its latch softly and the frame does not flex at all. Wet hair is heavy, clings, darkens the cloth it touches and drips. A garment on a hanger swings and settles when shaken and again when hung on a door handle. A dinner plate is hot enough that she holds it by the rim with her fingertips. Paper folded against a chest creases sharply; a printed sheet folded twice and set on a table stays where it is put. Headphone cups compress hair and spring back. Unglazed clay sits on painted timber with real friction and the pot never moves. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand, a body or a light shockwave has reached it, and no plant moves at any point for any reason.

ACTING: the mother is EXASPERATED, not wounded. Her whole register is a woman being repeatedly irritated by a teenager and having no idea what else to do about it — the flat unimpressed look, the eyes going up to the ceiling and coming back down, the one hand up and dropped, the five-degree head shake, the breath through the nose, the brisk unceremonious tidying. She never flinches at a door, never startles, never looks stricken, never gets emotional and never plays the victim. She never shouts, never grabs and never raises a hand. The daughter's attitude is entirely physical and entirely fifteen: the one-shoulder shrug used twice on purpose, the dead-faced stare, the headphone cup held off the ear, the lamp switched back on without breaking eye contact, the hanger hung on the door handle, the feet taken off the couch slowly one at a time, the door pushed quietly shut in her mother's face, the walk straight out the front without a glance. She is never cruel and never triumphant and she never smirks — she is simply done negotiating. Neither ever does the same thing at the same time; every response arrives a full beat after the other's action. Both blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously. Neither looks at the lens.

AUDIO: diegetic sound only. Room tone that is quieter and emptier than the same house five years earlier. Three door closings — two of a bedroom door upstairs and one of the front door downstairs — each firm rather than violent, each with a latch cracking home, a light shock through the floorboards, and a small picture frame tipping onto timber with a flat knock. One door pushed quietly shut with a soft latch click. Wet hair dripping on floorboards. A towel dragged off shoulders. A hanger shaken and hooked over a door handle. Two fingers tapping a printed sheet, twice. Paper folded twice and set on timber. Two knuckles on a door frame. A wall switch clicking off and on. A pencil not stopping. A ceramic plate set down on timber and picked back up. Paper taken from a hand and folded once. Bare adult feet and socked teenage feet on boards at clearly different weights. A hand laid flat on a couch back. Adult breaths let out through the nose, several times, at slightly different lengths. Faint tinny sound leaking from headphones with no melody and no words in it — just a thin percussive hiss. No speech, no words, no whisper and no vocal sound beyond breath from anyone at any point. NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

LOCKS: ten hard-cut shots across thirty seconds, each with its own lens, camera height and physical move, none locked off, none opening on a still. Nine collisions in a row with nothing between them — the wet hair, the skirt, the phone, the report card, the desk lamp, the plate, the drawing, the mirror, and the front door. ONLY TWO DOORS EXIST IN THIS SEQUENCE: the daughter's bedroom door and the front door, closed three times between them, firmly and never violently. NOTHING IS EVER DAMAGED — no cracks in any plaster, the calligraphy never falls, nothing breaks, and the only thing that ever goes over is one small picture frame on the console, three times, stood back up twice. The mother is ANNOYED AND DISAPPOINTED throughout, never shocked, never hurt and never a victim — flat looks, eyes to the ceiling, a hand up and down, a breath through the nose. NOBODY WATERS OR TOUCHES OR LOOKS AT THE PLANT at any point; it sits on its high shelf unchanged in every frame it appears in. It never moves and has no face. The daughter never cries and never smirks. Nothing moves without a hand, a body or a light shockwave reaching it first. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms words, and nobody looks at the lens.

TEN SHOTS — 30 seconds. Hard cuts only, nine of them, instantaneous, no dissolves, no fades, no transitional frames. Three seconds per shot. Real-time throughout, no slow motion, no ramping, no speed change anywhere.
NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.
ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE — CRITICAL: nobody in this sequence speaks, ever. Every argument in this montage is conducted entirely with hands, shoulders, chins, eyes and distance, and not one mouth ever opens to form a word. No spoken words, no talking, no whispering, no shouting, no muttering, no calling out, no vocalising of any kind. No character's mouth ever forms words, parts as if about to speak, or moves as if speaking at any point, in the foreground or the background, in focus or out. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue. Suppressing the audio alone is not enough — the mouths themselves must never move as if speaking.
NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point. The framed black brush calligraphy on the west wall is a physical painted artwork hanging on plaster. The report card the mother holds is seen from behind or edge-on and its printing is never legible.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

THE ESCALATION — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE STRUCTURE: this is ten collisions in a row with nothing between them, and the pressure only goes one direction. Early beats are small corrections the daughter absorbs. Middle beats she starts giving back. Late beats she stops engaging entirely, which is worse. By the last shot she is not fighting anymore — she has simply left the room and the mother is standing in the wreckage of an argument she was having alone. Nobody wins anything.

THE THREE SLAMS AND THE HOUSE TAKING IT — CRITICAL: three doors are slammed in this montage and each one is bigger than the last, and the house carries the damage forward between shots so the audience sees it accumulate. WRITE THE IMPACT PHYSICALLY EVERY TIME. On every slam: the door frame flexes and the latch cracks home, the whole run of floorboards carries the shock, the framed black brush calligraphy on the west wall jumps on its hook and settles further off level than it was, dust lifts off the top edge of its frame, the two small standing picture frames on the television console rock on their feet, and the record player lid ticks against its cabinet.
FIRST SLAM: the calligraphy jumps and settles about three degrees off level. One picture frame rocks and stays up. The mother straightens both afterward.
SECOND SLAM: the calligraphy jumps harder and settles eight degrees off. One picture frame goes over face down on the console. A hairline crack appears in the plaster running up from the top corner of the door frame. The mother straightens the calligraphy and stands the frame back up.
THIRD SLAM: the calligraphy comes off its hook entirely — a real drop, glass and dark timber landing flat on the console below, not breaking, rocking twice and coming to rest badly askew. Both picture frames go over. The crack in the plaster runs further. THE MOTHER DOES NOT STRAIGHTEN ANYTHING THIS TIME.
Household harmony, face down on the furniture. Nobody ever remarks on it.

THE PLANT IS PRESENT AND IGNORED — CRITICAL: the daughter's withering ivy stands on the high shelf in the background of several of these shots and NOBODY TOUCHES IT, tends it, waters it, looks at it or acknowledges it at any point in this entire sequence. There is no watering in this montage. The plant is simply there, up on its shelf, getting slightly worse between shots — a leaf on the record cabinet in the early shots, two by the middle, three by the end — while two people below it argue about hair and shoes and lamps and never once look up. Its condition changes only between shots, never on camera.

THE PLANT IS WITHERING, NOT DYING — CRITICAL: it is a mature plant that has lost its vigour. Less green than it was — the leaf colour dulled toward a grey-sage, the surfaces matte where they used to be waxy — and less full, with the crown thinner and looser and a few bare stretches of stem showing between leaves. A handful of leaves are slightly cupped and one or two carry a fine dry rim at the margin. It still has most of its foliage, its runners still hang over the rim, and it is unmistakably alive. It is NOT dead, NOT brown, NOT crisp, NOT skeletal, NOT bare and NOT collapsed. It never moves, never reacts, never leans and never responds at any point, to anybody or anything, and it has no face and no expression. It is as still as furniture in every frame.

NEITHER OF THEM IS THE VILLAIN — CRITICAL: the mother is frightened and converts every feeling into a task, and she never once shouts, never grabs, never looms and never raises a hand. Her weapon is turning away to something else with her hands. The daughter is fifteen and gives back attitude in the exact register of a fifteen-year-old — eye-rolls, shrugs, headphones, a shoulder turned, a door — and she is never cruel and never triumphant. Both are exhausted by each other.

PHYSICS: a slammed door flexes its frame, cracks its latch home and sends a shock through the floorboards that reaches every object resting on every surface in the room — heavier objects rock and lighter ones go over. A framed artwork on a hook jumps, swings, settles off level, and on the third impact lifts clear of the hook and drops flat onto the console below with real weight, rocking twice before settling. Plaster cracks propagate from a corner and do not close. Wet hair is heavy, clings, darkens the cloth it touches and drips. A garment on a hanger swings and settles when the hanger is shaken and again when it is hung on a door handle. A dinner plate is hot enough that she holds it by the rim with her fingertips. Paper folded against a chest creases sharply, and a printed sheet folded twice and set on a table stays exactly where it is put. Headphone cups compress hair and spring back. A door pushed closed rather than slammed clicks its latch softly and the frame does not flex. Fallen leaves are weightless and do not move once down. Unglazed clay sits on painted timber with real friction and the pot never moves. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand, a body or a shockwave has reached it, and no plant moves at any point for any reason.

ACTING: the mother is never angry and never shouts — every correction is fear wearing the face of housework, and her tells are a set jaw, a breath out through the nose, and turning away to a task with her hands. She straightens the calligraphy after the first slam and after the second, and the fact that she does not straighten it after the third is the single most important thing she does in this montage. The daughter's attitude is entirely physical and entirely fifteen: the one-shoulder shrug used twice on purpose, the dead-faced stare, the headphone cup held off the ear, the lamp switched back on without breaking eye contact, the hanger hung on the door handle, the feet taken off the couch slowly one at a time, the door pushed quietly shut in her mother's face. She is never cruel and never triumphant and she never smirks — she is simply done negotiating, and by the last two shots she has stopped engaging at all, which is worse than fighting. Neither ever does the same thing at the same time; every response arrives a full beat after the other's action. Both blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously. Neither looks at the lens.

LOCKS: ten hard-cut shots across thirty seconds, each with its own lens, camera height and physical move, none locked off, none opening on a still. Ten collisions in a row with nothing between them — the wet hair, the skirt, the phone, the report card, the desk lamp, the plate, the drawing, the mirror, and two more doors. NOBODY WATERS THE PLANT IN THIS SEQUENCE and nobody touches it, looks at it or acknowledges it at any point; it stands on its high shelf getting quietly worse in the background while two people below it argue about everything else. Three doors are slammed, each bigger than the last, and the house carries the damage forward between shots: the calligraphy settles three degrees off, then eight, then comes off its hook entirely and lands flat on the console; the picture frames rock, then one goes over, then both; a crack opens in the plaster and runs further. The mother straightens things after the first two slams and does not after the third. The plant is WITHERING, not dying: duller and thinner but still leafed and still alive. It never moves and has no face. The mother never shouts, never grabs and never raises a hand. The daughter never cries and never smirks. Nothing moves without a hand, a body or a shockwave reaching it first. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms words, and nobody looks at the lens.

TEN SHOTS — 30 seconds. Hard cuts only, nine of them, instantaneous, no dissolves, no fades, no transitional frames. Roughly three seconds per shot. Real-time throughout, no slow motion, no ramping, no speed change anywhere.
NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.
ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE — CRITICAL: nobody in this sequence speaks, ever. No spoken words, no talking, no whispering, no shouting, no muttering, no calling out, no vocalising of any kind. Every argument in this montage is conducted entirely with hands, shoulders, chins, eyes and distance, and not one mouth ever opens to form a word. No character's mouth ever forms words, parts as if about to speak, or moves as if speaking at any point, in the foreground or the background, in focus or out. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue. Suppressing the audio alone is not enough — the mouths themselves must never move as if speaking.
NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point. The framed black brush calligraphy on the west wall is a physical painted artwork hanging on plaster.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

THE ALTERNATION — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE STRUCTURE: the montage alternates strictly between an argument and a watering. Argue, water, argue, water, all the way through. The audience must make the connection themselves without a word: every time these two collide, the mother goes to the plant afterward and pours more water into it, and the plant gets worse anyway. She is drowning it while believing she is saving it, and she never once suspects that the problem is the room she is standing in.

THE OVERWATERING ACCUMULATES — CRITICAL: this is the through-line and it must build in visible physical stages across the four watering shots. FIRST watering: a normal pour, the soil darkening, a little water reaching the saucer. SECOND: a longer pour, the saucer full to its rim, the soil surface glossy and slow to drink. THIRD: water standing well above the soil line and taking seconds to sink, the saucer overflowing, a dark wet ring spreading into the painted timber of the shelf beneath, one leaf lying on the record cabinet below. FOURTH: the soil pale and crusted with a whitish mineral bloom on top, the saucer brimming and stagnant, the wet ring in the shelf now permanent and dark, two more leaves down on the cabinet, and a fine fungus gnat or two nowhere near the plant. Each time she pours she checks the result with more anxiety than the last, and each time it has not worked.

THE PLANT IS WITHERING, NOT DYING — CRITICAL: the daughter's ivy on the high shelf is a mature plant that has lost its vigour. Less green than it was — the leaf colour dulled toward a grey-sage, the surfaces matte where they used to be waxy — and less full, with the crown thinner and looser and a few bare stretches of stem showing between leaves. A handful of leaves are slightly cupped and one or two carry a fine dry rim at the margin. It still has most of its foliage, its runners still hang over the rim, and it is unmistakably alive. It is NOT dead, NOT brown, NOT crisp, NOT skeletal, NOT bare and NOT collapsed. It never moves, never reacts, never leans and never responds at any point, to anybody or anything, and it has no face and no expression. It is as still as furniture in every frame. Its condition changes only between shots, never on camera.

NEITHER OF THEM IS THE VILLAIN — CRITICAL: the mother is frightened and converts every feeling into a task, and she never once shouts, never grabs, never looms and never raises a hand. Her weapon is turning away to something else with her hands. The daughter is fifteen and gives back attitude in the exact register of a fifteen-year-old — eye-rolls, shrugs, headphones, a shoulder turned, a door — and she is never cruel and never triumphant. Both are exhausted by each other. The comedy and the ache are the same thing.

She lifts one hand and makes a small circling motion at her own head, then points down at the floorboards where water is dripping. The daughter looks at her, looks at the floor, and shrugs one shoulder with her mouth closed. The mother's jaw sets. She takes the towel off the daughter's shoulders and puts it back on properly, squarely, both hands. The daughter lets her, dead-faced, then walks off pulling it straight off again. HARD CUT.

SHOT 3 · 6–9s · THE FIRST WATERING · 30 degrees [65mm], camera at 140 cm, pushing in forty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the record cabinet. Frame CENTRE: the mother at the shelf wall, on the balls of her feet, the enamel can raised. Frame RIGHT: bare plaster.
She pours — a normal, measured pour, the soil darkening evenly, a little water reaching the saucer. She sets the can down on the cabinet, rises onto her toes again and turns one leaf over with a fingertip to look at its underside. Her brows draw in at the inner ends. She wipes the leaf with the pad of her thumb. She lowers back onto her heels and stands looking up at it for a beat and a half. HARD CUT.

SHOT 4 · 9–12s · THE DESK LAMP · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 100 cm in the daughter's bedroom, arcing right forty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the empty windowsill with its pale unfaded ring. Frame CENTRE: the desk, the task lamp lit, the daughter at it with headphones on. Frame RIGHT: the door, and the mother in it.
Late. The daughter is at the desk under the lamp, headphones on, drawing — plants, wild and overgrown, sprawling off the edges of the page. The mother appears in the doorway. She taps the door frame twice with two knuckles. No response. She reaches in and switches the lamp off at the wall. The daughter turns, slow, pulls one headphone cup off her ear, holds it there, and looks at her with absolutely nothing in her face. A beat. The mother taps her own wrist twice. The daughter switches the lamp back on without breaking eye contact and turns back to the desk. HARD CUT.

SHOT 5 · 12–15s · THE SECOND WATERING · 34 degrees [58mm], camera at 90 cm angled up, rising thirty centimetres. Frame CENTRE: the shelf and the pot from below, the mother's arms coming into frame from the bottom.
A longer pour this time, held well past where the first one stopped. The saucer fills to its rim. The soil surface goes glossy and stops drinking, a shallow film standing on top of it. She picks it up, looks at it, and closes it in her fist. HARD CUT.

SHOT 6 · 15–18s · THE SHOES · 50 degrees [35mm], camera at 110 cm at the entry, drifting forward sixty centimetres. Frame CENTRE: the daughter in the grey hoodie and jeans, backpack on, coming in fast and kicking her trainers off anywhere. Frame RIGHT: the mother.
The trainers go in two directions, one landing on its side. The daughter walks straight past. The mother, without a word and without hurrying, crouches, picks up both trainers and sets them side by side against the wall, perfectly square, heels aligned. The daughter does not look up, does not turn her head, does not acknowledge the plate or the hand that put it there. Her pencil does not stop. She pours again. The soil is pale and crusted with a whitish mineral bloom across its surface and the water sits on top of it, brimming the saucer, stagnant. The dark ring in the shelf's painted timber is permanent now. Nothing about the plant is better than it was thirty seconds ago. She sets the can down, steps back, and looks up at it with both arms at her sides. Her chest rises and falls. She has no idea what she is doing wrong. PHYSICS: water has real behaviour — it darkens dry soil unevenly and sinks fast on the first pour, sits as a film and sinks slowly on the second, stands proud and takes seconds to drain on the third, and pools stagnant on the fourth. It overflows a saucer in a sheet, runs over a painted edge, soaks into timber and spreads a dark ring outward with a defined damp edge that never fully dries. The enamel can is heavy full and light empty and the difference shows in her wrist and elbow. Wet hair is heavy, clings, darkens the cloth it touches and drips. A towel goes dark where it takes water. A trainer kicked off resists, comes free suddenly and lands on its side. A dinner plate is hot enough that she holds it by the rim with her fingertips. A door closed with finality cracks its latch home and the frame flexes. Headphone cups compress hair and spring back. Fallen leaves are weightless and do not move once down. Unglazed clay sits on painted timber with real friction and the pot never moves. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand or a body has touched it, and no plant moves at any point for any reason.

ACTING: the mother is never angry and never shouts — every correction is fear wearing the face of housework, and her tells are a set jaw, a breath out through the nose, and turning away to a task with her hands. The hand raised to knock and not knocking in shot nine is the most important beat she has. The daughter's attitude is entirely physical and entirely fifteen: the one-shoulder shrug, the dead-faced stare, the headphone cup held off the ear, the lamp switched back on without breaking eye contact, the towel pulled straight back off. She is never cruel and never triumphant and she never smirks — she is simply done negotiating. Neither ever does the same thing at the same time; every response arrives a full beat after the other's action. Both blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously. Neither looks at the lens.

AUDIO: diegetic sound only. Room tone that is quieter and emptier than the same house five years earlier. Water poured into soil, four times, each one sounding different from the last — absorbed, then hesitant, then standing and spilling, then flat and stagnant. Enamel set down on timber. A saucer overflowing and running over a painted edge. Wet hair dripping on floorboards. A towel dragged off shoulders. Two knuckles on a door frame. A wall switch clicking off and on. A pencil not stopping. A ceramic plate set down on timber and picked back up. Trainers kicked off and landing, then set down square. Bare adult feet and socked teenage feet on boards at clearly different weights. A door latch cracking home. A palm laid flat on timber. Faint tinny sound leaking from headphones with no melody and no words in it — just a thin percussive hiss. No speech, no words, no whisper and no vocal sound beyond breath from anyone at any point. NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

LOCKS: ten hard-cut shots across thirty seconds, each with its own lens, camera height and physical move, none locked off, none opening on a still. The montage strictly alternates argument and watering. The four waterings escalate in visible physical stages from a normal pour to standing stagnant water, a permanent dark ring soaked into the shelf, a whitish crust on the soil and three fallen leaves on the cabinet below — and the plant is no better at the end than the beginning. The plant is WITHERING, not dying: duller and thinner but still leafed and still alive. It never moves, has no face and is never touched by the daughter. The mother never shouts, never grabs and never raises a hand. The daughter never cries and never smirks. Nothing moves without a hand or a body touching it first. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms words, and nobody looks at the lens.

FOUR SHOTS — 24 seconds total. Shot 1 runs 0–7s, shot 2 runs 7–13s, shot 3 runs 13–19s, shot 4 runs 19–24s. Hard cuts between them, instantaneous, no transitions, no dissolves, no fades. Real-time throughout, no slow motion, no overcranking, no ramping.
NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.
ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE — CRITICAL: nobody in this sequence speaks, ever. No spoken words, no talking, no whispering, no shouting, no muttering, no calling out, no vocalising of any kind. The girl is alone and silent throughout. No character's mouth ever forms words, parts as if about to speak, or moves as if speaking at any point, on camera or off. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue. Suppressing the audio alone is not enough — the mouth itself must never move as if speaking.
NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point. No signage, no house number and no packaging carries readable text in any frame, and the backpack carries no logo, no brand mark and no lettering of any kind.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

SHE IS CARRYING SOMETHING PRECIOUS — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE WHOLE PERFORMANCE: everything she does in this sequence is governed by the two objects in her bicycle basket. She has a backpack on and she does not put either object in it — they would knock together in there, and she is not willing to risk that, so they ride in the basket in the open where she can see them. She rides carefully rather than fast — slower than a ten-year-old would normally ride, both hands on the bars, checking down into the basket twice on the way, easing over the kerb instead of bumping it, braking early and gently. She leans the bike against the house with real care rather than dropping it. She lifts the pot and the box out one at a time, not together. She carries them the way you carry things you are frightened of dropping — forearms in tight, elbows locked to her ribs, shoulders slightly raised, chin tucked to watch them. The backpack stays on her back the entire sequence and is never taken off, never opened and never set down. Not one moment of this is careless and not one moment is dramatic. She is ten years old and quietly, completely serious about two objects.

THE POT IS PAINTED, THE PLANT IS NOT IN IT — CRITICAL: the craft pot she is carrying is EMPTY. It is bare fired clay with nothing planted in it — no soil, no plant, no seedling, nothing growing. It has been painted by her at school: a wavering red band around the belly with one heavy drip, a row of blue thumbprints, and a wobbly yellow sun, all in matte poster paint on grey-buff clay, its interior bare and unpainted, no saucer. It is 20 cm tall and 18 cm across the rim and takes both her hands to hold. It is a completely separate object from the ivy on the shelf and the two are never confused.

THE IVY ON THE SHELF IS BIGGER THAN THE PLATE AND DOES NOT MOVE — CRITICAL: the supplied great room plate shows the small young Act 2 ivy on the high shelf. In this sequence that plant is several years older and correspondingly fuller — a healthy even crown of glossy heart-shaped leaves on firm stems with two runners spilling over the rim and hanging partway down the clay, still in the same plain unglazed terracotta pot on the same matching saucer, in the same position on the same span of the shelf. Override the plate's plant scale and keep everything else about the room exactly as the plate has it. The ivy does not move, react, turn, lean or respond at any point, to her or to anything else. It has no face and no expression. It is as still as furniture for the entire sequence and she never touches it, never reaches for it and never gets near it.

CONTACT FIRST, THEN MOTION — CRITICAL: nothing in any shot moves, tips, slides, swings, drifts or falls until a hand or a body has visibly touched it. The bike does not lean until she leans it. The shoes do not come off until her heel is on them. The box does not settle until her hands set it down. She navigates every piece of furniture with real clearance and never passes through, clips into or overlaps the sofa, the coffee table, the record cabinet or a wall.

The sun and the plant are compressed at the same rate: one full day of light travel across twenty seconds, and one full day of slow decline across the same twenty seconds. The decline is CONTINUOUS and visible in motion at all times — never a jump, never a cut, never a morph, never a dissolve between states, never a step change, never a still plant that is suddenly different. Something on this plant is moving for the entire duration.
The specific motion is the real motion of a vine losing tension under compression. Stems that were holding themselves up SLOWLY LOSE THEIR STIFFNESS — the droop travels outward from the base to the tip, each stem sagging in a smooth continuous arc, the tip sinking furthest and arriving last, with the whole crown settling lower and wider across the twenty seconds. Where a growing tip would quest and circle, these tips do the opposite: they sink, drift, and make one or two small failed attempts to lift and correct before giving in and continuing down. Individual leaves CURL — the blade rolling gently inward from the edges toward the midrib, continuously, each leaf at its own rate and none of them in unison, so that flat glossy leaves become slightly cupped and then slightly folded. The edges brown as they curl: a fine dry rim of brown creeping inward from the leaf margin, advancing visibly and continuously, following the curl rather than leading it. The rate of decline is uneven and organic — it deepens in the hard direct light and pauses almost entirely in the cool shade, which is the inverse of the growth lapse. It is never mechanical, never evenly paced, never linear and never robotic. Every sag carries a slow-in, a small failed recovery and a settle. It is never a sparkle, never a glow, never a shimmer, never a pulse, never a magical effect, never a wilting special effect — it is a plant thinning, quickly, and nothing else.

It is still unmistakably alive and still mostly green. It is not dead, not brown, not crisp, not skeletal, not bare, not collapsed, and its soil is not cracked. The compression is in the speed, not the severity — this is one day out of many and the damage of a single day is small.

PHYSICS: bedcovers lift with real weight and drag on themselves rather than flying. Bare feet compress on cold timber boards and the toes curl. A small box eased over floorboards catches once on a board join and is lifted over rather than forced. A lamp switch clicks and the filament comes up over about a tenth of a second rather than instantly, and the lamp's arm holds wherever it is set by friction in its joints. A chair lifted rather than dragged makes almost no sound. A screw lid takes two hands and a quarter turn to free. Poster paint tipped from a jar falls as a thick slow blob that spreads slowly in a palette well and holds a peak where it lands. Squeezed from a tube it comes out as a ribbon that coils on itself. Wet bristles tapped on a glass rim shed droplets that run back down the inside. Water in a jam jar clouds pink, then muddy, in visible swirls that settle. Bristles wiped on a stiff rag splay and spring back and leave colour behind on the cloth. Paint goes onto bare porous timber wet and thick, sinking into the grain and darkening it at the edges of every stroke, sitting proud in the middle, and running downward under gravity within a second or two where it is loaded too heavily, slowing as it thins. Two wet colours meeting bleed into each other at the join. Brushes tipped into a box land in a loose scatter and lean against each other and the walls. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand, a foot or a body has touched it.

ACTING: she is ten years old and she has decided something. The first shot is the decision arriving — lying awake with her glasses on, one look at the door, jaw setting, chin lifting — and everything after it is execution. She is careful rather than frightened: quiet with the covers, quiet with the box, lifting the chair rather than dragging it, two glances at the door. And then the moment the lamp comes on and the brush is in her hand, all of the care drops away and her face goes completely absorbed and completely unguarded — the only time in this act that it does. Her setup is methodical in the way a child who has been taught properly is methodical: brush from the pot, water, tap it off, colour into the palette, load from the palette. She does not look pleased with herself and does not perform delight. She works. When she sits back to look at it her expression is level and considering rather than triumphant. Putting the supplies into the box at the end is a small deliberate act of claiming and it should be played plainly. She blinks at uneven intervals, breathes visibly, and never holds a still expression or a fixed posture for more than a beat. She never looks toward the lens.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved grain, ceramic holds glaze thickness and crazing, brass holds tarnish, tile holds grout and wear. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

THE CAMERA IS A HUMAN BEING WITH A CAMERA ON THEIR SHOULDER — CRITICAL, THIS GOVERNS EVERY SHOT: this is heavy, tactile, imperfect handheld throughout and it must never for one frame read as mounted, stabilised, gimbal-smoothed or mechanically driven. Every shot carries a live cant that drifts between three and twelve degrees and never settles at zero. The frame BREATHES — a slow small vertical rise and fall, roughly one cycle every three to four seconds, riding an operator's lungs. Every reframe is a real human reframe: it LAGS the action by a beat, OVERSHOOTS slightly, and CORRECTS BACK with a small settle, rather than arriving perfectly. When she moves fast the camera is a fraction late catching her and has to hunt. When she stops the frame keeps drifting for half a second before it steadies. There are small unbidden weight shifts, a knee dip on the low shots, and a faint sway on the high one. It is never shaky in a violent or nauseating way and never a whip pan — it is close, physical, slightly unstable and always alive. THE ANGLES ARE DELIBERATELY VARIED AND UNCOMFORTABLE: floor level, mirror-side, directly overhead, tight profile from below the jaw. No two consecutive shots share a height or an axis.

IT IS DUSK AND THE PLATE'S LIGHT IS OVERRIDDEN — CRITICAL: the supplied bathroom plate shows bright midday sun blazing through the window and throwing hard bright patches across the tiled floor and the pink wainscot. THAT IS GONE. This is DUSK, the last twenty minutes of light. Through the frosted window comes only a low, cool, dim blue-grey glow with the very last trace of warmth at its bottom edge — no sun, no hard patch on the floor, no bright wash on the wall, no cast shadow with a hard edge anywhere. The room sits low, cool and soft, everything readable but nothing bright. The pink wainscot reads muted and dusty. The white of the tub and the basin reads blue-grey. There is NO electric light on in the room at any point — no bulb, no pendant, no fixture switched on — and the only illumination in all six shots is that failing window light plus a faint warm spill from the landing through the open door behind her. No pure black anywhere in any frame at any depth.

SHE IS OUT OF BREATH AND THAT IS THE FIRST THING WE HEAR — CRITICAL: she comes in HUFFING AND PUFFING, chest going, shoulders rising and falling, mouth open, breathing hard through her mouth in short uneven pulls. It is not exertion from running — it is the breathing of a child who has been holding something in and has just got somewhere private. It settles gradually across the sequence and is almost gone by the last shot, which is when the other thing arrives.

SHE IS UPSET FOR THE FIRST TIME — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE POINT OF THE LAST TWO SHOTS: across this film she has been flat, level and unreadable when things go wrong. Here, alone, with nobody to hold it for, it finally shows. Her brows draw together at the inner ends and STAY there, the corners of her mouth pull down a fraction and hold, and her eyes go glassy and bright along the lower lash line. NOTHING SPILLS. No tear runs, no tear falls, no tear reaches a cheek. Her face does not crumple, her lip does not tremble, her breathing does not hitch and she makes no crying sound of any kind. She does not wipe her eyes. She lets it be on her face for the first time in the picture, and then she puts it away again before the cut. Restraint is everything — the smallest possible version reads as devastating and anything larger reads as a tantrum.

CONTACT FIRST, THEN MOTION — CRITICAL: nothing moves until a hand or a body has visibly touched it. The tap does not run until her fingers have turned it. Her sleeves do not move until she pushes them. She navigates the tub, the washstand and the door with real clearance and never passes through, clips into or overlaps any of them.

PHYSICS: leather shoes knock hard and bright on ceramic tile, quite different from timber, and the sound carries in a small tiled room. Knitted sleeves shoved up an arm bunch thick at the elbow and stay where they are pushed. A brass tap turns with resistance and the water arrives after a half-beat delay, running loud into a ceramic basin and changing pitch as the bowl pools and drains. Water sheets off skin and runs pink, then brown, then muddy, swirling before it goes down. DRIED POSTER PAINT ON SKIN THINS AND LOOSENS UNDER WATER AND SCRUBBING BUT DOES NOT COME OFF — it stays in every crease, under every nail and in a ring at each wrist no matter how hard she works. Wet hands leave dark prints on a ceramic basin rim. Coming up onto the toes takes a real shift of balance with the hands taking weight on the rim and the heels visibly leaving the tile. Tears that well but do not fall change the surface of the eye without moving, and a blink redistributes rather than releases them. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. THE GAIT — CRITICAL: the cat moves with true feline mechanics and the paws must never move as a matched pair while walking or trotting. A cat walks and trots in a DIAGONAL TWO-BEAT — the left forepaw and the right hindpaw swing and land together, then the right forepaw and the left hindpaw. From this POV that means the forepaws ALTERNATE, one at a time, left then right then left, each entering the lower frame independently and on its own beat, never simultaneously and never symmetrically. Each forepaw reaches forward, is placed deliberately, takes weight, and is lifted again while the other is already reaching. A cat also direct-registers — each hind foot lands almost exactly where the forefoot on that side just left — so the frame advances in small precise increments rather than lurching.

The ONLY moment both forepaws appear together is the front-foot pair of a bound or a landing, and even then one leads the other by a fraction and the two never arrive in perfect unison.

Other true feline mechanics to hold throughout: the shoulders roll and the frame rises and falls very slightly with each forelimb, giving an asymmetric side-to-side sway rather than an even bob. Claws extend on the placement stroke and retract on the lift. On any narrow surface the paws place along a single near-straight line, one almost in front of the other, so the frame tracks a tightrope path. Before any jump the whole frame lowers, holds dead still, and makes two or three tiny lateral sighting adjustments — a rangefinding wobble — with the haunches loading beneath, then launches. ACTION TIMING:

SHOT 1 · 0–5s · THROUGH THE STREETS · 46 degrees [40mm], camera at 140 cm, tracking backwards ahead of them across about seven metres at their pace. Frame CENTRE: all four coming toward the lens down the slope, spread across the frame rather than in a line, half-running. Frame LEFT and RIGHT: lit shop fronts and awnings sliding past.
They are already moving, somewhere between a fast walk and a jog, with no urgency behind it — just momentum. THE TALL ONE is ahead again without meaning to be, her bob swinging. THE CURLY ONE cuts across behind the daughter and shoulders her sideways as she passes; the daughter staggers two steps, recovers, and shoves her back harder. THE SMALL ONE lets out one loud sudden honking laugh at this, head back, and it sets THE CURLY ONE off, who throws her head right back and laughs with her whole body while still running. Every mouth is open — LAUGHING, NEVER SPEAKING. They pass through a pool of sodium light and out of it. HARD CUT.

SHOT 2 · 5–9s · THE CORNER · 54 degrees [32mm], camera at 110 cm, arcing right seventy centimetres as they round a corner past it. Frame LEFT: an iron railing and ordinary potted plants on a step in the near plane. Frame CENTRE: the four of them coming round the corner into the alley mouth. Frame RIGHT: the alley opening up in the mid plane, its caged bulb small and warm in the depth.
THE TALL ONE takes the corner too wide and has to grab a downpipe to stop herself, swinging around it. THE SMALL ONE, still laughing, runs straight into THE TALL ONE's back and rebounds. THE CURLY ONE overtakes both of them on the inside. The daughter comes last, walking now, still breathing hard from the run, her hand pressed to her side and her mouth open, wiping her eye with the back of her wrist. She is laughing without much sound left in her. They all turn into the alley. HARD CUT.

SHOT 3 · 9–14s · THE BAG · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 70 cm, low on the wet paving, pushing in eighty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the four flattened cardboard panels propped against the brick in the mid plane. Frame CENTRE: the daughter crouched over her backpack on the ground, the other three around her. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT: the caged bulb and its tight pool in the mid plane. Frame RIGHT: two dented bins and a stack of pallets in the near plane.
9–11s — she sets the backpack down on the wet stone, drops to a crouch and unzips it. She takes out <<<9b989147-625a-4e62-93d5-45ede3b054c2>>> one at a time — four cans, cream bodies, coloured caps, BLOOM in black capitals with a green heart. She hands one up to THE CURLY ONE without looking, one to THE TALL ONE, and holds one out to THE SMALL ONE, who takes it this time with both sleeve-covered hands and immediately looks worried about it.
11–14s — all four shake their cans at once, four different rhythms, the balls rattling hard. THE CURLY ONE hauls two of the cardboard panels off the wall and lays them flat on the paving. THE TALL ONE props the other two upright against the brick. The daughter pulls her cap off with her teeth, spits it into her palm, and gets down on her knees over a flat panel. HARD CUT.

SHOT 4 · 14–19s · THE PAINTING · 34 degrees [58mm], camera at 60 cm, low, tracking laterally right across two metres past all four of them at work. Frame moves across: the daughter kneeling over a flat panel, THE CURLY ONE beside her, THE TALL ONE at an upright panel, THE SMALL ONE at the last one.
The daughter is painting PLANTS — wild sprawling overgrown forms, huge looping stems, big soft leaves, blooms opening off the sides, running right off the edges of the board. No letters, no numbers, no words, no tags, no signature, just growth. Her whole arm works from the shoulder and her free hand is flat on the board to steady it. THE CURLY ONE is doing something enormous and shapeless and enthusiastic. THE TALL ONE is bent almost double over her upright panel doing something small and careful low down. THE SMALL ONE is holding her can at arm's length like it might go off and putting down one extremely tentative dot. The daughter looks over at THE SMALL ONE's single dot, then at THE SMALL ONE, and THE SMALL ONE laughs her enormous honking laugh at her own dot. Mouths open, no words. HARD CUT.

SHOT 5 · 19–24s · THE MESS · 50 degrees [35mm], camera at 95 cm, arcing left sixty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the upright panels and THE TALL ONE. Frame CENTRE: the daughter and THE CURLY ONE on the ground over the flat boards. Frame RIGHT: THE SMALL ONE and the bins.
THE CURLY ONE, reaching across, swings her can too wide and lays a stripe of colour straight across the daughter's grey sleeve. The daughter looks at her sleeve. Then at THE CURLY ONE. Then she reaches over with one deliberate finger and draws a line down THE CURLY ONE's cheek. THE CURLY ONE's whole head goes back and she laughs so hard she sits down on the wet paving. THE TALL ONE folds at the waist over her own knees, shoulders shaking, almost silent. THE SMALL ONE honks. The daughter is laughing properly now, open-mouthed, her ponytail shaking, one hand braced on the board and the other still holding a can. This is the happiest she is anywhere in this film. HARD CUT.

SHOT 6 · 24–27s · THE LIGHTS ARRIVE · 46 degrees [40mm], camera at 120 cm AT THE ALLEY MOUTH looking down the alley's length away from the street, holding and drifting back thirty centimetres. Frame CENTRE: the four of them a few metres in, on and around the cardboard. Frame LEFT and RIGHT: the brick walls running away into the depth. The lights come from BEHIND THE CAMERA.
24–25s — a wash of BLUE slides into frame from the bottom and near edges and travels UP the alley away from the lens, running across the brick on both sides. Then RED. Then blue again, alternating, sweeping deeper into the alley past them and throwing all four of their shadows FORWARD, away from the camera, long and hard on the paving ahead of them. NO VEHICLE, NO LIGHT BAR, NO HEADLIGHT, NO PERSON AND NO SILHOUETTE IS EVER VISIBLE at any point — only the colour arriving on surfaces. There is no siren and no engine.

The laughing stops in stages, not all at once — THE CURLY ONE is still going for another half second on the ground before she registers everyone else has stopped. The daughter is already moving: she grabs her backpack by one strap without zipping it and gets a hand under THE CURLY ONE's arm to haul her up off the wet stone. HARD CUT.

SHOT 7 · 27–30s · AWAY · 63 degrees [28mm], camera at 90 cm AT THE ALLEY MOUTH, low, holding position and rising twenty centimetres. The camera does not follow them. Frame CENTRE: the alley running away into the depth, and all four of them RUNNING AWAY FROM THE LENS down its length, getting smaller. Frame LEFT and RIGHT: brick, downpipes and bins in the near plane, washed in blue and then red.
They run away from camera in four completely different ways — THE TALL ONE in huge loose strides with her bob flying and her arms too long, out ahead within three steps; THE CURLY ONE flat out and graceless with her tote hammering against her hip and paint on her cheek; THE SMALL ONE with her hands finally out of her sleeves and going properly, last and gaining; and the daughter with her backpack held against her chest by one strap and a can still in her other hand. Their shadows are thrown ahead of them, away from the lens, stretching and shortening as the blue and red alternate behind. Nobody is frightened and nobody looks back except THE TALL ONE, once, over her shoulder. They reach the darker far end and are gone. LAST FRAME: the empty alley running away from the lens, the four cardboard panels abandoned on the wet paving and against the brick with their wild overgrown painted plants facing up and out, four spray cans lying where they were dropped, and the blue and red still sweeping slowly up the brick with nobody left in it.

PHYSICS: four different gaits and four different runs with four different rhythms and weight transfers, none synchronised at any point. Fine straight hair swings as one soft mass and falls forward under gravity when a head goes down, and flies loose in a run. Dense curls move as a heavier mass with more lag and more bounce. Low buns barely move. A high ponytail lifts on a landing and settles a beat after the feet. A canvas tote swings against a hip on a pendulum a beat behind the stride and hammers on a run. A backpack held by one strap swings and pulls its carrier off balance. A shoulder shove transfers real momentum and both bodies stagger and correct. An aerosol can rattles hard when shaken and the sound changes pitch as it empties. Spray paint goes onto corrugated cardboard wet and saturated, soaking into the board and darkening it, sitting proud on the flutes and running downward on the upright panels where the nozzle is held too long. Flattened cardboard is stiff but bows under its own weight when lifted and slaps flat when laid down on wet stone. A wet stripe transferred to fabric soaks in and stays. Wet paving holds shallow puddles that carry reflections of the caged bulb and, later, of the blue and red. A body laughing hard loses postural control — knees go, a hand goes down, someone sits. Bodies going from stationary to running compress through the knees first and the arms follow. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand or a body has touched it.

ACTING: this is the only sequence in the film where the daughter is fully at ease, and unlike every other scene it is allowed to be loud and physical and funny. She shoves, she laughs open-mouthed, she draws on her friend's face, she works with her whole arm. Her face out here is unguarded in the same way it is when she paints alone at her desk, except she does not have to hide it and there is nobody to hide it from. THE FOUR LAUGHS ARE FOUR DIFFERENT LAUGHS AND MUST NEVER SYNCHRONISE: the tall one folds at the waist almost silently, the small one honks suddenly and enormously, the curly one throws her head all the way back with her whole body, the daughter laughs breathlessly with her shoulders and one hand braced. They set each other off in sequence rather than together, and the laughing stops in stages at the end rather than all at once. When the lights come they are not terrified — they are teenagers who know what that colour means and how much time they have, and the reaction is quick and practised. Nobody is guilty, because they have not damaged anything. MOUTHS OPEN FOR LAUGHTER AND BREATH AND NEVER FOR A WORD. They blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates, and never do the same thing at the same time. Nobody looks at the lens.

AUDIO: diegetic sound only. The open night air of a small town, wide and airy. Four sets of footsteps at four clearly different rhythms and weights — heavy boots, light trainers, scuffed trainers, high-tops — on cobbles, then on wet paving, half-running. REAL AUDIBLE LAUGHTER, four distinct laughs that never sync: a nearly silent shaking one with only breath in it, a sudden loud honk, a full-bodied head-back one, and a breathless winded one. Hard breathing through open mouths after running. A canvas tote knocking against a hip. A backpack strap sliding on a shoulder. A shoulder shove and two bodies staggering. A backpack unzipping. Four aerosol balls rattling at four different rhythms. A cap pulled off with teeth and spat into a palm. Flattened cardboard hauled off brick and slapped down flat onto wet stone. A nozzle hissing in short bursts and long pulls, the pitch changing as a can empties. Wet paint running on cardboard. A body sitting down hard on wet paving. Then at 24 seconds, NO SIREN AND NO ENGINE — just the ordinary night, the laughing stopping in stages, and four sets of feet breaking into a run on wet stone at four different rhythms, receding away from the lens and getting quieter, breathing hard, a tote hammering. Then nothing but the buzz of a caged bulb. No speech, no words, no whisper and no vocalisation that shapes a word from any of the four at any point. NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

LOCKS: seven hard-cut shots across thirty seconds, all of it in deep night with no daylight, no dusk and no blue hour anywhere. Four fifteen-year-olds half-run and shove and LAUGH their way through a sodium-lit town and into a brick service alley. THEY LAUGH OUT LOUD WITH OPEN MOUTHS AND NEVER SPEAK A WORD — mouths open for laughter, breath and effort only, never for a consonant or a vowel. The daughter sets her backpack down on the wet stone, unzips it and hands a spray can to each of them. They paint on FOUR LARGE FLATTENED CARDBOARD PANELS found in the alley — two laid flat on the ground, two propped against the brick — never on the wall and never on anybody's property. Wild sprawling overgrown plants, huge loops and blooms, NO LETTERS AND NO WORDS ANYWHERE. Paint gets on a sleeve and a face and everybody loses it. Then blue and red light arrives FROM THE ALLEY MOUTH BEHIND THE CAMERA and sweeps up the brick away from the lens, and THEY RUN AWAY FROM IT AND AWAY FROM CAMERA, deeper into the alley, getting smaller, their shadows thrown ahead of them. THE CAMERA DOES NOT FOLLOW. No vehicle, no light bar, no officer, no figure, no silhouette, no siren, no engine — only colour on brick. The cardboard is left behind. There are no soul plants outdoors anywhere in this sequence. Nothing moves without a hand or a body touching it first. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms a word, and nobody looks at the lens.

FOUR SHOTS — 24 seconds. Shot 1 runs 0–7s, shot 2 runs 7–12s, shot 3 runs 12–18s, shot 4 runs 18–24s. Hard cuts between them, instantaneous, no dissolves, no fades, no transitional frames. Real-time throughout, no slow motion, no ramping, no speed change anywhere.
NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.
ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE — CRITICAL: nobody in this sequence speaks, ever. The entire exchange at the front door is conducted with a raised hand, a pointed finger, a look and a shoulder, and not one mouth ever opens to form a word. No spoken words, no talking, no whispering, no shouting, no muttering, no calling out, no vocalising of any kind. No character's mouth ever forms words, parts as if about to speak, or moves as if speaking at any point. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue. Suppressing the audio alone is not enough — the mouths themselves must never move as if speaking.
NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point. The only text in this sequence is the printing on the cover and pages of the physical book the mother holds, which is real ink on a real object inside the scene, seen at an angle with real perspective, real page curl and real shadow — never a graphic laid over the picture. The framed black brush calligraphy on the west wall is a physical painted artwork hanging on plaster.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, paper holds real fibre and real wear, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

IT IS NIGHT AND THE HOUSE LIGHTS ARE ON — CRITICAL: this sequence happens after dark and every window in it is a dark pane, so ALL the light in every shot comes from practical fixtures that are switched on inside the house and visible or clearly implied in frame. THE ENTRY IS LIT BY ITS OWN CEILING FIXTURE — a small warm pendant hanging above the stone-tiled apron, its bulb burning at a low warm temperature, casting a bright pool straight down onto the tiles with soft falloff up the walls and a clear circular top-light on the daughter's shoulders and the crown of her head as she crosses beneath it. THE GREAT ROOM IS LIT BY THE CERAMIC TABLE LAMP standing on the side table by the couches, switched ON, its shade glowing warm from within and throwing a broad soft pool across the floorboards and up the west wall — this is the only source in that room and it reaches the high shelf at a low upward angle, so the pot is lit from below and slightly to one side, its saucer water carrying a bright highlight and the underside of the shelf catching a warm reflected wash. There is NO daylight anywhere in this sequence. The tall street window in the great room is a dark pane with a faint cool sheen and contributes nothing. The glass in the front door is dark. Both fixtures are physical practical objects that exist in the world of the shot and are legible as sources. No moonlight, no unmotivated fill, no light arriving from nowhere.

THE MOTHER IS ANNOYED, NOT WOUNDED — CRITICAL: she is not shocked, not hurt, not stricken and not a victim at any point. She is a tired woman being brushed past by a teenager, and she reads as EXASPERATED — a flat unimpressed look, eyes going up and coming back down, one hand raised and dropped, a breath out through the nose. When the front door goes she does not flinch or startle: she stands there a beat, exhales, and gets on with it. Only in the last shot does something else creep in, and it is CONCERN ABOUT THE PLANT rather than hurt about her daughter — a worried, practical, problem-solving frown, the face of somebody who has followed the instructions and cannot understand why it is not working.

THE WATER JUST SITS THERE — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE PAYOFF OF THE WHOLE SEQUENCE: when she pours, the water does not sink in. It pools on the surface of the soil and stays there, a standing film that barely moves, taking far too long to drain and not really draining at all. The soil beneath it is pale, compacted and slightly crusted at the edges where it meets the clay. The saucer is already brimming before she starts and overflows when she pours, running over the shelf's front edge into a dark ring already soaked into the painted timber. AND THE PLANT DOES NOT CHANGE. Not one leaf improves, lifts, greens or moves. It is exactly the same plant after the pour as before it. She watches the water sit on top of the soil for a full two seconds waiting for something to happen, and nothing does.

THE PLANT NEVER CHANGES AND NEVER MOVES — CRITICAL: the withering ivy is identical in every frame of this sequence, before the watering and after it. Same leaf count, same dullness, same slight droop, same cupping on the same leaves. It does not improve, does not decline, does not gain or lose a leaf, and never approaches death. It never moves, never reacts, never leans and never responds to anybody or anything, and it has no face and no expression. It is as still as furniture at all times.

THE PLANT IS WITHERING, NOT DYING: a mature plant that has lost its vigour. The leaf colour dulled toward a grey-sage, the surfaces matte where they used to be waxy, the crown thinner and looser than it once was with a few bare stretches of stem showing, five leaves slightly cupped, two carrying a fine dry rim at the margin, the two runners over the rim sagging rather than trailing firmly. It still has most of its foliage and is unmistakably alive. NOT dead, NOT brown, NOT crisp, NOT skeletal, NOT bare, NOT collapsed.
