She is not cruel and not triumphant, she simply does not care, and that is worse. In the great room the mother's register shifts from irritation to genuine practical concern — not about her daughter, about the PLANT. She waits for the water to sink and it doesn't. She tests the soil. She checks a leaf. She wipes the shelf. And then she goes and gets a book she has kept for fifteen years and reads it standing in the lamplight, looking from a diagram to a real pot and back, brows drawn, trying to find the sentence that explains it. She never cries, never shouts and never gets emotional. She blinks at uneven intervals, breathes visibly, and never holds a still expression for more than a beat. Neither of them looks at the lens.

PHYSICS: the water has real mass and depth — swells roll under the frame with weight, troughs sit deep, chop breaks and reforms, and eddies spiral with real rotational drag rather than sliding. Water sheets off its flanks in threads that separate into droplets mid-air, and it re-enters nose first, punching a compact hole in the surface with a crown of spray and a ring spreading outward and flattening behind it as the camera leaves it. The moored boats at the quay rock slowly on the swell, their masts describing small arcs, their mooring lines going slack and taut. Reeds in the shallows bend with the current and rebound. LOCKS: one unbroken twenty-second shot with no cuts. STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

THE PLANT IS THE LIFE BEING LIVED — CRITICAL, THE CENTRAL RULE OF THIS SEQUENCE: every window in this building holds a soul plant, and the state of each plant matches the state of the life happening in the room behind it. The room is the evidence and the plant is the reading, and the audience makes the connection themselves because the two are always in frame together. A room where nothing is being kept up — clothes on the floor, dishes left, curtains shut against the morning, a body that will not get out of bed — holds a plant that is thin, bare-stemmed and browning, its soil cracked and dry, dead leaves lying on the sill where nobody has cleared them. A room where a life is being actively maintained — bed made, floor clear, a body moving on purpose, water within reach — holds a plant that is dense, glossy and upright, its soil dark and damp, its saucer wet, a pair of small scissors and a few trimmed cuttings set tidily beside it. A room that is loud and messy with the ordinary chaos of a family holds several plants at once in several different states, because mess is not the same thing as decline and a full noisy house does not mean everybody in it is well.
CRUCIALLY, THE PLANTS DO NOT MOVE. Not one leaf on any plant in this sequence moves, reacts, turns, leans, opens or responds at any point, to anything or anybody. There is no plant animation of any kind, no reaction to a person, no reaction to sound, no reaction to breath, no reaction to touch. They are as still as furniture. The entire meaning is carried by their CONDITION beside the condition of the room, and by nothing else.
And NOBODY EVER LOOKS AT ONE. Not one person in this building looks at their plant, tends it on camera, glances at it, thinks about it or acknowledges it in any way. They are simply there, in the light, in every window, while people live their lives past them.

EVERY SOUL PLANT IS THE SAME PLANT — CRITICAL: every soul plant in this building is the identical species and the identical vessel — trailing ivy with glossy heart-shaped leaves, in a plain unglazed terracotta pot on a matching shallow terracotta saucer, bare orange-brown clay with visible throwing ridges and thumb marks, no glaze, no paint, no decoration, no ribbon, no label, no ornament, ever, on any of them, in any window. Only health, size and age differ. Ordinary houseplants may appear elsewhere in the rooms — a spider plant on a shelf, herbs in a tin — and they are entirely different objects with different leaf shapes in different containers, and they are never confusable with a soul plant.

TIME-LAPSE — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE WHOLE SHOT: this is a genuine botanical time-lapse and it must read as one. The sun and the plant are compressed at the same rate: one full day of light travel across twenty seconds, and one full day of growth across the same twenty seconds. The growth is CONTINUOUS and visible in motion at all times — never a jump, never a cut, never a morph, never a dissolve between states, never a step change, never a still plant that is suddenly different. Every stem is actively extending on screen for the entire duration.
The specific motion is the real motion of a climbing vine under compression: each growing tip CIRCUMNUTATES — it swings in slow irregular loops as it extends, questing left, forward, right and back, the arc widening as the stem lengthens, so the tip traces a loose wandering spiral through the air rather than a straight line. Stems squiggle and wander as they push out, correcting and overcorrecting, never travelling in a clean straight extension. Each new leaf emerges as a tight furled spear pressed against its stem, then unrolls — the roll opening from one edge outward, the blade widening and flattening in a continuous unfurl, the leaf lifting and turning to face the light as it finishes and then settling with a small overshoot. Older leaves reorient slowly across the day, rotating on their petioles to track the moving light, each one turning at its own rate and not in unison with its neighbours. The two runners over the rim lengthen visibly, their tips swinging out from the clay and back against it in the same circling quest, the longer one gaining about five centimetres across the shot.
The growth rate is uneven and organic — it surges slightly in the strong mid-morning and mid-afternoon light and slows almost to nothing in the deep shadow around midday and at the very end of the day. It is never mechanical, never evenly paced, never linear and never robotic. Every extension carries anticipation, follow-through and a soft settle. It is never a sparkle, never a glow, never a shimmer, never a pulse, never a magical effect, never a burst of light — it is a plant growing, quickly, and nothing else.

PHYSICS: the pot is fired clay with real weight, braced against the mother's chest, and its few leaves shift and settle with the rhythm of each tread and each step rather than holding rigid. Stair treads creak under both sets of feet at clearly different weights and rhythms — the adult's even and rolling, the child's fast and doubled on the way down and then careful and doubled after she is checked. The girl's palm skids audibly along the plaster as she rushes and slides to a stop. Her shoulder collision compresses the sofa arm visibly along its whole padded length and rebounds her body half a step, her braids swinging out on the impact and settling a beat later. The mother's reach to the shelf takes a real shift of balance with her heels leaving the floor and her spine extending, and her weight comes back down through her heels with a small overshoot. On the shelf, the unglazed base scrapes across painted timber, rocks once and settles, and again in two short stages when nudged back. Her kneel takes real balance with one hand briefly on the floorboards. The loose thread has real tension — it pulls taut, puckers the seam it comes out of, goes slack, and springs back when released. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly and nothing lands silently, and no object in any shot moves before a hand or a body has visibly touched it.

ACTING: the mother is tired and busy and entirely present — practical rather than absent, thinking about the next thing rather than about nothing. Her check on the stairs carries no anger at all, just the automatic authority of somebody with their hands full on a staircase, and the raised brows and the flat mouth do all of it. When she kneels and holds her daughter's cheek, she is doing a task and something else is leaking through it — the hand that stays a fraction too long and the thumb moving across the cheekbone are the whole character, because she cannot simply hold her, so she checks her instead. The head pat at the end is affection at the speed of housework: two flat unhurried pats and then gone. The girl gives her almost nothing back — face flat, mouth level, eyes sliding off and returning, the jaw shift and the slow blink her only tells — and she never stops working the thread, which is where her actual attention is. She never cries and never has a tantrum; the pout at the end is small and closed and silent. Her final look up at the shelf is the point of the whole sequence: not longing performed, just a small person measuring a distance. Both of them blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates and depths, and never do the same thing at the same time — every action is sequential and reactive, with the girl's responses arriving a full beat after her mother's. Neither of them ever looks toward the lens.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

ONE PLANT, AND THE SHELF IS EMPTY UNTIL SHE PUTS IT THERE — CRITICAL: there is exactly one plant in this entire sequence and it is the one in the mother's hands. The long cream-painted plank shelf on the west wall carries its household objects packed along its NEAR end only — the row of leaning books, the small standing clock, the pair of brass candlesticks and the shallow bowl. THE MOTHER IS NOT ON RAILS — CRITICAL: she is a specific tired woman carrying an awkward object through her own house and every second of her screen time shows it. Her walk is uneven — she slows without reason and picks up again, shortens a stride to clear the coffee table leg and lengthens the next, her weight rolling fully from hip to hip with her torso counter-rotating against her shoulders and her head leading each turn. She adjusts the pot against her chest twice, hitching it higher with a small bump of her forearm and shifting her grip from underneath to around the body of the clay. A loose strand of hair falls across her face and she blows it upward without breaking stride, then tucks it behind her ear with the back of one wrist because both hands are full. She rolls her right shoulder once. Her chest and shoulders rise visibly with breath at her own rhythm, deeper on some breaths than others. She blinks at uneven intervals, never metronomic. She glances at things in passing. She never walks in a straight line at a constant speed, never holds a fixed posture, and never carries the pot at a fixed angle. Never neutral, never mechanical, never dead-faced.

THE GIRL MISJUDGES DISTANCES AND NOBODY PHASES THROUGH ANYTHING — CRITICAL: this child's depth perception is slightly off and it shows in small physical ways that are never remarked upon and never played for comedy by her. Twice in this sequence her body makes contact with furniture she was trying to walk past: her right shoulder catches the arm of the nearer couch and she rebounds off it half a step, and later her hip clips the corner of the low coffee table hard enough to shift it a centimetre across the rug. Neither is a stumble, neither is a trip, neither is broad — she does not fall, does not windmill, does not react with any drama. She hits the thing, absorbs it, and keeps going as though nothing happened, because to her nothing did. Every other piece of furniture is navigated with real clearance by both figures — no body ever passes through, clips into or overlaps a couch, a coffee table, a side table, a console, a cabinet or a wall. Every near miss is visibly negotiated with a turn of the shoulders or a shortened stride.

Running north from the kitchen end: the KITCHEN at the south end, then the LIVING SPACE carrying the framed black brush calligraphy with the vintage cream television on its low timber console against the west wall and the two facing couches with the low coffee table between them on a woven rug, then the GREAT ROOM carrying the long high cream-painted plank shelf with the record player cabinet beneath it against the same west wall, and beyond that the tall street-facing window with its own small cream sofa. 6–8s — the mother's hands stay in the water for a beat and a half. Then she turns the tap off with a wet wrist, straightens, and turns — wiping both wet hands down the front of her apron as she comes round, twice, the linen going dark where they pass. Her eyes drop. HARD CUT.

SHOT 3 · 8–13s · THE HAND · 20 degrees [100mm], camera at 90 cm, very tight, pushing in twenty-five centimetres and staying locked on the hands throughout. Frame CENTRE: the girl's small hand held palm-up in her mother's, filling most of the frame. Frame LEFT: the curve of <<<2f21feb8-d298-4a97-ae85-5e4e30907d7e>>>, soft and partly out of focus, held in the mother's other hand and pushed to the very edge. Frame RIGHT: the linen of the apron and the counter edge, soft.
8–9.5s — the mother reaches out and TAKES BOTH AT ONCE in one motion — one hand closing around the pot, the other closing around the girl's wrist. The pot goes soft and to the edge of frame immediately. THE HAND IS THE SUBJECT.
9.5–13s — she turns the small hand palm-up. Every detail of it is now legible in the raking window light: red, blue and yellow dried thick across the palm, cracked into flakes along every crease, ringed solid round the wrist, packed under the fingernails, a dried run of it down the side of one finger. The mother turns the hand one way, then the other, tilting it into the light. Her own thumb rubs once hard across the palm and THE PAINT DOES NOT COME OFF. Her grip is firm but not rough. She turns the hand over to check the back of it too. This takes the whole shot. She never once looks at the pot in her other hand. HARD CUT.

SHOT 4 · 13–18s · THE CUPBOARD AND THE POINT · 34 degrees [58mm], camera at 100 cm, arcing right forty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the low base cupboards beneath the counter in the mid plane. Frame CENTRE: the mother releasing the hand and turning away to crouch. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT: the girl standing where she was, now empty-handed. Frame RIGHT: the room running back toward the hallway.
13–14s — the girl lifts her free hand and POINTS — away past her mother, back through the room toward the great room and the high shelf, off frame. She holds it. Her eyes go from her mother's face along her own arm and back.
14–16s — the mother's eyes follow the point for barely half a beat and come straight back. She SHAKES HER HEAD once, twice, small and definite, about five degrees each way, mouth closed. Then she lets go of the wrist, turns away, crouches at the counter, PULLS OPEN A LOW BASE CUPBOARD and puts <<<2f21feb8-d298-4a97-ae85-5e4e30907d7e>>> inside on the bottom shelf among ordinary household things. She pushes the door shut. She never looks at the pot while doing it.
16–18s — she straightens up, turns back, and POINTS — one arm up and out, two sharp jabs toward the ceiling and the hallway beyond, unmistakably meaning UPSTAIRS. Her mouth stays closed. She holds the point. HARD CUT.

SHOT 5 · 18–22s · HER FACE · 20 degrees [100mm], camera at 115 cm, close on the girl's head and shoulders, pushing in twenty centimetres very slowly. Frame CENTRE: the girl's face, three-quarters to the lens, lit from one side by the window light. Frame LEFT and RIGHT: the kitchen soft and out of focus behind her, the mother's shape moving back toward the sink at the far edge.
18–19.5s — she is standing exactly where she was, both hands empty at her sides, her painted palms turned slightly outward. Her mouth is closed and level. Her brows draw together a few millimetres at the inner ends. Her eyes are up where her mother was.
19.5–21s — AND HER EYES BEGIN TO WELL, VERY SLIGHTLY. A thin brightening along the lower lash line of both eyes. One new wet catchlight sitting where there was none before. The surface of the eye going glassy in the side light. NOTHING SPILLS. Nothing runs. Nothing reaches a cheek. Her lip does not tremble. Her breathing does not hitch. She makes no sound at all.
21–22s — she blinks once, slowly, and the wet is still there after it. She does not wipe her eyes. Her jaw shifts a fraction. Her eyes drop from where her mother was, down and away, and settle on nothing. Then she turns her head to go. LAST FRAME: the girl in close-up with her eyes barely wet and completely still, her painted hands empty at her sides, the kitchen soft behind her and her mother already back at the sink out of focus at the frame edge.

PHYSICS: linen apron fabric pulls, creases and springs back when tugged, and its waist tie shifts with it. Wet hands leave two dark damp streaks down an apron front that stay dark. A tap turned off with a wrist runs down and stops with a last drip into a full sink. The pot is fired clay with real weight even empty. Dried poster paint on skin is matte, thick, cracked into plates along every crease and completely immovable to a dry thumb — it does not smear, does not lift and does not shine. An adult hand closing on a child's wrist compresses the skin around it and the small fingers splay slightly. A low base cupboard door swings on its hinges with a soft timber knock and the pot's unglazed base scrapes once as it is set down inside. A crouch and a rise take real balance. Tears that well but do not fall change the surface of the eye without moving — the lower lid holds them and a blink redistributes rather than releases them. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly and nothing is ever dropped. No object moves before a hand or a body has touched it.

ACTING: the girl is ten and hopeful and it is all in her body — the quick short steps, the insistent double tug, the pot held ready, the point held while her eyes go back and forth. She is asking a question and she is sure the answer is yes. The mother is exasperated rather than cruel, and the whole sequence turns on what she attends to: she takes the pot and the hand at the same moment and gives all her attention to the hand. She is not rejecting a gift, because she never registers it as one, which is worse. She never shouts, never grabs roughly, never looms and never raises a hand in anger. The last shot belongs entirely to the girl and it must be played with total restraint: no crumpling, no trembling, no sobbing, no sound, no wiping. Just a level face, brows drawn a few millimetres, and eyes that go glassy and stay that way. A ten-year-old holding perfectly still while something small gives way behind her eyes. Both blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates, and never do the same thing at the same time. Neither looks at the lens.

AUDIO: diegetic sound only. A quiet warm house on a weekday afternoon. Running water in a full sink, ceramic knocking softly against ceramic under it, a dish set on a draining board. Small shoed footsteps on floorboards, quick and short-stepped. Linen tugged twice at a hip. A tap turned off with a wet wrist and one last drip. Wet hands wiped down an apron front, twice. A short sharp intake of breath through a nose. The dry sound of a thumb rubbing hard across dried paint on skin. Fired clay changing hands. A low cupboard door pulled open on its hinges, an unglazed base scraping once on a timber shelf, and the door pushed shut with a soft timber knock. Bare adult feet on floorboards. The tap turning back on in the last shot, distant and behind her. Faint birdsong and a distant town murmur through the kitchen window. In the final shot, almost nothing — one slow small breath through a nose, and the tap running softly somewhere behind. NO SNIFFING, NO CATCH IN THE BREATH, NO CRYING SOUND OF ANY KIND. No speech, no words, no whisper and no vocal sound beyond breath from either of them at any point. NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

LOCKS: five hard-cut shots across twenty-two seconds, each with its own lens, camera height and physical move, none locked off, none opening on a still. A ten-year-old walks in from the hallway past the sofa into the kitchen with the painted pot hugged in ONE arm and her other hand free, and tugs twice at her mother's apron. The mother is at the sink with her back turned; she turns the tap off, wipes both wet hands down her apron and turns round. SHE TAKES THE POT AND THE GIRL'S HAND IN THE SAME MOTION, AND THE CAMERA STAYS ON THE HAND — a tight shot of a small paint-covered palm turned over in an adult hand, cracked and ringed at the wrist and packed under the nails, turned into the light, thumbed once and not coming off, while the pot sits soft and forgotten at the frame edge. The girl points toward the great room and the high shelf; the mother shakes her head twice, small and definite. She crouches, opens a LOW BASE CUPBOARD beneath the counter, puts the pot inside on the bottom shelf and shuts the door — not up high, not confiscated, just put away — then points twice at the ceiling: upstairs. THE LAST SHOT IS A CLOSE-UP OF THE GIRL'S FACE AND HER EYES WELL VERY SLIGHTLY AND NOTHING SPILLS — no tear falls, no lip trembles, no sound, no wiping, just a level face and a glassy eye. The mother is exasperated and never cruel, never shouting and never raising a hand. Nothing moves without a hand or a body touching it first. NOBODY SPEAKS, NO MOUTH EVER FORMS A WORD, and neither of them looks at the lens.

TWO SHOTS — 28 seconds total. SHOT 1 runs 0:00–0:24 as one unbroken continuous take with no cuts, no transitions and no dissolves of any kind. ONE HARD CUT at 0:24. SHOT 2 runs 0:24–0:28. Real-time throughout, no slow motion, no overcranking, no ramping, no speed change anywhere.

NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no captions, no subtitles, no titles, no watermarks, no logos, no interface, no numbers, no letters added anywhere in frame. The only lettering that exists is the painted signage physically present on the buildings, the billboard and the shopfront within the world.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Human proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction and chipping, wood holds carved grain, brick and stone hold chipping and wear, metal holds dents and oxidation, cloth awnings hold real weight, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE FRAME IS PULLED, NOT CARRIED — CRITICAL: this camera is not stabilised and does not float. It is dragged forward by an animal hauling itself along on its own forelimbs, and every single stride is visible in the frame. On each forelimb placement the frame surges FORWARD and DROPS as the paw takes weight and the shoulder loads under it, then RISES and swings slightly to that side as the limb pulls the body over and past it. The result is a continuous rocking rise-and-fall with a lateral roll layered on top, alternating side to side, never even, never smooth, never repeating identically. The horizon tips and rights itself constantly. The motion is a pull rather than a bob — each surge carries real forward momentum and the frame coasts a fraction between surges rather than travelling at constant speed. At a trot the rocking is quick and shallow. At a bound it becomes a deep heave — the frame compressing down hard on the front-foot landing, driving up and forward as the body gathers, then floating momentarily at the top of each arc before the next crash down. Faster means more violent, never smoother. NEVER a level self-stabilised horizon, never a gimbal glide, never a floaty drone, never a dolly, never mechanically smooth, and never a human handheld register.

THE GAIT — CRITICAL: the paws must never move as a matched pair while walking or trotting. A cat moves in a DIAGONAL TWO-BEAT, so from this POV the forepaws ALTERNATE one at a time — left, then right, then left — each entering the lower frame independently on its own beat, never simultaneously and never symmetrically. Each forepaw reaches forward into frame, is planted, takes the full weight of the body while the frame surges over it, and is torn back out of frame as the other is already reaching. Claws extend on the placement stroke and retract on the lift. On any narrow surface the paws place along a single near-straight line, one almost in front of the other. Before every jump the whole frame LOWERS toward the surface, goes completely still, and makes two or three tiny lateral sighting shifts with the haunches loading beneath. In flight the frame is smooth and ballistic with no rock at all — the only stillness in the entire shot. On landing the forelimbs punch into frame one a fraction before the other, absorb deep, the frame drops hard and rebounds once. The only moment both forepaws appear together is the staggered front-foot pair of a bound or a landing, and even then one leads the other by a fraction and they never arrive in unison. NEVER a symmetrical two-beat hop, an even mechanical bounce, a human crawl, a bipedal walk cycle or a repeating identical loop.

THE LENS NEVER RISES ABOVE CAT HEAD HEIGHT — CRITICAL: at every point in SHOT 1 the lens sits at the eye height of a small cat standing on whatever surface its paws are on — roughly 22 to 25 centimetres above that surface and never more. It does not rise, does not lift, does not crane, does not gain a vantage and never at any moment looks down on the world from above an animal's own eyeline. On the rooftops it sits 25 centimetres above the tiles. On the steps it sits 25 centimetres above the tread. On the pavement it sits 25 centimetres above the paving, below every adult knee. During a jump the arc peaks no more than about 50 centimetres above the take-off surface and comes straight back down. There is no high shot, no overhead, no elevated angle and no moment where the camera is taller than the animal carrying it.

THE CAT SHOULDERS THROUGH EVERYTHING — CRITICAL: this animal is moving with real urgency and it does not go around obstacles it can go through. It drives straight into the potted plants crowding its route and they react physically to it. Leaves and trailing tendrils slap directly across the lens and whip past, bending as the body forces through them and springing back behind. Terracotta pots get shouldered as it passes — the pot rocking on its base, grating a short distance across tile or stone, and settling. On the stairway it threads a narrow gap between two pots that are too close together, both of them rocking hard as it forces through. A small pot gets clipped and knocked over entirely on the roof terrace, rolling a short way before stopping against a larger one. Foliage is not scenery in this shot; it is physical, it obstructs, and it is displaced by a body moving fast through it. Everything it touches must be visibly disturbed and must visibly settle afterward.

ASSETS:

THIS SCENE: controls geography, materials and light direction only, always seen from 25 centimetres above the paving. 100% match to the reference.
<<<3eb7937b-02cc-4a04-82f5-b0fc1df31b47>>> — a greengrocer storefront, tall windows, painted timber facade with hand-lettered signage, wooden crates of produce stacked outside on the pavement, awning overhead. THIS SCENE: each working at their own trade along the route, in motion throughout, seen from below at cat height. 100% match to the reference.
<<<a210eea0-51b1-44c1-b444-df3b88141518>>> — children roughly five to nine years old in individual casual school clothes, each with distinct hair and build. THIS SCENE: playing on the pavement and the stone steps, running, crouching, chasing, in constant motion. 100% match to the reference.
<<<0f72b3ab-d02e-4eda-aab3-aa06eba8bdc8>>> — a family group in casual everyday clothing. THIS SCENE: walking down the stone steps together, one carrying a potted plant against their hip. 100% match to the reference.
<<<db3202ad-7916-4baf-8b43-604265d2f4c0>>> — a family group in casual everyday clothing. THIS SCENE: on a stoop tending their plants together, an adult tipping a watering can and a crouching child pressing a finger into the soil. 100% match to the reference.
THE CAT — a small short-haired cat, roughly 23 centimetres at the shoulder. Even mid-grey fur with faint darker tabby banding on the flanks and a paler cream-grey belly. All four paws are clean white, the white ending in a clean line just above the wrist on the front legs and mid-shin on the back. A small white patch at the chin and throat. Round face, wide-set green-gold eyes, upright ears with the left one nicked at the tip, long pale whiskers, a fairly long tail with a white tip. Compact, lean and a little scruffy. THIS SCENE: never seen from outside at any point in SHOT 1 — the camera IS this cat and it is never reflected, never revealed and never enters its own frame except for its own white forepaws entering the bottom of frame during placements, crouches, jumps and landings, and the occasional blurred whisker or ear tip crossing the very edge of frame. It is seen fully and from outside only in SHOT 2. 100% match to this description.

THE PREMISE: this town has quietly agreed that everyone keeps a plant, treated as a completely ordinary part of daily life. Potted plants are everywhere and load-bearing along the whole route — on every windowsill, roof terrace, stoop and step, climbing drainpipes and porch posts, filling window boxes and balconies, lining stairways and pavements, riding in bike baskets and on carts. People carry them, water them, and set them down beside themselves while they work, and nobody comments on it or looks at anyone else's. Every plant is healthy and green. The premise is never explained.

THE TOWN IS ALIVE: the town is busy and populated throughout, and every person is mid-action doing something specific and ordinary — never standing idle, never posed, never waiting. Bodies at every depth move at their own independent tempo and keep moving continuously, and none of them pauses when the cat passes. Nobody looks into the lens, except that one or two people glance down at the passing cat with a small unremarkable smile and carry straight on.

GEOMETRY MAP — SHOT 1: the route runs continuously downhill and never doubles back. It begins high on a rooftop ridge with the town spread below and the low sun at the far end of the valley. It drops onto a lower roof, runs that ridge past chimney pots and a rooftop terrace crowded with pots, drops again onto a stone stair landing, descends a long flight of worn stone steps between buildings with pots crowding both edges, emerges onto the pavement of a busy street with storefronts at frame LEFT and the painted billboard raised above them, runs the length of that pavement weaving between adult legs, ducks beneath a wooden handcart being pushed across its path, and comes out the far side with the greengrocer's crates ahead at frame CENTRE-RIGHT. Depth planes throughout: the cat's own white forepaws in extreme foreground when visible, the immediate surface underfoot razor sharp, human legs and street furniture in the mid-ground, the town and the low sun in the background.

GEOMETRY MAP — SHOT 2: outside the greengrocer. The camera is external, at roughly 60 centimetres off the pavement, positioned about three metres out from the shopfront. The stacked wooden crates sit at frame CENTRE-RIGHT in the mid plane against the shop facade. The shop window and its hand-lettered signage fill the far plane behind them at frame RIGHT. Two townspeople stand at frame LEFT in the mid plane, side on to camera, one holding a paper bag of produce and the other a potted plant under one arm, in the middle of an unhurried everyday exchange. Passing legs cross the near plane at frame LEFT throughout.

FIRST FRAME: already travelling. The frame is already mid-stride along the rooftop ridge, already surging over a planted white forepaw, already rocking, the town already below. No still hold and no establishing beat.

OPTICS: 84 degrees horizontal field of view [22mm] classic wide, held for the entire 28 seconds across both shots. Deep focus so the immediate surface, the legs of passers-by and the distant town all read at once. Slight barrel character at the frame edges. No focal drift, no zoom, no lens change at any point, including across the cut.

CAMERA — SHOT 1: the animal's own head, pulled forward by its forelimbs as described above. Surging, rocking, rolling, never level and never stabilised. Pace varies constantly — a long driving trot, a sudden full stop, a low crouch and freeze, then an explosive burst. Fast lateral head-whips lock onto things and hold dead still on them for a beat with no drift, then release.
CAMERA — SHOT 2: a slow lateral track moving rightward across the shopfront, covering about a metre and a half over the four seconds, at a constant rate, never stopping. Smooth and mounted, with the faintest organic breath. This is the only stabilised camera in the piece and the change must be felt.

LIGHT: motivated natural light, low warm early sun sitting at the far end of the valley, throwing light back toward the lens for much of the route. Roof tiles, chimney tops, awning edges, railings, pot rims, shoulders and hair are rimmed in bright amber. Down in the stairway and the street the light drops into soft warm shade with generous bounce off pale plaster. Long soft shadows run toward the lens. Windows glow warm from inside. Foliage catches the backlight and glows with subsurface warmth at the leaf edges. In SHOT 2 the same low sun rakes across the shopfront from frame RIGHT, catching the crate edges, the produce and the cat's white paws. Shadows lifted and tinted warm, no pure black anywhere in frame at any depth.

COLOUR: roughly 70% warm cream, dusty rose, sage and faded cornflower clapboard with worn stone, tile and timber; 20% amber gold from the low sun; 10% sap green from the plants, bare terracotta from the pots, and scattered accents from clothing.

ATMOSPHERE: the air carries real density at every depth — a continuous scattering gradient from the lens to the far ridgeline, filling the entire frame including the foreground, blacks lifted at every plane with high micro-contrast inside the lift. Depth reads in clearly separated layers: paws and immediate surface razor sharp, legs and street furniture holding, the town softening, the far ridge softest and brightest. Bodies pass through the air without disturbing it, leaving no wakes and no trails. No fog, no mist, no smoke in the air, no volumetric shafts, no god rays, no drifting particulate.

White forepaws enter the lower frame one at a time in alternating rhythm, each planted along the narrow ridge almost directly in front of the last, claws catching the tile on placement and retracting on lift. The frame drops onto each paw and surges up and over it, rolling to that side, then the other. It whips left to a chimney pot passing close, locks dead still on it for a beat, then whips back. At this speed the gait becomes a bound and the rocking becomes a deep heave: the frame crashes down on the staggered front-foot landing, drives up and forward, floats for a fraction at the top of the arc, and crashes down again. The frame lowers almost to the paving, white forepaws placing carefully and silently one at a time, and slips beneath the cart. The underside of the deck passes close overhead, wheels turning heavily either side, the baker's boots stepping past. The grey cat with white paws enters frame from the LEFT at 0:24, already at a fast trot across the paving in front of the shop, its body low and its tail level behind it. At 0:25 it gathers, drops into a brief crouch beside the crates at frame CENTRE-RIGHT, and springs up onto the top crate — the leap short and precise, the front paws landing staggered, the crate rocking once on the stack under the impact and settling. It turns once on the spot, sits down, and at 0:26.5 begins washing — lifting one white forepaw to its mouth, licking the pad, then drawing the paw over the ear and back, unhurried and completely absorbed. Legs pass across the near plane at frame LEFT. Last frame: the cat on the crate mid-wash, the shopfront behind it, the exchange continuing at frame left.

PHYSICS: real gravity, inertia and bodyweight. Each paw placement carries the cat's full weight and the pad compresses and splays against the surface. Claws catch and scrape audibly on tile and stone. Every landing carries genuine impact absorbed through the forelimbs. Terracotta pots rock on their bases with real mass, grate across tile and stone, and settle with a wobble rather than stopping dead; the one that goes over falls with real acceleration and rolls until something stops it. Foliage bends under contact with proper lag and damping and springs back afterward, overshooting once before settling. Every human footfall lands with weight and a proper contact shadow. The handcart has real mass, its wheels loaded and turning slowly, the deck flexing slightly as it rolls. Carried pots load the arms of whoever holds them, their leaves lagging behind the motion and settling after. Water pours with true volume and darkens soil where it lands. Clothing swings and settles with each step. Cloth awnings lift and fall with real weight. In SHOT 2 the crate takes the cat's weight and rocks once on the stack before settling. Nothing floats, nothing slides, nothing teleports, and nothing moves that has not been touched.

ACTING: natural eye blinking and active brow micro-expression on every figure close enough to read, no frozen mask-face and no dead eyes. PHYSICS: the pot is fired clay with real weight, braced against the mother's chest, and its few leaves shift and settle with the rhythm of each tread and each step rather than holding rigid. Her loose hair has real weight and lag — it swings a beat behind every turn of her head, falls forward across her cheeks when she leans down, lifts off her neck as her chin rises to the shelf, and settles after the movement stops. Stair treads creak under both sets of feet at clearly different weights and rhythms — the adult's bare, even and rolling, the child's shod, fast and doubled on the way down and then careful and doubled after she is checked. Leather soles scuff and grip on painted treads and knock on bare floorboards. The girl's palm skids audibly along the plaster as she rushes and slides to a stop. Her shoulder collision compresses the sofa arm visibly along its whole padded length and rebounds her body half a step, her braids swinging out on the impact and settling a beat later. The mother's reach to the shelf takes a real shift of balance with her heels leaving the floor and her spine extending, and her weight comes back down through her heels with a small overshoot. On the shelf, the unglazed base scrapes across painted timber, rocks once and settles, and again in two short stages when nudged back. Her kneel takes real balance with one hand briefly on the floorboards. The loose thread has real tension — it pulls taut, puckers the seam it comes out of, goes slack, and springs back when released. The sofa cushion compresses deeply under the climbing child and rebounds around her as she pushes back into it. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly and nothing lands silently, and no object in any shot moves before a hand or a body has visibly touched it.

ACTING: the mother is tired and busy and entirely present — practical rather than absent, thinking about the next thing rather than about nothing. Her check on the stairs carries no anger at all, just the automatic authority of somebody with their hands full on a staircase, and the flat hand and the raised brows do all of it with her mouth completely still. When she kneels and holds her daughter's cheek, she is doing a task and something else is leaking through it — the hand that stays a fraction too long and the thumb moving across the cheekbone are the whole character, because she cannot simply hold her, so she checks her instead. The head pat is the cruellest small thing in the sequence and it must be quick: two fast pats delivered on the way past, without a look down, affection at the speed of housework, and then she is gone from the room. The girl gives her almost nothing back — face flat, mouth level and closed, eyes sliding off and returning, the jaw shift and the slow blink her only tells — and she never stops working the thread, which is where her actual attention is. She never cries and never has a tantrum; the pout is small and closed and silent, arriving only after her mother has left. Both of them blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates and depths, and never do the same thing at the same time — every action is sequential and reactive, with the girl's responses arriving a full beat after her mother's. Neither of them ever looks toward the lens, and neither mouth ever opens or moves as if speaking.

No speech, no words, no whisper and no vocal sound beyond breath from anyone at any point in any shot. NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

LOCKS: five shots, four hard cuts, each shot with its own lens, its own camera height and its own physical camera move, none locked off, none opening on a still frame. The mother's hair is loose, medium length, dark auburn and falling to just below the jaw in every single frame — never pinned, never tied, never in a bun. She comes down the last treads of an enclosed staircase carrying a small terracotta pot with five or six countable leaves in it while her daughter hurries down behind her in brown leather shoes trying to get past; the mother stops, holds a flat palm across her at the child's chest height and raises her brows, and her mouth never opens and never forms a word — the gesture is the whole correction — and the girl pulls up short and falls in behind with her shoulders and chin down. In the great room the far span of the high shelf above the record player cabinet is EMPTY until the mother rises onto the balls of her feet and sets the pot on it — there is exactly one plant in this sequence and it is the one in her hands. The girl trails in behind her, clips the sofa arm with her shoulder exactly once, stops there, leans her weight against it and picks at a loose thread. Her mother kneels, cups her cheek, tips the small face left and right and looks into each eye while the girl stares back flat, both mouths closed the entire time. The mother stands, pats the small head twice quickly on her way past without looking down, and walks out of the room entirely. Only then does the girl let go of the thread, climb onto the sofa and sit with her lip out. The last shot leaves both of them and pushes slowly in on the small terracotta pot alone on its shelf, which does not move. The camera never once points south. The girl wears her shoes in every frame. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms words, and nobody looks at the lens.

TWELVE-SHOT MONTAGE — 28 seconds total. Hard cuts only, no dissolves, no fades, no wipes, no transitional frames of any kind. Roughly two to two and a half seconds per shot. Constant real-time speed inside every shot — no slow motion, no ramping, no speed change anywhere at any point.
NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.
ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE: nobody in this sequence speaks, ever. No spoken words, no talking, no whispering, no shouting, no muttering, no calling out. No character's mouth ever forms words or moves as if speaking at any point in any shot. Everything between these two people is carried by face, hand, shoulder and body. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue.
NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point. The framed black brush calligraphy on the west wall is a physical painted artwork hanging on plaster. The child's chalk and crayon marks are wobbly drawn shapes — leaves, stems, a lopsided pot, a tall figure and a short figure — and contain no letters, no numbers and no words of any kind. The television screen is switched off, dark and blank in every shot it appears in.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

HARD CUT MONTAGE — CRITICAL: twelve separate shots joined by eleven hard cuts. Every cut is instantaneous with no dissolve, no cross-fade, no blur, no motion smear and no transitional frame of any kind. No two consecutive shots share a lens, a camera height, a framing or a camera move. Not one shot is locked off — every single shot carries its own physical camera movement with a stated travel distance. Every shot opens with the camera already moving and the action already underway, never on a still held frame and never on the exact geometry of any supplied plate. Every shot ends mid-action, cutting away before the beat completes, never on a settled pose. Time jumps forward between every shot by weeks or months and the jump is legible in the bodies, the cloth, the hair and the light, never in a caption and never in a visual effect.

THE CHILD GROWS AND THE MOTHER WEARS DOWN — CRITICAL: this is a physical age progression across roughly two years and it must be readable without a single caption. The girl starts at 100 cm and finishes at 112 cm, and the growth is legible in specific staged ways: at the start she needs both hands and a full body-launch for things she manages with one hand and a step-up by the end; her head is proportionally largest in the first shots and settles closer to her body by the last; her balance improves visibly, from a wobbling two-footed hop to a clean single-foot step; her grip changes from a full fist wrap to a three-finger pinch; her speech-free noises change from open-mouthed effortful breathing to quiet nose breathing. She passes through four wardrobe and hair states in strict order, always warm in colour and never grey and never black. Her cuffs gain chalk dust, her knees go from clean to grazed and back to scabbed, her socks slip further and then stop slipping because she has learned to pull them up. The mother stays inside her unchanging palette of cream, pale sage, bare tan, soft blue and white with no pattern and no ornament of any kind, and her hair stays short — but the way she wears it degrades from neat and pushed back, to flattened on one side, to damp at the temples and shoved behind one ear. Her tiredness accumulates physically and never emotionally: her shoulders sit lower by the end, she pushes up off her own thigh to stand twice, one hand goes to the small of her back, and the skin under her eyes goes slightly darker and slightly looser. SHE IS NEVER ANGRY IN ANY SHOT. Every correction she makes is fear wearing the face of practicality — she lifts, removes, wipes and redirects quickly and without heat, and the closest she comes to anything sharper is a jaw set and a breath let out through the nose. The child never cries at any point in this sequence, not once, not a single tear, and never has a tantrum — she goes quieter instead, and that is the whole arc.

THE ONE PLANT AND THE ORDINARY PLANTS — CRITICAL: the soul plant is the small young trailing ivy in the plain unglazed terracotta pot on its matching shallow saucer, standing on the far span of the high cream-painted plank shelf directly above the record player cabinet, 195 cm above the floorboards and far above the child's reach. It is the same pot and the same plant in every shot it appears in — bare orange-brown clay with visible throwing ridges and thumb marks, no glaze, no paint, no decoration ever, a sparse crown of glossy heart-shaped leaves on thin visible stems with bare soil showing between them, growing only very slightly fuller across the twelve shots. It never leaves that shelf, is never carried, never moves house and is never touched by the child. Ordinary houseplants fill the backgrounds and are completely different objects — a leggy fern in a woven basket in the corner, a small flowering plant on the record player cabinet, a row of herbs on the kitchen sill — different leaf shapes, different containers, never terracotta, never heart-shaped, never confusable with the soul plant. THE IVY IS THE ONLY THING IN THIS ENTIRE SEQUENCE THAT MOVES WITHOUT BEING TOUCHED: once, in the final shot, one stem lifts and one furled leaf opens. It happens the way a leaf opens, physically and quietly, with a small anticipatory tightening first, then the opening, then a soft overshoot and settle, over a short duration. It is not a time lapse, not a sparkle, not a glow, not a shimmer, not a pulse and not a wind effect. Every other object in every other shot moves only after a hand or a body has visibly made contact with it first.

CONTACT FIRST AND NOBODY PHASES THROUGH ANYTHING — CRITICAL: nothing in any shot moves, tips, slides, swings, drifts or falls until a hand or a body has visibly touched it, without exception. The laundry basket does not shift until small hands are gripping its rim. The drawer does not open until fingers are hooked over its edge. The chalk does not mark the floorboards until it is in contact with them. The towel does not move until it is taken. Both figures navigate every piece of furniture with real clearance — no body ever passes through, clips into or overlaps a couch, a coffee table, a cabinet, a console, a basket, a tub or a wall. Where a body does make contact it is a real physical collision with a real physical consequence, never an intersection.

CAMERA: twelve separate physical moves, one per shot, each with its own travel distance and rate, stated per shot. Every move is mounted and smooth with the faintest organic breath, never handheld shake, never mechanical, never locked off, and never fully stopping before the cut.

Water sheets off a small body and runs back into the tub, and the towel goes heavy and dark where it touches wet skin. Soil packs under three fingers and holds its shape, and the twig stands because it has been pushed in, not because it grew. Cushions compress and rebound. The terracotta pot never moves on its shelf. ACTING: the mother is never once angry across these twelve shots — every removal, every sweep, every redirection is fear moving fast and calling itself housework, and the only heat she ever shows is a jaw set and a breath out through the nose. Her physical decline is the spine of her performance: she starts upright and finishes with her shoulders lower, her hand at her back, her weight pushed off her own thigh to stand, and the skin under her eyes darker and looser. Two beats carry her whole interior life and neither is spoken: the thumb that wipes water from under her daughter's eye in the bath without her seeming to think about it, and the hand that stops on the tin cup in shot nine and stays there a beat and a half too long before she empties it anyway. She understands completely and she does it anyway, and that is the tragedy of her. The child is bright and physical and undefeated in the early shots — a small engineering department attacking a shelf with a basket and a drawer — and across the sequence her methods get quieter and better: the fist grip becomes a pinch, the two-footed hop becomes a clean step, the loud open-mouthed breathing becomes quiet nose breathing, and the drawings and the building move from the open floor to the gap behind the couch. By shot eleven she waters what she can reach and does not look up at what she cannot, and that is the whole arc landing without a single tear. Both of them blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates and depths, and never do the same thing at the same time — every action is sequential and reactive, with the child's responses arriving a full beat after her mother's. Neither of them ever looks toward the lens.

A small girl shoves a laundry basket across the floor to the wall beneath a shelf and it slides out from under her. She draws two figures and a pot in chalk on the floorboards and her mother sweeps them up without looking at them. She stands books upright along her own bare bedroom sill. One unbroken camera move from the first frame to the last, following the mother down the last of an enclosed staircase, north up the full length of the house, and finally arcing around to look back south down the same run. STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.
THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.
ONE PLANT, AND THE SHELF IS EMPTY UNTIL SHE PUTS IT THERE — CRITICAL: there is exactly one plant in this entire sequence and it is the one in the mother's hands. The long cream-painted plank shelf on the west wall carries its household objects packed along its NEAR end only — the row of leaning books, the small standing clock, the pair of brass candlesticks and the shallow bowl. The FAR end of that same shelf, the stretch directly above the record player cabinet, is completely and visibly empty at the start of the shot. No pot, no plant, no saucer, no ring mark, no shadow of one, nothing. That far span is exactly where the pot she is carrying ends up, and it stays there for the remainder of the shot. Do not render a plant on the shelf before her hands place it there. Do not render a second plant anywhere in the house at any point, on any sill, in any corner, in any depth. The ivy itself is a modest young plant, much smaller than the pot suggests: a sparse crown of five or six glossy heart-shaped leaves in total, clearly countable, on thin visible stems with bare soil showing between them, and exactly two short runners spilling over the rim and hanging only a little way down the outside of the clay without reaching the base. It is not full, not dense, not layered, not cascading, and it does not crowd the pot it stands in.
THE MOTHER IS NOT ON RAILS — CRITICAL: she is a specific tired woman carrying an awkward object through her own house and every second of her screen time shows it. Her walk is uneven — she slows without reason and picks up again, shortens a stride to clear the coffee table leg and lengthens the next, her weight rolling fully from hip to hip with her torso counter-rotating against her shoulders and her head leading each turn. She adjusts the pot against her chest twice, hitching it higher with a small bump of her forearm and shifting her grip from underneath to around the body of the clay. A loose strand of hair falls across her face and she blows it upward without breaking stride, then tucks it behind her ear with the back of one wrist because both hands are full. She rolls her right shoulder once. Her chest and shoulders rise visibly with breath at her own rhythm, deeper on some breaths than others. She blinks at uneven intervals, never metronomic. She glances at things in passing. She never walks in a straight line at a constant speed, never holds a fixed posture, and never carries the pot at a fixed angle. Never neutral, never mechanical, never dead-faced.
THE GIRL MISJUDGES DISTANCES AND NOBODY PHASES THROUGH ANYTHING — CRITICAL: this child's depth perception is slightly off and it shows in small physical ways that are never remarked upon and never played for comedy by her. Twice in this sequence her body makes contact with furniture she was trying to walk past: her right shoulder catches the arm of the nearer couch and she rebounds off it half a step, and later her hip clips the corner of the low coffee table hard enough to shift it a centimetre across the rug. Neither is a stumble, neither is a trip, neither is broad — she does not fall, does not windmill, does not react with any drama. She hits the thing, absorbs it, and keeps going as though nothing happened, because to her nothing did. Every other piece of furniture is navigated with real clearance by both figures — no body ever passes through, clips into or overlaps a couch, a coffee table, a side table, a console, a cabinet or a wall. Every near miss is visibly negotiated with a turn of the shoulders or a shortened stride.
ONE UNBROKEN HOUSE, ONE UNBROKEN LIGHT — CRITICAL: from the moment they come off the bottom stair the whole ground floor lies open ahead in a single continuous depth with no walls and no doors dividing it. Running north from the kitchen end: the KITCHEN at the south end, then the LIVING SPACE carrying the framed black brush calligraphy with the vintage cream television on its low timber console against the west wall and the two facing couches with the low coffee table between them on a woven rug, then the GREAT ROOM carrying the long high cream-painted plank shelf with the record player cabinet beneath it against the same west wall, and beyond that the tall street-facing window with its own small cream sofa. The enclosed staircase is a narrow straight run boxed in by plaster on both sides with a plain timber handrail, sitting on the east side beside the living space — only the last few treads and a short length of that handrail ever appear in frame and they are cropped away entirely once the figures are off the bottom tread. The two supplied location plates were photographed at different times of day and that difference is discarded completely: one single warm mid-morning register holds identically across the staircase, the living space, the great room and the kitchen end, with no visible shift, dip or lift in exposure, brightness or colour temperature at any point in the move, in either direction along the run. When the camera turns at the end and looks back south, the living space and the kitchen beyond it must be relit to match the great room exactly — not the warmer, lower, later light of their own plate.

Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

HARD CUT MONTAGE — CRITICAL: twelve separate shots joined by twelve hard cuts. Every cut is instantaneous with no dissolve, no cross-fade, no blur, no motion smear and no transitional frame of any kind. No two consecutive shots share a lens, a camera height, a framing or a camera move. Not one shot is locked off — every single shot carries its own physical camera movement with a stated travel distance. Every shot opens with the camera already moving and the action already underway, never on a still held frame and never on the exact geometry of any supplied plate. Every shot ends mid-action, cutting away before the beat completes, never on a settled pose. Time jumps forward between every shot by weeks or months and the jump is legible in the bodies, the cloth and the light, never in a caption and never in a visual effect.

THE ONE PLANT AND THE ORDINARY PLANTS — CRITICAL: the soul plant is the small young trailing ivy in the plain unglazed terracotta pot on its matching shallow saucer, standing on the far span of the high cream-painted plank shelf directly above the record player cabinet, 195 cm above the floorboards and far above the child's reach. It is the same pot and the same plant in every shot it appears in — bare orange-brown clay with visible throwing ridges and thumb marks, no glaze, no paint, no decoration ever, a sparse crown of glossy heart-shaped leaves on thin visible stems with bare soil showing between them, growing only very slightly fuller across the twelve shots. It never leaves that shelf, is never carried, never moves house and is never touched by the child. Ordinary houseplants fill the backgrounds and are completely different objects — a leggy fern in a woven basket in the corner of the great room, a small flowering plant on the record player cabinet — different leaf shapes, different containers, never terracotta, never heart-shaped, never confusable with the soul plant. THE IVY IS THE ONLY THING IN THIS ENTIRE SEQUENCE THAT MOVES WITHOUT BEING TOUCHED: once, in the final shot, one furled leaf opens. It opens the way a leaf opens, physically and quietly, with anticipation and a small overshoot and settle, over a short duration. It is not a time lapse, not a sparkle, not a glow, not a shimmer, not a pulse. Every other object in every other shot moves only after a hand or a body has visibly made contact with it first.

TIME PASSES IN THE BODIES AND THE CLOTH — CRITICAL: the child grows perhaps two centimetres across the twelve shots, her limbs lengthening a fraction and her balance improving, and she cycles through four wardrobe and hair states, becoming progressively more dishevelled and then, at the end, quieter and tidier than she was. Her cardigan gains crayon wax at the cuff and a pulled thread. Her socks slip further down. Her knees go from clean to grazed. Her braids come out and her hair goes loose and then up. The mother's clothes stay inside her unchanging palette of cream, pale sage, bare tan, soft blue and white with no pattern and no ornament of any kind, and her hair stays short — but the way she wears it degrades: neat and pushed back at first, then flattened on one side, then damp at the temples and shoved behind one ear. Her tiredness accumulates physically and never emotionally: her shoulders sit lower by the end, she pushes up off her own thigh to stand, the skin under her eyes goes slightly darker and slightly looser, and one hand goes to the small of her back twice. SHE IS NEVER ANGRY IN ANY SHOT. Every correction she makes is fear wearing the face of practicality — she lifts, removes, wipes and scrubs quickly and without heat, and the closest she comes to anything sharper is a jaw set and a breath let out through the nose. She never raises a hand in threat, never grabs, never looms. The child never cries at any point in this sequence, not once, not a single tear, and never has a tantrum — she goes quieter instead, and that is the whole arc.

CONTACT FIRST AND NOBODY PHASES — CRITICAL: nothing in any shot moves, tips, slides, swings, drifts or falls until a hand or a body has visibly touched it, without exception. The stool does not scrape until small hands are gripping its seat. The books do not shift until they are picked up. The water does not leave the cup until the cup is tipped. The wax does not appear on plaster until the crayon is in contact with the plaster. The wall does not lighten until the cloth is dragged across it. Both figures navigate every piece of furniture with real clearance — no body ever passes through, clips into or overlaps a couch, a coffee table, a cabinet, a console, a stool or a wall, and every near miss is visibly negotiated with a turn of the shoulders, a raised elbow or a shortened stride.

FIRST FRAME: already in motion. Shot one opens with the stool already halfway across the floorboards under the child's hands, already scraping, the camera already tracking with it, and the child already mid-stride. Nothing is held, nothing is static, no establishing frame.

OPTICS: each shot carries its own locked horizontal field of view, stated per shot below and unchanging within that shot. No zoom, no focal change and no lens breathing inside any shot. Every change in scale within a shot comes from the camera physically moving.

CAMERA: twelve separate physical moves, one per shot, each with its own travel distance and rate, stated per shot. Every move is mounted and smooth with the faintest organic breath, never handheld shake, never mechanical, never locked off, and never fully stopping before the cut.

LIGHT: warm daylight throughout, direction and time of day shifting shot to shot to carry the passage of time, quality always soft and always warm. Broad soft daylight from the tall north window at the far end of the house, raking south along the west wall and skimming the face of the high shelf. Cooler daylight enters from the south kitchen end and fills the opposite depth. Several shots sit in low late-afternoon light coming almost level along the floorboards; two sit in flat overcast mid-morning; one sits in warm amber dusk with the last of the light on the upper wall only. Generous warm bounce off pale plaster fills every shadow at every hour. Shadows soft-edged, lifted and tinted warm amber, never crushed. The television glass holds a soft grey sheen and is never pure black. No pure black anywhere in any frame at any depth in any shot. COLOUR: peak warmth, the warmest register in the film so far. Roughly 30% warm cream and bone in plaster and walls, 22% honey and umber in floorboards, stool, console, cabinet and coffee table, 18% warm amber and gold in the raking light, 12% cream in couch upholstery, 10% butter yellow and dusty rose across the child's cardigan, overalls, jumper and trousers, 8% pale blue, pale sage, white and tan across the mother, plus terracotta orange and sap green in the pot and its leaves. ATMOSPHERE: a continuous soft scattering gradient in every shot, filling the entire frame including the foreground and thickening steadily with distance so the far end of the house always sits paler than the near. Macro contrast low with blacks lifted at every depth, micro contrast high on knitted wool, corduroy, couch weave, plaster tooth, timber grain, clay throwing ridges, enamel chipping, wet cloth and leaf surface. Gentle bloom at the windows only. No fog, no mist, no smoke in the air, no volumetric shafts, no god rays, no drifting particulate, no dust motes.

PHYSICS: the stool is light enough to drag and too awkward to lift — it judders across each board join and catches in the gaps, and it rocks under the child's weight with her compensating at the ankles. The stacked hardbacks slide against one another and shift under her feet before the mother takes them. The child's lift is a real lift — the mother's spine straightens, her shoulders take the load, and the child's legs continue their running motion for a beat in the air. Water behaves with real mass: the thrown slug rises, decelerates, breaks into separate volumes and falls, soaking cloth in dark patches that spread and darken the boards where it lands. The enamel can is heavy full and light empty and the difference shows in the mother's wrist and elbow. Wax sits proud on the plaster tooth and smears before it lifts, and the wet plaster darkens on contact and dries pale from the edges inward. The cloth drips when lifted and sheets water when wrung. The scrubbing brush bristles splay against the wall and spring back. Couch cushions compress and rebound. The terracotta pot never moves on its shelf. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly and nothing lands silently, and no object in any shot moves before a hand or a body has visibly touched it — with the single exception of the leaf in shot twelve.

ACTING: the mother is not cruel and is never once angry — every removal, every lift, every scrub is fear moving fast and calling itself housework, and the only heat she ever shows is a jaw set and a breath out through the nose. Her physical decline across the twelve shots is the spine of her performance: she starts upright and finishes with her shoulders lower, her hand going to her back, her weight pushed off her own thigh to stand, and the skin under her eyes darker and looser. The moment in shot nine when she finds the hidden drawing and stops with her hand halfway to it is the single most important beat in the sequence — she is looking at a child who has learned to hide, she understands it completely for one and a half seconds, and then she washes it off anyway, and that is the whole tragedy of her. The child is bright and physical and undefeated in the early shots — a whole small engineering department attacking a shelf — and by the end she has simply gone quiet. Not sad, not broken, not crying, just smaller in her movements: the arm working from the wrist instead of the shoulder, the shoulder hunched near the ear, the checking glance over the shoulder, the drawing made small enough to hide, and finally the eyes that do not go up to the shelf at all in shot eleven because she has stopped asking. Both of them blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates and depths, and never hold a still expression or a fixed posture for more than a beat in any shot. Neither of them ever looks toward the lens.

A faint distant town hum, louder in the shots nearer the north window. Timber stool legs juddering and scraping across floorboards and catching in the board joins.
