LOCKS: twelve hard-cut shots across twenty-six seconds, each with its own lens, its own camera height and its own physical camera move, none locked off, none opening on a still frame, none ending on a settled pose. A small girl drags a stool to the wall beneath a shelf she cannot reach and comes up a metre short. She stacks four books on the stool and her mother lifts her off it and takes the books away without heat. She draws a wobbly ivy on the bare plaster in red wax and her mother scrubs it off on her knees. She throws a cup of water upward at the shelf and it comes back down on her own face. Her mother mops the boards. Her mother waters the plant with a can, effortlessly, while the girl watches from below with her chin lifted. Months later the girl draws again, smaller and lower and hidden behind a couch, checking over her shoulder while she works. Her mother finds it, stops with her hand halfway to it for a beat and a half, and washes it off anyway. Her mother sits down on the bottom stair in the dusk with the can still beside her and presses the heel of her hand into one eye. The girl kneels in the corner and carefully waters an ordinary fern she can reach, and does not look up at the shelf at all. In the last shot she sits on the floorboards looking up at the terracotta ivy far above her, and one furled leaf opens on its own — the only thing in the entire sequence that moves without being touched. The mother is never angry and the girl never cries. Time passes in the bodies, the cloth and the light and nowhere else. Nobody looks at the lens.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

THERE IS EXACTLY ONE DOOR IN THIS HOUSE — CRITICAL: the only door anywhere in this sequence is the front door, a solid panelled timber leaf hung on hinges with a round brass knob, set in the far wall of the entry. The opening between the entry and the front room is NOT a door — it is a wide cased opening in the wall with chunky painted timber casing on both sides and across the top, and nothing hanging in it. It has no door leaf, no knob, no handle, no hinges, no latch and no threshold plate, and nothing ever swings, opens or closes there. Both spaces are permanently open to one another through it. Do not add a door, a frame with a leaf in it, or any second openable door anywhere in this sequence.

THE ROUTE THROUGH THE HOUSE — CRITICAL: she enters through the front door in the far wall of the entry. From the threshold she crosses the entry floor toward frame LEFT and passes through the wide cased opening in the entry's left-hand wall. That opening leads into the front room, which she enters through the front room's RIGHT-hand wall. Once inside she turns and crosses leftward and forward to the sofa, which stands beneath the tall window on the far wall of the front room. This is the only route and she follows it exactly: front door, across the entry leftward, through the cased opening, into the front room, leftward and forward to the sofa.

SHOES AND SOCKS COME OFF IN TWO PAIRS — CRITICAL: the mother removes footwear in two complete sets, one leg at a time, and each set is a shoe immediately followed by its own sock before she moves to the other leg. FIRST the good leg: shoe off, then that sock off, both set down together. THEN the hurt leg: shoe off, then that sock off, both set down together. Never both shoes first and then the socks afterward, and never both socks at once. Each shoe and each sock is handled as its own distinct object with its own contact and its own release, but they come away easily and without struggle — the leather releasing with one clean tug, the cotton sliding off over the heel and toes in one smooth peel. Nothing sticks, nothing catches and nothing has to be worked at. Both small feet end up bare.

THE PLANT RESPONDS TWICE AND NOBODY SEES IT — CRITICAL: the ivy reacts twice in this sequence, once to pain and once to care, and it does so entirely alone. In both plant shots there is no person anywhere in frame — no hands, no shoulders, no bodies, no silhouettes and no shadows cast by a person. Neither the mother nor the girl ever looks toward the shelf, turns toward it, or registers in face or body that anything has happened there. The movement is witnessed by the camera alone. It carries no sparkle, no glow, no light effect, no shimmer and no visual flourish of any kind — the plant simply moves, quietly and physically, the way a living thing moves.

THE FLINCH IS A CONTRACTION, NOT A BREEZE — CRITICAL: in the first plant shot the ivy tightens inward on itself in one quick reflexive contraction. The few leaf edges curl fractionally in toward their own centre veins, the leaf faces tip downward, the thin stems draw in toward the crown and the two runners lift and shorten as they tense. It happens fast, in well under a second, and then holds tight and still. It is not a sway, not a flutter, not a wobble and not wind moving through foliage — every part of the plant moves inward at once, as a body flinches. Nothing else in that frame moves at all.

THE BREATH IS AN OPENING, NOT A TIME LAPSE — CRITICAL: in the second plant shot the ivy releases and lifts across several seconds with real botanical weight. The tension goes out of the thin stems first, then they rise and straighten, the few leaves rotating fractionally outward and opening from their curl into a firmer wider spread, the two runners easing back down over the rim, and the whole small crown settling with a faint overshoot and recovery. It does not snap, does not pop, does not accelerate and does not repeat. The plant does not grow, does not sprout new leaves and does not extend — it only releases and lifts. Exactly one continuous opening, once.

EVERY MOVEMENT HAS A VISIBLE PHYSICAL CAUSE — CRITICAL: nothing in this sequence moves on its own and no object is ever operated off screen or by implication. The front door does not move until a hand has closed around its knob; each shoe does not come off until fingers have taken its heel and pulled; each sock does not move until fingers have taken it and peeled; the trouser leg does not rise until fingers have gripped its hem and pulled; the cloth does not move until a hand has taken it; the bandage does not wrap until fingers have drawn it around. Nothing shifts, tips or slides by itself. Contact first, then motion, always, for every object without exception. The single exception is the ivy, which moves by itself with nobody near it and nobody touching it.

PHYSICS: the front door carries real mass, swinging inward with visible momentum and slowing on its arc, then decelerating and clicking at the frame when she pushes it closed. The hobble is genuine — the hurt leg is stiff and unloaded, the hip on that side stays high, and the whole torso pitches to the good side on every step with the arms swinging out for balance. Her hand flattens against the casing of the opening as she passes through it. The sofa cushion compresses under her weight and rebounds where she shifts. Each leather shoe releases with one clean tug and a small soft pop of suction, the heel counter deforming as the fingers hook it, and lands on the floorboards with a soft leather knock. Each cotton sock stretches as it is peeled, turning slightly inside out over the heel, and hangs limp as it is laid down. The corduroy hem resists and bunches as she drags it up over the knee, holding its fold. The cloth is heavy with water and releases a real stream when squeezed against the bowl rim. At the flinch the leg jerks against the mother's grip and her fingers slide slightly on the bare ankle before holding. The bandage has real fabric tension, compressing the knee slightly and creasing where it turns. The mother's knees and shins press into the floorboards with visible weight. The ivy's thin stems carry real botanical stiffness in both plant shots — the contraction is fast and elastic with everything moving inward together, and the release is slow with the leaves rotating on their own small inertia and the runners lagging behind the crown. ACTING: the girl coming in is stoic — jaw set, mouth closed, brows drawn, working hard not to make a thing of it, and she never cries at any point in this sequence. While her shoes and socks are being taken off her face is patient and slightly resigned; she lifts each foot fractionally to help without being asked, and wiggles her bare toes once after the first sock comes off. The flinch is the biggest thing her face does and it is sharp, involuntary and total — eyes screwed shut, mouth pulled back off the teeth, the whole body recoiling — and it passes within a second. The mother's face is entirely absorbed and entirely soft throughout — brows level, mouth relaxed, eyes down on the work, no impatience and no tension anywhere in the jaw or shoulders. The undressing is done with visible care, especially on the hurt side, and she never once looks up at her daughter's face while doing it. The hand on the cheek at the end is unhurried and open, and the girl pressing her face into it is the last thing that happens between them. Both of them blink at uneven intervals and breathe at clearly different rates throughout, and neither ever holds a still expression for more than a beat. Neither of them looks toward the plant at any point and neither looks toward the lens.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point. The television screen is switched off, dark and blank throughout.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

EVERY BODY IS ALIVE AT ALL TIMES — CRITICAL: neither person in this sequence ever moves like a puppet on a path, and nobody ever simply walks from one place to another. Every second of screen time carries continuous small involuntary human business underneath the main action. The mother walking is never neutral — she adjusts her grip on the pot, glances down behind her to check where her daughter's feet are, shifts the weight against her chest, blows a loose strand of hair off her face, slows fractionally without reason and picks up again, rolls a shoulder. The girl walking is never neutral — she skips a step to keep up, drags a hand along the back of a couch as she passes it, looks sideways at the television, stumbles half a step and recovers, wipes her nose on her wrist, watches her own feet and then the pot again. Standing is never neutral either — the weight rocks from one hip to the other, fingers move, breath is visible in the chest and shoulders, the eyes flick to something irrelevant and come back, a foot scuffs the boards. Both blink at irregular intervals. Neither ever freezes between beats and neither ever holds a pose. At every moment they are doing several small things at once, and never the same small thing at the same time.

NOBODY PHASES THROUGH ANYTHING — CRITICAL: both figures walk around every piece of furniture with real clearance and real navigation. Neither one ever passes through, clips into or overlaps a couch, a coffee table, a side table, a console or a wall at any point. The route down the length of the house threads between the two facing couches and around the coffee table, and both bodies visibly adjust their line and their shoulders to make the gap. When the girl follows too closely behind her mother, the mother slows and glances down to avoid stepping back onto her, and the girl checks her own stride and swerves slightly to the side. Every contact between a body and an object is a real contact — a hand trailing along upholstery, a hip passing close to a table edge — and every near miss is visibly navigated.

PHYSICS: a panelled door on real hinges swings forward into a room against its own mass with faint hinge friction. A TIMBER CHAIR under a seated body shifts a few millimetres and creaks faintly when that body is pulled and turned. KNITTED WOOL GRIPPED IN FISTS bunches into thick folds and drags the garment out of shape across the shoulders. A pencil on paper drags with friction and lifts cleanly. Tears run down and follow the contour of a cheek under gravity. GROWING STEMS CARRY REAL WEIGHT AS THEY EXTEND — the trailing lengths sag under their own increasing mass, bend over the box's edge and lie down onto the desk timber rather than floating, and the whole mass settles heavier as it fills out. A LEAF UNFURLING moves only at its own hinge and its own edge. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT, and the growth is the single exception because it is the plant's own biology and not an external force.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved figure, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

PHYSICS: a panelled door on real hinges swings against its own mass with faint hinge friction and seats into its frame with a quiet latch click, and it decelerates before it lands rather than stopping dead. A SMALL PAINTED TIMBER BOX HAS LIGHT BUT REAL WEIGHT — it swings slightly when carried, its weight increases noticeably as soil and a root ball go into it, and it settles solidly when set down on timber or stone. A ROOT BALL IS A DENSE CLOD that holds its shape when lifted, sheds loose crumbs from its underside, and drops into a box with a soft heavy landing. DRY SOIL runs between fingers, falls straight down under gravity, scatters on landing and never rises into the air. THE IVY IS DEAD WEIGHT — its stems and leaves swing passively with whatever carries them, settle late, and then hang completely still. Broken terracotta shards lie exactly where they fell and are never touched, never disturbed and never moved at any point. Soft slippers and bare knees make quiet muffled contact on timber floorboards. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT.

ACTING: she has come back with a solution she thought of herself, and she carries it out carefully and without ceremony. THE PERFORMANCE IS IN HER HANDS for most of the sequence — the care in how she lifts the root ball, the patience in going back over the boards a second time, the softness of the palm laid on the box — and in her face only at the window and at the door. She is quiet, purposeful and tender, never sad, never dramatic, never triumphant and never proud of herself. SHE NEVER CRIES AND HER EYES STAY COMPLETELY DRY. She does not sigh heavily, does not hang her head, does not slump and does not look for anyone's reaction. SHE LEAVES THE SHARDS EXACTLY WHERE THEY ARE and never gathers them, never sweeps them and never touches them. THE MOTHER IS COMPLETELY UNCONSCIOUS AND UNAWARE — she never stirs, never wakes, never opens her eyes and never reacts, and her snoring is played straight and never for comedy. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT for the daughter: she breathes visibly, she blinks at uneven irregular intervals, and her fingers work slightly against whatever she is touching. THREE FOR THE MOTHER: her chest rises and falls unevenly, her lips flutter loosely on an exhale without ever shaping a word, and one hand settles a fraction where it lies. THE TWO OF THEM NEVER ACT AT THE SAME MOMENT — the mother is inert and the daughter carries every beat, and any settle of the mother's arrives a full beat after the daughter's hands have finished. NOBODY LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no captions, no subtitles, no burned-in dialogue, no auto-captions, no karaoke text, no lower thirds, no titles, no watermark, no logo, no timecode, no interface or social overlay of any kind. THE PAINT CAN LETTERING IS A PHYSICAL PRINTED OBJECT IN THE WORLD — each aerosol carries the word BLOOM printed in dark capitals across its cream body with a solid green heart beneath it and a band of colour below matching its cap, ink printed on curved metal, standing at an angle in real perspective, scuffed and slightly worn, never an overlay and never flat on the frame. STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved figure, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

First: two hands on one brush lay a single stroke of butter-yellow acrylic on the blank canvas, roughly 7cm long, running diagonally from lower-left to upper-right at about 20 degrees off horizontal, and because two wrists push at two different angles the line deviates slightly at its midpoint, thickens at its start and thins where the pressure eased. Second: the older woman's left hand sets the palette flat on her own left thigh, her index and middle fingers extend into the same two-finger squaring gesture she has used all her life, the hand rises about 12cm toward the canvas, and it STOPS about 20cm short of the paint and hangs there, motionless, for six tenths of a second — not trembling, not advancing, not retreating — then the fingers curl slightly toward the palm, the gesture dies on its own, and the hand comes down and rests flat on her knee. No dialogue, no voice-over, no whispering, no muttering, no humming, no singing; neither woman's mouth ever forms words, shapes syllables or moves as though speaking, and neither mouths anything silently. Both smiles are closed-lipped, with no teeth showing, and they carry the whole feeling in the eyes — lower lids lifting, outer corners creasing deeply, cheeks rising. Every emotional beat arrives late and builds: a reaction begins as one small involuntary thing about three tenths of a second after its cause, spreads across the face over the next half second, and settles. Nothing snaps on, nothing switches state between frames, nothing is telegraphed before its cause, and no expression is struck as a pose and held. Faces are asymmetric — one corner of a mouth moves before the other, one brow lifts further than its partner, the eyes always start it and the mouth always answers, and a smile that fades unwinds in the reverse order it was built. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, wood holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes before releasing. Weight shifts fully from hip to hip when walking, torsos counter-rotate against shoulders, heads lead turns and bodies follow a beat later. Between actions the characters never freeze — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust. This is patient, tender, observational character animation with real physical charm.

THE ROOM EMPTIES AND THEN STAYS EMPTY — CRITICAL: at the start of this sequence the last of the class is still filing out through the door, and by the end of the first shot every one of them has gone. From the second shot onward no other child appears anywhere in frame at any point — no bodies in the background, no silhouettes at the door, no one passing the windows. The room holds only the teacher and the girl and the abandoned evidence of a class that has just left: pushed-out chairs, drying pots on the tables, jars of dirty water and brushes lying where they were dropped.

THE THREE LOOKS COME BEFORE THE CROUCH — CRITICAL: before the teacher lowers herself, the girl performs three distinct looks in a fixed order, each one clearly readable and briefly held before releasing to the next. First she looks toward the door, watching the last children leave. Then she looks down at her own painted pot sitting on the table beside her. Then she looks up — steeply up, because the teacher is standing over her — into the teacher's face. Three looks, in that order, and only after the third does the teacher begin to lower.

THE CROUCH IS THE POINT OF THE SCENE — CRITICAL: the teacher lowers herself all the way down to the girl's eye level and stays there. She does not bend at the waist, does not stoop over her, does not lean down from standing and does not talk down at her from above. She goes fully down onto her heels in a low crouch so that her eyes and the girl's eyes are level with each other, and she holds that position for the rest of the sequence. The two faces are at the same height in frame from the moment she lowers until the sequence ends. The steep upward look immediately before it and the levelled eyelines immediately after it must make the change unmistakable. No adult in this film has ever done this before.

TWO BOXES, VERY DIFFERENT — CRITICAL: two wooden boxes appear in this sequence and they must never be confused. The teacher's own box is heavily painted, layered and old. The box she gives the girl is completely blank, bare and new. They are the same size and shape and nothing else about them matches. The blank one carries no paint, no marks, no colour and no decoration of any kind at any point.

THE PAINTED POT STAYS ON THE TABLE AND STAYS WET — CRITICAL: the girl's decorated clay pot stands on the table beside her for the entire sequence and is never picked up, moved, carried, handed over or touched by anyone. It is only ever looked at. Its paint is still wet throughout — glossy and light-catching, standing proud of the porous clay with soft rounded edges — and the heavy drip below the red band is still slowly travelling down the clay, visibly a little longer by the end of the sequence than at the start.

EVERY MOVEMENT HAS A VISIBLE PHYSICAL CAUSE — CRITICAL: nothing in this sequence moves on its own and no object is ever operated off screen or by implication. A box does not lift until hands have closed around it; a lid does not come off until fingers have taken it and pulled; a box does not turn until it is turned by hands; a door does not swing until a body has pushed through it. Nothing shifts, tips or slides by itself. Contact first, then motion, always, for every object without exception.

THAT DOOR OPENS TOWARD THE CAMERA — CRITICAL, AND IT INVERTS THE USUAL RULE BECAUSE OF WHERE WE ARE STANDING: the door is hinged INSIDE this room and opens INTO this room, and the camera is standing inside this room. THE SWING, IN ORDER: the door is closed, flat in the plane of its own wall, its painted face turned toward us, recessed inside its architrave with an even shadow gap all round and a thin bright strip of light glowing along the floor beneath it — the brass knob turns — THE FREE EDGE OF THE LEAF SEPARATES FROM THE FRAME AND COMES FORWARD OUT OF THE WALL PLANE TOWARD THE CAMERA, the painted face turning to catch the room light and becoming foreshortened as it advances — the leaf continues swinging forward until it stands angled into the room, its free edge NEAR the camera and its hinged edge FAR, against the door wall — and where the door used to be there is now an OPEN DOORWAY with a lit space beyond it. Once open, THE LEAF STAYS EXACTLY WHERE IT IS LEFT, angled into the room, for the whole rest of the sequence. It never closes, never swings back, never sweeps across the lens and never leaves frame.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no captions, no subtitles, no burned-in dialogue, no auto-captions, no karaoke text, no lower thirds, no titles, no watermark, no logo, no timecode, no interface or social overlay of any kind. THE MOTHER IS ON TOP OF THE BED, NOT UNDER THE COVERS — CRITICAL: she has plainly had a bad night and moved around a great deal. SHE LIES ON TOP OF THE SAGE GREEN COVERLET, fully outside the bedding, wearing what she went to bed in. THE COVERLET IS STILL ON THE BED beneath her but it is dragged crooked and rucked into folds under her weight, one corner pulled loose from the foot of the mattress and hanging. SHE IS LYING AWKWARDLY AND OFF-CENTRE: not square to the bed, not neatly on her side of it. THE DAUGHTER'S FIRST INSTINCT IS THE PILLOW, NOT THE MESS — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE HEART OF THE SEQUENCE: when she comes into the room she sees the broken pot on the floor and registers it — but SHE DOES NOT GO TO IT AND DOES NOT TOUCH IT. Her attention moves off it and onto her mother, and what she does is PICK THE FALLEN PILLOW UP OFF THE FLOOR AND PUT IT BACK ON THE BED, easing it under her mother's head to make her comfortable. That is the only thing she does in the room. She does not sweep up the shards, does not gather the soil, does not right the plant, does not tidy anything and does not wake her mother. THE MESS IS LEFT EXACTLY WHERE IT IS.

SHE IS CONCERNED AND CONFUSED, NOT DISTRAUGHT — CRITICAL: her whole register is worry and puzzlement, and it stays contained. HER BROWS ARE RAISED AND DRAWN IN at the inner ends — the specific shape of concern, not fear and not grief. Her eyes are wide and searching. Her mouth stays closed or very slightly parted. SHE DOES NOT CRY — no tears, no welling, no brightening along the lash line, no wet catchlight, no glassiness, no sniff, no trembling lip, no crumpling and no hand to her face. She does not gasp, does not startle and does not panic. In the final shot her feet quicken and her weight goes forward, but it stays quiet and controlled and never becomes running, fleeing, stumbling or fright.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved figure, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

PHYSICS: a panelled door on real hinges swings forward into a room against its own mass with faint hinge friction, and a brass knob turns against real spring resistance. A hand gripping the free edge of a door leaf wraps the timber and compresses slightly against it. Soft slippers make quiet muffled contact on timber floorboards. A PILLOW HAS REAL SOFT WEIGHT — it sags and folds over the hands lifting it, its filling shifting inside the case, and it compresses and settles when a head is lowered onto it. A SLEEPING HEAD LIFTED A FEW CENTIMETRES is heavy and loose, the neck slack, and it settles down into the pillow rather than being placed. A body lying on top of a coverlet rucks and drags it beneath its weight, and the mattress and the bedding depress under a knee coming onto the edge. Broken terracotta shards and spilled soil lie exactly where they fell and are never disturbed, never touched and never moved at any point. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT.

ACTING: she is a child who has come to check on someone and is finding something she cannot make sense of — and her instinct is care rather than tidying. THE PERFORMANCE IS IN HER BROWS AND HER EYES throughout, and in the gentleness of her hands with the pillow. SHE REGISTERS THE BROKEN POT AND CHOOSES HER MOTHER OVER IT, and that choice is the whole point of the scene. She is concerned and confused, never frightened, never grieving and never dramatic. SHE NEVER CRIES AND HER EYES STAY COMPLETELY DRY. She does not gasp, does not startle, does not cover her mouth, does not call out and does not clean anything up. THE MOTHER IS COMPLETELY UNCONSCIOUS AND UNAWARE — she never stirs, never wakes, never opens her eyes and never reacts, even while being moved, and her snoring is played straight and never for comedy. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT for the daughter: she breathes visibly, she blinks at uneven irregular intervals, and her fingers work slightly against whatever she is touching. THREE FOR THE MOTHER: her chest rises and falls unevenly, her lips flutter loosely on an exhale without ever shaping a word, and one hand settles a fraction where it lies. THE TWO OF THEM NEVER ACT AT THE SAME MOMENT — the mother is inert and the daughter carries every beat, and any settle of the mother's arrives a full beat after the daughter's hands have finished. NOBODY LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no captions, no subtitles, no burned-in dialogue, no auto-captions, no karaoke text, no lower thirds, no titles, no watermark, no logo, no timecode, no interface or social overlay of any kind. STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved figure, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

SHOT 2 · 7–16s · OVERHEAD, THE NEEDLE DROPS · 34 degrees [58mm], camera DIRECTLY OVERHEAD looking straight down at the record player on the cabinet from about 130 cm above it, lens perpendicular so the platter and the record read as true circles and the machine sits square to the frame. Her hand is steady but alive — small live adjustments in the fingers, never frozen.

The record begins rotating clockwise beneath the suspended stylus, starting from dead still and coming up to speed over about a second with a visible acceleration rather than snapping instantly to full rate, the CTRL label at the centre beginning to spin and blurring slightly at its printed edges as it settles into a steady turn. The stylus stays hovering above it while the record picks up speed underneath.
12–14s — SHE DROPS THE NEEDLE. Her fingers lower the arm the last centimetre and the stylus settles into the outer groove, the arm tip dipping very slightly as it takes the surface, the cantilever giving a fraction. Her hand comes away — and her OTHER HAND IS ALREADY ENTERING FRAME at the right, moving toward the control knobs before the first hand has fully cleared. She turns it in one movement and does not turn it back. THE SURFACE NOISE GETS LOUDER as she does — the crackle and hiss rising in level with the turn, and nothing else arriving with it. NO MUSIC BEGINS.
20–21s — her fingers release the knob, and her hand does not snap away — it lifts, hovers a moment over the deck, then drops out of the bottom of frame as her weight visibly shifts off the cabinet above. LAST FRAME: the record turning steadily under the tracking tonearm, the CTRL label spinning at the centre, the volume knob left at its new position, the ceramic cat untouched at the frame edge, the bare cabinet top around it, and the raking daylight across it.

PHYSICS: a tonearm lifted off its rest has real weight in the hand and its counterweight balances it at the pivot. A stylus lowered into a groove settles with a tiny dip and the cantilever gives a fraction under it. A platter starts from rest and accelerates up to speed over about a second rather than snapping instantly to full rate, and once at speed turns at a constant rate with no strobing, no stutter and no frame-stepping. A tracking tonearm creeps inward across the record almost imperceptibly. A fluted control knob turns against real detent resistance and stays where it is put. Flat shoes on timber make soft contact with the boards, with a light quick cadence. Loose wide-leg trousers move a beat behind the leg. Hair is heavy and swings a beat behind the head, settling with a visible overshoot. A ceramic figurine on a cabinet does not move when someone works beside it. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT — with the single exception of the platter, which starts turning under the hovering stylus because the machine is running.

ACTING: this is a small practised routine she has done a thousand times, and it plays as easy competence rather than ceremony. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT: she breathes visibly, blinks at uneven intervals, and her fingers make small live adjustments against whatever they are holding. STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Head slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouette built from soft rounded primary solids. Face simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple nose, brows and mouth carrying the performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: timber holds carved figure, plaster holds a tooth, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, painted metal holds dents and chips. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never evenly paced. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

FIRST FRAME: already in motion and already mid-embrace, and not on the supplied plate's own geometry. The frame opens close on the daughter's face over her mother's shoulder, the camera already mid-drift and already carrying its handheld float — no static first frame, no settling into position, no establishing hold. PHYSICS: real gravity and real mass throughout. GROWING STEMS CARRY WEIGHT — a lengthening runner sags several millimetres between contact points before its next rootlet catches, and a rose head tips its stem downward a few millimetres as its petals open and mass moves outward. Each rootlet makes visible contact with plaster, timber, iron or a mirror frame before load transfers to it. Leaves and roses cast true contact shadows where they meet the wall, the desk, the bedpost, the window casing and the ceiling junction. THE PAINTED CRATE HOLDS ITS SOIL AND NEVER MOVES UNDER THE GROWTH — no rock, no creep, no slide, no drift across the desk. The desk does not flex. THE ROW OF CANS IS NEVER DISTURBED. A BODY KNEELING on floorboards holds its weight through the knees with the knitted robe folded and pooled around them. COARSE KNITTED WOOL UNDER OPEN HANDS compresses and drags; gathered into fists it bunches into thick folds and pulls the whole garment out of shape across the shoulders and back. A timber chair under a seated body shifts a few millimetres and creaks faintly when that body pulls and turns. Tears run down and follow the contour of a cheek under gravity. Nothing floats, nothing slides, nothing teleports, nothing stops instantly, and nothing is displaced by anything other than its own growth.

ACTING: this is the moment the film has been withholding and it is played completely. THE DAUGHTER'S PERFORMANCE RUNS IN ONE UNBROKEN LINE — held and wet with her eyes open on the plant, then the tears break, then her eyes close, then her hands open wide and take hold of her mother's robe and her body and pull her in, then she sobs. She does not recover, does not compose herself and does not pull back at any point. THE OPENING OF HER HANDS IS THE KEY BEAT — fingers spread wide and flat before they close, a child taking hold of a parent she has not been held by in years. THE MOTHER IS FULLY COMMITTED FROM THE FIRST FRAME — already down on her knees, already holding her, and she never lets go, never loosens, never pulls away to look at her and never breaks the embrace. Her performance is entirely in her hands and the back of her head. NEITHER OF THEM NOTICES THE PLANT AFTER THE FIRST SHOT — through the whole bloom they are holding each other and not looking, and the growth is never performed for and never reacted to. THE TWO OF THEM NEVER ACT AT THE SAME MOMENT — one moves and the other answers a full beat later, never together. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT for each: both breathe visibly and unevenly, both blink at uneven irregular intervals and never simultaneously with each other, and both work their fingers against whatever they are holding. THE GROWTH ITSELF IS GENTLE — patient and unhurried, never grasping, never whipping, never lunging, never predatory, never reaching for anybody. NOBODY LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point, and every look goes clearly off-axis past the near edge of the lens.

AUDIO: fully diegetic, every sound with a visible source in frame. Low warm room tone. Distant birdsong outside the closed windows. RAGGED UNEVEN BREATHING FROM BOTH OF THEM throughout, catching and irregular, AS BREATH ONLY — NO SOB SOUND, NO CRY, NO WAIL, NO WHIMPER, NO GASP AND NO VOCAL SOUND OF ANY KIND from either of them at any point. Coarse knitted wool compressing under open palms, then bunching and dragging in gripping fists. Cotton jersey shifting. A timber chair creaking faintly and shifting a few millimetres. THE GROWTH HAS ITS OWN SOUND AND IT IS ORGANIC AND SMALL — a faint dry rustle as leaf coils unroll, a soft papery separation as rose petals roll back, a fine creak and tick of stems lengthening, and a tiny tick as each rootlet meets plaster, timber, iron or a mirror frame. IT IS NEVER MUSICAL — never a chime, never a tone, never a swell, never a whoosh, never a rising note. NO SOUND FROM THE PAINT CANS — nothing rattles, nothing hisses, nothing sprays. NO DOOR SOUND, NO FOOTSTEPS, NO VOICES AND NO CHATTER at any point. NO OTHER SOUND FROM ANYWHERE IN THE HOUSE. No speech, no words and no murmuring at any point. NO BGM of any kind at any point, INCLUDING UNDER THE BLOOM.

THE ROOM STARTS COMPLETELY BARE — CRITICAL, AND IT IS THE FIRST RULE OF THIS PROMPT: for the first thirteen seconds this bedroom has NO FLOWERS, NO BLOSSOM, NO BUDS, NO PETALS, NO VINES, NO CLIMBING FOLIAGE AND NO GREENERY ANYWHERE — not on the walls, not on the ceiling, not at the windows, not on the bed, not on the desk, not on the floor, not outside the windows and not at any depth of any frame. THE ONLY GREEN THING IN THE ROOM IS THE SMALL DYING IVY IN THE PAINTED CRATE ON THE DESK, and it is dull, sparse and browned. Every flower and every vine that exists later grows out of that crate on camera. The room does not begin dressed and does not arrive pre-flowered.

THE GROWTH IS BIOLOGICAL AND NOT MAGICAL — CRITICAL: from thirteen seconds onward the ivy recovers and spreads visibly on camera, and it does so as A PLANT DOING PLANT THINGS VERY FAST. NO SPARKLE, NO GLITTER, NO GLOWING PARTICLES, NO MOTES, NO LIGHT TRAILS, NO LENS FLARE, NO HALO, NO AURA, NO PULSE, NO ENERGY, NO SWIRL AND NO MAGIC OF ANY KIND. Nothing emits light and nothing glows from within. No wind blows through the room. THE GROWTH ADVANCES ON FOUR INDEPENDENT CLOCKS THAT NEVER FALL INTO STEP AND NEVER PULSE TOGETHER: stems lengthen at a steady constant rate that never surges; one leaf begins unrolling from a tight coil roughly every second at a different point on the vine, each taking about a second to open, staggered so no two open on the same frame; buds swell slowly over several seconds each, beginning at scattered moments, many still closed at the final frame; and flowers release open in a fast late motion, scattered, several still opening as each shot ends. CONTACT PRECEDES ADVANCE EVERY TIME — a tendril tip touches a surface first and flattens against it, and only then does the stem beyond it lengthen. This is continuous organic growth, never a morph, never a dissolve, never a crossfade between two states of a room.

THE GROWTH NEVER TOUCHES EITHER PERSON — CRITICAL: no stem, no runner, no leaf and no flower ever reaches toward, wraps around, brushes, crosses or makes contact with the mother or the daughter at any point, and none ever grows between them or over them. It spreads across the desk, up the walls, along the ceiling line and over the bed frame, and it goes around them. Neither of them is ever entangled, obscured or interrupted by it. The floorboards stay completely bare of vine.

THE EMOTION IS THE WHOLE POINT AND IT IS SILENT — CRITICAL: this is the release of eighteen years of held tension and it must be fully played, not indicated. The order is locked: she is being held with her eyes open and wet, looking at the plant — then the first tears break and run — then her eyes CLOSE and her face gives in completely — then she pulls in hard and sobs. THE SOBBING IS TOTAL AND COMPLETELY SILENT: her shoulders jump and shake in irregular bursts, her back moves under her mother's arm, her fists grip, her breath goes ragged and audible AS BREATH ONLY. NO SOB SOUND, NO CRY, NO WAIL, NO WHIMPER, NO GASP AND NO VOCALISATION OF ANY KIND from either of them. The mother is already fully committed to the embrace from the first frame and never lets go, never pulls back and never breaks it.

NO BGM — no score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no rising tone, no chimes, no strings, no piano, no choir, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point, INCLUDING UNDER THE BLOOM, which is the single most likely place for music to appear and must not have any.

ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE: nobody speaks anywhere in this sequence. No words, no talking, no calling out, no whispering, no muttering, no vocalising of any kind. NEITHER MOUTH EVER FORMS A WORD and neither moves as if speaking at any point — they open for BREATH only. Neither says the other's name and neither mouths anything silently. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no captions, no subtitles, no burned-in dialogue, no auto-captions, no karaoke text, no lower thirds, no titles, no title cards, no credits, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no UI or interface overlays, no Chinese characters, no Korean characters. The frame is clean of all overlay graphics from first frame to last. THE PAINT CAN LETTERING IS A PHYSICAL PRINTED OBJECT IN THE WORLD — each aerosol carries the word BLOOM printed in dark capitals across its cream body with a solid green heart beneath it and a band of colour below matching its cap, ink printed on curved metal, standing at an angle in real perspective, scuffed and lightly worn, catching the room light on the raised edges of the print. It is never an overlay and never flat on the frame.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. NOT a game engine and NOT a game-cutscene aesthetic. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems, and the knitted wool of the mother's cardigan carries a coarse open knit that bunches and drags under gripping fists. Foliage is sculpted mass with clean leaf silhouettes and clean petal edges, never photo-scanned, never rendered vein by vein. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved figure, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust, and leaves already opened keep a low idle drift of two or three millimetres.

PHYSICS: real gravity and real mass throughout. GROWING STEMS CARRY WEIGHT — a lengthening runner sags several millimetres between contact points before its next rootlet catches, and a flower head tips its stem downward a few millimetres as its petals open and mass moves outward. Each rootlet makes visible contact with plaster, timber or iron before load transfers to it. Leaves cast true contact shadows where they meet the wall, the desk, the bedpost and the ceiling junction. THE PAINTED CRATE HOLDS ITS SOIL AND NEVER MOVES UNDER THE GROWTH — no rock, no creep, no slide, no drift across the desk. The desk does not flex. THE ROW OF CANS IS NEVER DISTURBED. A BODY KNEELING on floorboards holds its weight through the knees with the knitted cardigan folded and pooled around them. KNITTED WOOL GRIPPED IN FISTS bunches into thick folds and drags the garment out of shape across the shoulders. A timber chair under a seated body shifts a few millimetres and creaks faintly when that body pulls and turns. Tears run down and follow the contour of a cheek under gravity. Nothing floats, nothing slides, nothing teleports, nothing stops instantly, and nothing is displaced by anything other than its own growth.

ACTING: this is the moment the film has been withholding and it is played completely. THE DAUGHTER'S PERFORMANCE RUNS IN ONE UNBROKEN LINE — held and wet with her eyes open on the plant, then the tears break, then her eyes close and her face gives in, then her arms go round and she sobs. She does not recover, does not compose herself and does not pull back at any point. THE MOTHER IS FULLY COMMITTED FROM THE FIRST FRAME — already down on her knees, already holding her, and she never lets go, never loosens, never pulls away to look at her and never breaks the embrace. Her performance is entirely in her hands and the back of her head. NEITHER OF THEM NOTICES THE PLANT AFTER THE FIRST SHOT — through the whole bloom they are holding each other and not looking, and the growth is never performed for and never reacted to. THE TWO OF THEM NEVER ACT AT THE SAME MOMENT — one moves and the other answers a full beat later, never together. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT for each: both breathe visibly and unevenly, both blink at uneven irregular intervals and never simultaneously with each other, and both work their fingers against whatever they are holding. THE GROWTH ITSELF IS GENTLE — patient and unhurried, never grasping, never whipping, never lunging, never predatory, never reaching for anybody. NOBODY LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point, and every look goes clearly off-axis past the near edge of the lens.

AUDIO: fully diegetic, every sound with a visible source in frame. Low warm room tone. Distant birdsong outside the closed windows. RAGGED UNEVEN BREATHING FROM BOTH OF THEM throughout, catching and irregular, AS BREATH ONLY — NO SOB SOUND, NO CRY, NO WAIL, NO WHIMPER, NO GASP AND NO VOCAL SOUND OF ANY KIND from either of them at any point. Coarse knitted wool bunching and dragging in gripping fists. Cotton jersey shifting. A timber chair creaking faintly and shifting a few millimetres. THE GROWTH HAS ITS OWN SOUND AND IT IS ORGANIC AND SMALL — a faint dry rustle as leaf coils unroll, a soft papery separation as petals release, a fine creak and tick of stems lengthening, and a tiny tick as each rootlet meets plaster, timber or iron. IT IS NEVER MUSICAL — never a chime, never a tone, never a swell, never a whoosh, never a rising note. NO SOUND FROM THE PAINT CANS — nothing rattles, nothing hisses, nothing sprays. NO DOOR SOUND, NO FOOTSTEPS, NO VOICES AND NO CHATTER at any point. NO OTHER SOUND FROM ANYWHERE IN THE HOUSE. No speech, no words and no murmuring at any point. NO BGM of any kind at any point, INCLUDING UNDER THE BLOOM.

LOCKS: five hard-cut shots across thirty seconds, in this exact order — she is held and looking at the plant with her eyes open and wet, she closes her eyes and gives in and sobs, the plant comes back to life on the desk, the vine takes the walls and the bed, the whole room in bloom. THE EMBRACE IS ALREADY FULLY UNDERWAY IN THE FIRST FRAME and is never broken, never loosened and never released. THE EMOTIONAL ORDER IS LOCKED: eyes open and wet on the plant, tears break and run, eyes close, arms go round, silent sobbing — and it never reverses and she never composes herself. BOTH SETS OF TEARS ACTUALLY RUN and the crying is COMPLETELY SILENT with breath only. THE ROOM IS COMPLETELY BARE OF FLOWERS AND VINE FOR THE FIRST THIRTEEN SECONDS and every vine and flower afterwards grows out of the painted crate on camera. THE GROWTH IS BIOLOGICAL — colour, then uncurling, then thickening and new leaves, then flowers, on four independent clocks that never fall into step — WITH NO SPARKLE, NO GLOW, NO PARTICLES, NO LIGHT CHANGE AND NO MAGIC. IT NEVER TOUCHES EITHER PERSON, never grows between them or over them, never crosses the open floorboards and never disturbs the row of paint cans. COVERAGE CAP: walls, joinery, windows, bed frame and pictures stay clearly readable through the vine, and no surface is fully buried. THE CRATE NEVER MOVES. THE FOUR CANS STAND CAPPED AND UNTOUCHED and the BLOOM lettering is ink printed on curved metal in perspective, never an overlay. THE MOTHER IS THE UNWORN VERSION with a full auburn bob and no grey anywhere, and NO JEWELLERY IN ANY FRAME on either of them. The room's furniture, floor and window positions hold unchanged from first frame to last with only the vine added on top. Every shot a different height and a different angle. Light direction and colour temperature stay constant across all cuts. The air holds uniform density with blacks lifted at every plane and no pure black in any frame. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms a word, and nobody looks at the lens.

THREE SHOTS. TOTAL RUNTIME 25 SECONDS.
SHOT 1 — 0s to 13s. SHOT 2 — 13s to 21s. SHOT 3 — 21s to 25s.
CUT POLICY: two hard cuts, instantaneous, on the frame. No dissolve, no fade, no crossfade, no wipe, no transitional frames, no speed ramp, no slow motion, no retiming. Every shot plays in continuous real time at natural speed.

NO BGM — no score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE: she is alone and nobody speaks anywhere in this sequence. No words, no whispering, no muttering, no vocalising of any kind. HER MOUTH NEVER FORMS A WORD and never moves as if speaking at any point, on camera or off — it opens only for breath. No mouthed dialogue. NO VOICE COMES FROM BEHIND EITHER DOOR.

NOBODY ELSE IS EVER SEEN: no child, no baby, no other adult appears in frame, in a doorway, as a shadow or as a silhouette at any point. Both doors stay shut except for the one she comes through, and nothing is ever glimpsed beyond either of them.

NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering burned into the frame anywhere. Real physical in-world text exists only as the handwritten date on the photograph mount described below.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Head slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouette built from soft rounded primary solids. Face simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple nose, brows and mouth carrying the performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: timber holds carved figure, plaster holds a tooth, painted joinery holds brush direction and soft chips, card holds a soft paper tooth, ink holds real pen texture. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never evenly paced. Poses readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

DOORS OPEN INWARD, ALWAYS — CRITICAL: the door she comes out of swings INTO the room behind her, away from the landing and away from the camera. IT NEVER SWINGS OUT TOWARD THE LANDING and never swings toward the lens at any point. She comes through the opening and the leaf stays on the far side of the frame in the room beyond, and she pulls it closed toward herself. The other door stays fully shut for the entire clip and is never opened.

SHE IS QUIET BECAUSE SOMEONE IS ASLEEP — CRITICAL: everything she does is deliberately soft. But there is NO PANIC ANYWHERE IN THIS CLIP — she never freezes, never startles, never flinches, never gasps, never holds her breath, never goes wide-eyed and never reacts in alarm to anything. Nothing happens that she has to react to. No board creaks, no sound comes from anywhere else in the house. She is careful out of love, not fear.

A locked rear wheel breaks traction and the back end steps out sideways, scrubbing speed with a hard grinding contact on stone and leaving a faint dark mark, and the rider's weight goes back to keep it under control. A bike stopping hard at an angle rocks once on its springs before settling. A released bicycle falls under its own weight, pivoting as it goes because the mass is unevenly distributed, and lands hard on stone with a clatter of metal, a spinning wheel and a pedal turning under its own inertia before settling. A long timber ladder is heavy and awkward and swings with real momentum when levered upright — it arrives faster than it settles, knocks hard against a wall, bounces once, scrapes sideways as the feet find purchase, and the side rails shiver briefly after it stops. Hair moves as a sculpted mass with a beat of lag. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand, a foot or a body has touched it.

PHYSICS: linen apron fabric pulls, creases and springs back when tugged, and its waist tie shifts with it. Wet hands leave two dark damp streaks down an apron front that stay dark. A tap turned off with a wrist runs down and stops with a last drip into a full sink. The pot is fired clay with real weight even empty — hugged in one arm it presses into the ribs and the girl's opposite shoulder rides higher to compensate, and lifted in two hands her forearms tighten. Dried paint on hands and clothes is matte and cracked at the edges and does not shine. A low base cupboard door swings on its hinges with a soft timber knock and the pot's unglazed base scrapes once as it is set down inside on the shelf. A crouch and a rise take real balance. Floorboards sound different from the harder surface at the kitchen end. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly and nothing is ever dropped. No object moves before a hand or a body has touched it.

ACTING: the girl is ten and hopeful and it is all in her body — the quick short steps, the insistent double tug, the pot lifted out and offered at her own chest height, the point held while her eyes go back and forth. She is asking a question and she is sure the answer is yes. The mother is exasperated rather than cruel and the whole beat turns on the ORDER she sees things in: paint, paint, paint, and only then the pot. Her sharp intake of breath, the head-to-knee sweep of her hand, the hard-drawn brows and the small definite head shake are all the reaction of a tired woman looking at more work, not a woman rejecting a gift — she never thinks of it as a gift at all, which is worse. She never shouts, never grabs, never looms and never raises a hand. The last beat belongs to the girl: no tears, no trembling lip, no meltdown, just a flat level face and a slight narrowing of the eyes as she processes and connects what has happened. She is doing quiet real-time maths about her mother. Both blink at uneven intervals and never simultaneously, breathe at clearly different rates, and never do the same thing at the same time — every response arrives a full beat after the other's action. Neither looks at the lens.

She takes the pot in one practised motion, crouches, opens a LOW BASE CUPBOARD beneath the counter, puts it inside on the bottom shelf and shuts the door — not up high, not confiscated, just put away. Then she points twice at the ceiling: upstairs. The girl stands a beat with empty hands and a flat level face, brows drawing slightly and eyes narrowing as she works it out, and goes. Her mouth never opens to form a word, never parts as if about to speak and never moves as if speaking at any point, on camera or off. NOBODY ELSE IS IN THIS SEQUENCE — CRITICAL: she is completely alone. No mother, no adult, no other person in frame, in the doorway, as a shadow, as a reflection or heard anywhere. No footsteps but hers, no voice, no door opening. The house is asleep around her.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved grain, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

THE LIGHT STATE IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE PLATE — CRITICAL: the supplied bedroom plate shows the desk lamp switched ON and the string of small bulbs faint. IN THIS SEQUENCE THAT IS REVERSED. For shots one and two the DESK LAMP IS OFF and dark, and the only light in the room is the STRING OF SMALL WARM BULBS looped on the wall behind the bed head, glowing low and warm, plus faint cool moonlight coming through the two windows and laying pale rectangles on the floorboards. Then in shot three SHE SWITCHES THE DESK LAMP ON and it becomes the dominant source for the rest of the sequence — a hard warm pool on the desktop and her hands, with the string lights and the moonlight still present but secondary. That switch is the visual event of the sequence.

SHE IS BAREFOOT THROUGHOUT — CRITICAL: no shoes, no slippers, no socks. Bare feet on the floorboards, on the rug and under the desk chair the entire time, and her feet are visible and doing real things — curling on cold boards, one tucking behind the other ankle, toes gripping a chair rung.

SHE IS QUIET BECAUSE SOMEONE IS ASLEEP — CRITICAL: every action carries the care of a child who does not want to be heard. She lifts the covers rather than throwing them. She puts her feet down one at a time. She slides the box out from under the bed slowly rather than dragging it. She sets everything down rather than dropping it. She glances at her closed bedroom door twice across the sequence. She is not frightened and not furtive in a cartoon way — she is simply careful, and the care is constant.

WHAT SHE PAINTS TONIGHT IS THE FIRST COAT ONLY — CRITICAL: <<<eab42c4f-cf38-49fc-b0ce-24bb1ad73d09>>> in its final form is EIGHT YEARS of accumulated overpainting — layered, drip-laden, corners rubbed pale, colour on colour on colour. SHE CANNOT REACH THAT IN ONE NIGHT AND MUST NOT. What she completes in this sequence is THE FIRST COAT: bold, simple, wet and freshly applied onto bare pale timber — broad bands of pink and green across the lid and the front slats, a scatter of dots, one bloom shape, brush direction plainly visible, a few heavy runs starting where she loaded the brush too much, and plenty of bare timber still showing through between the marks. It reads unmistakably as the BEGINNING of the box in the final reference — the same palette, the same energy, the same kind of marks — while being obviously one night's work rather than eight years of it. The paint is visibly WET at the end, catching the lamp light with a sheen that dry paint would not have.

CONTACT FIRST, THEN MOTION — CRITICAL: nothing moves until a hand, a foot or a body has visibly touched it. The covers do not lift until her hands are on them. The box does not slide until her fingers are under its edge. The lamp does not come on until her hand is on its switch. The lid does not come off until she lifts it. She navigates the bed, the desk and the chair with real clearance and never passes through, clips into or overlaps any furniture.

PHYSICS: bedcovers lift with real weight and drag on themselves rather than flying. Bare feet compress on cold timber boards and the toes curl. A small box eased over floorboards from under a bed catches once on a board join and is lifted over rather than forced. A lamp switch clicks and the filament comes up over about a tenth of a second rather than instantly. A chair pulled out on timber can scrape and she keeps it lifted so it does not. Poster paint goes onto bare porous timber wet and thick and sinks into the grain, darkening it, sitting proud on the surface, and running downward under gravity within a second or two where it is loaded too heavily, slowing as it thins. Brush bristles splay against a jar rim and spring back. Water in a jam jar clouds pink and then muddy brown as brushes are rinsed in it. A wet brush laid across a palette rocks once and settles. Brushes tipped into a box land in a loose scatter and lean against each other. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand, a foot or a body has touched it.

ACTING: she is ten years old and she has decided something. The first shot is the decision arriving — lying awake, one look at the door, jaw setting, chin lifting — and everything after it is execution. She is careful rather than frightened: quiet with the covers, quiet with the box, quiet with the chair, two glances at the door. And then the moment the lamp comes on and the brush is in her hand, all of the care drops away and her face goes completely absorbed and completely unguarded — the only time in this act that it does.
