STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved figure, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges, metal holds dents and oxidation. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion in the opposite direction first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Poses are readable and held briefly at their extremes. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.

SHOT 1 · 0–5s · THE DOOR OPENS TOWARD US AND SHE IS THERE · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 120 cm inside the room facing the door wall, drifting left ten centimetres. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT: the closed panelled door with its architrave and small round brass knob, the thin bright light strip beneath it. Frame LEFT: the chest of drawers and the leaning mirror against the same wall, and the foot of the bed running away. Frame LOWER: worn floorboards with the edge of the daylight parallelogram reaching in from behind the camera.
0–2s — the door is closed and still. The shadow of two feet stands in the light strip beneath it and does not move. Warm daylight lies across the panelled face. Faint soft snoring is audible from off frame.
2–4s — THE BRASS KNOB TURNS, and THE DOOR SWINGS OPEN TOWARD THE CAMERA — the free edge separating from the frame and coming forward out of the wall plane, the painted face turning and growing larger and more foreshortened as it advances toward us and toward frame RIGHT, until the leaf stands angled into the room with its free edge near the lens. IT NEVER SHRINKS, NEVER RECEDES AND NEVER TRAVELS AWAY FROM US. Where the door was there is now an open doorway with the lit landing beyond it.
4–5s — <<<8557ad86-b274-4cff-a762-8e54407d85d4>>> stands in that opening — black tee, grey sweatpants, soft grey slippers, high ponytail with the fringe down — one hand still on the far knob, the other coming up to the free edge of the leaf. She does not step in yet. Her head is already turning into the room, past the camera and off to one side. HER BROWS DRAW IN AND UP. She breathes visibly, blinks once, her fingers work against the painted timber. HARD CUT.

SHOT 2 · 5–9s · HER FACE AT THE EDGE OF THE DOOR · 29 degrees [80mm], camera at 125 cm, holding with only the faintest float. THE FRAMING IS TIGHT AND ASYMMETRIC.
FRAME RIGHT, occupying the whole right half of the frame: THE OPEN DOOR LEAF ITSELF, seen close and near, angled into the room toward us, its painted panels and mouldings running vertically, its brass knob low in frame, and its vertical free edge running top to bottom roughly through the middle of the frame. Frame FAR LEFT: the pale plastered wall and the door architrave.
FRAME CENTRE-LEFT, in the gap between the leaf's edge and the architrave: HER, half-hidden by the door. ONLY THE NEAR HALF OF HER FACE AND BODY IS VISIBLE — her forehead, her fringe, both eyes, her nose and part of her mouth read clearly, with the leaf's vertical edge cutting down across her face just past the far side of her nose so the rest of her is hidden behind it. Her ponytail and the loose lengths of her hair fall past her shoulder. Her near shoulder and upper arm in the black tee read below. HER NEAR HAND IS UP ON THE FREE EDGE OF THE LEAF, fingers curled over the timber at about chest height, gripping it.
SHE IS LOOKING INTO THE ROOM PAST THE CAMERA — her eyeline goes forward and clearly off to one side, beside and slightly above the lens, never down the barrel. The room she is looking at is entirely off frame and never seen in this shot.
5–7s — she holds the door edge and looks in. HER EYES ARE WIDE AND HER BROWS ARE RAISED AND DRAWN IN. Her mouth is slightly parted for breath only. Her eyes make small quick passes as she takes the room in.
7–9s — HER EYES DART. They go down and off to one side and hold — landing on something low and off frame — then come back up and across and hold there. Then down again. Each is a real considered look with a beat on it, her head making tiny movements after her eyes, never a flick and never a scan. Her brows go up a fraction further with each pass. On the last one her fingers release the timber. She breathes visibly, blinks at uneven intervals, her jaw sets slightly. HARD CUT.

SHOT 3 · 9–14s · SHE STEPS IN, SEES THE MESS, AND CHOOSES AWAY FROM IT · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 115 cm beside the bed on the door-wall side, angled across the room, drifting right ten centimetres. Frame LEFT: the open doorway seen obliquely with the leaf angled into the room, and her stepping through it into the room proper. Frame RIGHT and in depth: the window wall, the armchair, the footstool, and ON THE FLOORBOARDS BENEATH THE WINDOW THE BROKEN POT — shards, spilled soil and the collapsed ivy, lit clearly by the daylight parallelogram. Frame LOWER: floorboards.
9–11s — she crosses the threshold and comes two steps into the room, soft slippers placing quietly. She slows and stops. Her weight settles onto one hip, her shoulders drop a little.
11–13s — HER HEAD TURNS TOWARD FRAME RIGHT AND HER EYES LAND ON THE BROKEN POT. She looks straight at it and HOLDS THE LOOK for a real beat. HER BROWS GO UP. Her mouth stays closed. Her free hand comes up and her fingers close loosely on the hem of her tee.
13–14s — AND THEN SHE LOOKS AWAY FROM IT. Her head turns back across and past the camera toward the bed, which is off frame behind and beside the lens, her eyeline going clearly off-axis and never down the barrel. She takes a step that way. SHE DOES NOT GO TO THE MESS AND NEVER TOUCHES IT. She breathes visibly, blinks unevenly, her fingers work on the hem. HARD CUT.

SHOT 4 · 14–17s · THE BROKEN PLANT ON THE FLOOR · 24 degrees [85mm], camera at 30 cm, LOW AT FLOOR LEVEL, holding still. Frame CENTRE and filling most of it: THE BROKEN TERRACOTTA POT on the timber floorboards beneath the window — several large curved shards of orange-brown clay lying where they fell with their fractured edges pale and raw, a dark spill of dry soil scattered across the boards around them, the root ball turned out on its side, a separate saucer fragment, and <<<c2d07563-1ab6-4485-ae4a-5ddb69397ba6>>> lying collapsed among the pieces, its dull greyish-green heart-shaped leaves browned and crisped at the edges, flat against the timber. Frame BEYOND, soft: the base of the armchair and the wall beneath the window. Frame UPPER, soft: the warm daylight falling across it all.
14–17s — NOTHING MOVES. The pot lies broken exactly where it fell. Not one shard shifts, not one crumb of soil moves, not one leaf stirs. THE PLANT DOES NOT LEAN, REACT, RESPOND, TURN OR ACKNOWLEDGE ANYTHING — it is furniture. The daylight lies across it and picks out every fractured edge, every crumb of dry soil and every crisped leaf tip. NOBODY IS IN THIS SHOT and no hand reaches into it. HARD CUT.

SHOT 5 · 17–25s · THE PILLOW · 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 110 cm facing the bed wall, drifting right ten centimetres. Frame CENTRE and RIGHT: THE BED with <<<19321f3a-7a60-4d04-acff-5e728b4e71be>>> lying ON TOP OF the sage coverlet — diagonal across the mattress, one shoulder down toward the middle, legs splayed and unaligned with one knee drawn up, one arm flung out across the empty half and the other trapped beneath her, HER HEAD HALF OFF THE PILLOW with only a corner of it under her cheek and her neck at an awkward angle. The coverlet is dragged crooked and rucked beneath her with one corner pulled loose at the foot. THE CERAMIC LAMP glows warm on the nightstand beside her head. Frame LOWER LEFT: THE FALLEN PILLOW, roughly sixty by forty centimetres, lying flat and crumpled on the floorboards beside the bed. Frame LEFT, soft in the depth: the window and, on the floor beneath it, the broken pot.
17–19s — <<<8557ad86-b274-4cff-a762-8e54407d85d4>>> comes into frame from the left and stops beside the bed, looking down at her mother. HER BROWS ARE RAISED AND DRAWN IN. Then HER EYES DROP TO THE PILLOW ON THE FLOOR and hold on it.
19–21s — she crouches down beside the bed, going onto one knee with the weight visible in her thigh and her free hand touching the boards for balance, and PICKS THE PILLOW UP with both hands — lifting it, its case rucked, its filling shifting and sagging over her hands with real soft weight. She stands back up with it held against her chest, her spine straightening under it, and takes a moment to get her balance.
21–24s — SHE PUTS IT BACK AND MAKES HER MOTHER COMFORTABLE. She leans over the bed carefully, one knee coming up onto the edge of the mattress, and eases the pillow into place beside her mother's head. Then she very gently slides one hand under her mother's cheek and lifts the head a few centimetres — barely — the head heavy and loose, the neck slack, the hair falling. She slips the pillow underneath with her other hand and LOWERS THE HEAD DOWN ONTO IT. THE HEAD SETTLES INTO THE PILLOW, compressing it, and the neck straightens out of its awkward angle. IT IS DONE SLOWLY AND CAREFULLY SO AS NOT TO WAKE HER, AND IT WORKS — the mother does not stir, does not wake and does not open her eyes. She snores softly through the whole thing.
24–25s — the daughter straightens up and stands beside the bed looking down at her mother for a beat, her brows still raised and drawn, her mouth closed. Her hands come down to her sides and her fingers work against her sweatpants. She breathes visibly and blinks unevenly. HARD CUT.

SHOT 6 · 25–30s · SHE GOES, LOOKING BACK · 45 degrees [40mm], camera at 90 cm beside the window facing the door wall, drifting left ten centimetres. FRAME LOWER RIGHT, NEAR THE LENS AND SOFT: THE BROKEN POT — shards, spilled soil and the collapsed ivy on the sunlit floorboards, close in the foreground. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT in depth: THE OPEN DOORWAY with the leaf still standing angled into the room where it was left, and the lit landing beyond. Frame LEFT and soft: the bed with the sleeping mother, her head now properly on the pillow. Frame CENTRE: the daughter crossing.
25–27s — she crosses the room toward the doorway, AND HER FEET HAVE QUICKENED — shorter, faster steps, her weight carried forward, her shoulders slightly ahead of her hips. It is quicker than anything she has done so far and it is still completely quiet, still soft slippers placing on boards, never running, never stumbling, never fleeing. AND SHE IS ALREADY LOOKING BACK — her body going one way and her head turned the other, back over her shoulder and DOWN TOWARD THE BROKEN POT IN THE NEAR FOREGROUND, her eyeline going low and off to the side past the near edge of the lens and never into it. HER EYES STAY ON THE MESS while she walks.
27–29s — she reaches the doorway and steps into it, one hand going to the architrave and gripping it, HER HEAD STILL TURNED BACK. She checks for one beat, still looking at the shards and the soil and the collapsed ivy. HER BROWS ARE RAISED AND DRAWN IN. HER EYES FLICK ONCE across to her mother on the bed and hold briefly, then come back down to the mess. HER EYES STAY COMPLETELY DRY — no welling, no brightening along the lash line, no wet catchlight.
29–30s — she turns away and goes, stepping out through the doorway onto the landing and out of frame, her hand releasing the architrave last. THE DOOR IS LEFT STANDING OPEN exactly where it was — she does not close it, does not pull it, does not touch the leaf. THE MESS IS LEFT EXACTLY AS IT WAS — nothing swept, nothing gathered, nothing righted, nothing moved. LAST FRAME: the broken pot on the sunlit floorboards in the near foreground, the empty doorway with the leaf angled into the room and the lit landing beyond, and the mother asleep on top of the bed with her head now settled on the pillow.

PHYSICS: a panelled door on real hinges swings forward into a room against its own mass with faint hinge friction, and a brass knob turns against real spring resistance. A hand gripping the free edge of a door leaf wraps the timber and compresses slightly against it. Soft slippers make quiet muffled contact on timber floorboards. A PILLOW HAS REAL SOFT WEIGHT — it sags and folds over the hands lifting it, its filling shifting inside the case, and it compresses and settles when a head is lowered onto it. A SLEEPING HEAD LIFTED A FEW CENTIMETRES is heavy and loose, the neck slack, and it settles down into the pillow rather than being placed. A body lying on top of a coverlet rucks and drags it beneath its weight, and the mattress and the bedding depress under a knee coming onto the edge. Broken terracotta shards and spilled soil lie exactly where they fell and are never disturbed, never touched and never moved at any point. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT.

ACTING: she is a child who has come to check on someone and is finding something she cannot make sense of — and her instinct is care rather than tidying. THE PERFORMANCE IS IN HER BROWS AND HER EYES throughout, and in the gentleness of her hands with the pillow. SHE REGISTERS THE BROKEN POT AND CHOOSES HER MOTHER OVER IT, and that choice is the whole point of the scene. She is concerned and confused, never frightened, never grieving and never dramatic. SHE NEVER CRIES AND HER EYES STAY COMPLETELY DRY. She does not gasp, does not startle, does not cover her mouth, does not call out and does not clean anything up. THE MOTHER IS COMPLETELY UNCONSCIOUS AND UNAWARE — she never stirs, never wakes, never opens her eyes and never reacts, even while being moved, and her snoring is played straight and never for comedy. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT for the daughter: she breathes visibly, she blinks at uneven irregular intervals, and her fingers work slightly against whatever she is touching. THREE FOR THE MOTHER: her chest rises and falls unevenly, her lips flutter loosely on an exhale without ever shaping a word, and one hand settles a fraction where it lies. THE TWO OF THEM NEVER ACT AT THE SAME MOMENT — the mother is inert and the daughter carries every beat, and any settle of the mother's arrives a full beat after the daughter's hands have finished. NOBODY LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point.

AUDIO: diegetic only. A quiet warm house in the morning with the room tone audible. Faint birdsong through the window. A brass knob turning and a panelled door swinging open on its hinges — once, at the start. Soft slippered feet placing quietly on timber floorboards. Fabric moving — loose cotton jersey and sweatpants. Fingers gripping painted timber. IN SHOT 4, ALMOST NOTHING — only room tone and faint birdsong, with the broken pot making no sound at all. A knee coming down onto floorboards. A pillow lifted off the floor with a soft rustle of case and filling. Bedding shifting under a leaning weight. The soft settle of a head into a pillow. SOFT IRREGULAR SNORING from the sleeping woman throughout, audible faintly from off frame in shots 1 to 4 and clearly in shots 5 and 6 — thick, heavy and unglamorous, on each intake, not loud and never comic, continuing unbroken while she is moved. Quicker slippered feet crossing the room at the end and stepping out through the doorway. NO OTHER SOUND FROM ANYWHERE IN THE HOUSE. No speech, no words, no murmuring and no vocal sound beyond breath and snoring at any point. NO BGM of any kind at any point.

LOCKS: six hard-cut shots across thirty seconds, ALL SIX SHOT FROM INSIDE THE MOTHER'S BEDROOM — the door opens toward us and she is there, her face at the edge of the door, she steps in and sees the mess and looks away from it, the broken plant on the floor, the pillow, she goes looking back. THE ROOM HAS ONE DOOR ONLY and the second leaf in the supplied plate does not exist. THE DOOR IS HINGED INSIDE THE ROOM AND SWINGS TOWARD THE CAMERA, GROWING LARGER — it never recedes, never shrinks and never travels away from the lens, and once open it stays open, angled into the room, until the end. THE DOORWAY IS ALWAYS LIT FROM THE LANDING BEYOND AND NEVER READS AS A DARK HOLE. THE MOTHER LIES ON TOP OF THE COVERLET, NOT UNDER IT — diagonal, splayed, head half off the pillow, the bedding dragged crooked beneath her, and ONE PILLOW ON THE FLOOR beside the bed. THE DAUGHTER SEES THE BROKEN POT, LOOKS AWAY FROM IT, AND PICKS UP THE FALLEN PILLOW INSTEAD — putting it back and easing it under her mother's head to make her comfortable, gently enough not to wake her. SHE NEVER TOUCHES THE MESS AND NEVER CLEANS ANYTHING UP. SHOT FOUR IS A LOW STILL CLOSE-UP OF THE BROKEN POT WITH NOBODY IN FRAME AND NOTHING MOVING. THE BROKEN POT IS THE ONLY SOUL PLANT IN THE SEQUENCE and no other plant, pot or planter appears at any depth in any frame. SHE LEAVES THROUGH THE SAME DOOR SHE CAME IN BY, HER FEET QUICKENED AND HER HEAD TURNED BACK OVER HER SHOULDER AT THE MESS, and it is left exactly as it was. HER EYES STAY COMPLETELY DRY THROUGHOUT. The plant never moves, never leans and never reacts. Nothing moves before it is touched. The mother never wakes and never speaks. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms a word, and nobody looks at the lens.

SIX SHOTS. TOTAL RUNTIME 30 SECONDS.
SHOT 1 — 0s to 5s. SHOT 2 — 5s to 9s. SHOT 3 — 9s to 14s. SHOT 4 — 14s to 17s. SHOT 5 — 17s to 25s. SHOT 6 — 25s to 30s.
CUT POLICY: five hard cuts, instantaneous, on the frame. No dissolve, no fade, no crossfade, no wipe, no transitional frames, no speed ramp, no slow motion, no retiming. Every shot plays in continuous real time at natural speed.

NO BGM — no score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE: nobody speaks anywhere in this sequence. No words, no talking, no calling out, no whispering, no muttering, no vocalising of any kind. THE DAUGHTER'S MOUTH NEVER FORMS A WORD and never moves as if speaking at any point — it opens for BREATH only. She does not call to her mother, does not say her name and does not mouth anything silently. THE MOTHER NEVER SPEAKS, NEVER MURMURS AND NEVER TALKS IN HER SLEEP — the only sound she makes is soft snoring. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue.

BOTH DOORS START CLOSED — CRITICAL: at the opening of this sequence BOTH panelled doors at the internal corner of the landing are FULLY CLOSED, exactly as the supplied landing plate shows them, each with a thin bright strip of light glowing along the floor beneath it. Nothing is ajar, nothing is cracked and nothing stands open. The mother's door is shut and stays shut until the daughter opens it herself in shot 2.

DOORS OPEN INWARD, ALWAYS — CRITICAL: THE RIGHT-HAND DOOR, the daughter's, SWINGS INTO HER OWN ROOM, away from the landing and away from the camera, when she comes out. THE LEFT-HAND DOOR, the mother's, SWINGS INTO THE MOTHER'S BEDROOM, away from the landing and away from the camera, when the daughter pushes it open. NEITHER DOOR EVER SWINGS OUT ONTO THE LANDING AND NEITHER EVER SWINGS TOWARD THE LENS at any point.

THE MOTHER IS ON TOP OF THE BED, NOT UNDER THE COVERS — CRITICAL: she has plainly had a bad night and moved around a great deal. SHE LIES ON TOP OF THE SAGE GREEN COVERLET, fully outside the bedding, wearing what she went to bed in. THE COVERLET IS STILL ON THE BED beneath her but it is dragged crooked and rucked into folds under her weight, one corner pulled loose from the foot of the mattress and hanging.

SHE IS LYING AWKWARDLY AND OFF-CENTRE: not square to the bed, not neatly on her side of it. Her body runs diagonally across the mattress, one shoulder well down toward the middle, her legs splayed and unaligned with one knee drawn up, one arm flung out across the empty half of the bed and the other trapped underneath her. HER HEAD IS NOT PROPERLY ON A PILLOW — it lies half on the mattress with only a corner of one pillow under her cheek, her neck at an uncomfortable angle.

AND ONE PILLOW IS ON THE FLOOR — CRITICAL: a second pillow has been pushed or knocked off the bed during the night and LIES ON THE FLOORBOARDS BESIDE THE BED, dropped flat and slightly crumpled where it landed, its case rucked. It has been there for hours. It does not move until the daughter picks it up.

THE DAUGHTER'S FIRST INSTINCT IS THE PILLOW, NOT THE MESS — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE HEART OF THE SEQUENCE: when she comes into the room she sees the broken pot on the floor and registers it — but SHE DOES NOT GO TO IT AND DOES NOT TOUCH IT. Her attention moves off it and onto her mother, and what she does is PICK THE FALLEN PILLOW UP OFF THE FLOOR AND PUT IT BACK ON THE BED, easing it under her mother's head to make her comfortable. That is the only thing she does in the room. She does not sweep up the shards, does not gather the soil, does not right the plant, does not tidy anything and does not wake her mother. THE MESS IS LEFT EXACTLY WHERE IT IS.

SHE IS CONCERNED AND CONFUSED, NOT DISTRAUGHT — CRITICAL: her whole register is worry and puzzlement, and it stays contained. HER BROWS ARE RAISED AND DRAWN IN at the inner ends — the specific shape of concern, not fear and not grief. Her eyes are wide and searching. Her mouth stays closed or very slightly parted. SHE DOES NOT CRY — no tears, no welling, no brightening along the lash line, no wet catchlight, no glassiness, no sniff, no trembling lip, no crumpling and no hand to her face. She does not gasp, does not startle, does not panic and does not rush.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: head slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouette built from soft rounded primary solids that reads instantly in blackout. Face simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple nose, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: timber holds carved figure, plaster holds a tooth, painted joinery holds brush direction and soft chips, brass holds a dulled patina, clay holds thumb marks and a fractured edge. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never evenly paced. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

SHOT 1 = 40 degrees [45mm], camera at 130 cm on the landing.
SHOT 2 = 34 degrees [58mm], camera at 130 cm on the landing.

CAMERA: gentle handheld register throughout, three to eight degrees of cant, floating and drifting with small organic corrections, never locked, never stabilized, never gimbal-glide. LIGHT: warm morning daylight, one consistent hour across all six shots with no shift at any cut. On the landing it rakes across the herringbone boards and up the plaster, warm and soft. PHYSICS: a panelled door on real hinges swings into a room against its own mass with faint hinge friction, and a brass knob turns against real spring resistance. A hand gripping the vertical edge of a door leaf wraps the timber and compresses slightly against it. Soft slippers make quiet muffled contact on herringbone timber and on floorboards. A PILLOW HAS REAL SOFT WEIGHT — it sags and folds over the hands lifting it, its filling shifting inside the case, and it compresses and settles when a head is lowered onto it. A SLEEPING HEAD LIFTED A FEW CENTIMETRES is heavy and loose, the neck slack, and it settles down into the pillow rather than being placed. A body lying on top of a coverlet rucks and drags it beneath its weight. Broken terracotta shards and spilled soil lie exactly where they fell and are never disturbed, never touched and never moved at any point. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT.

ACTING: she is a child who has come to check on someone and is finding something she cannot make sense of — and her instinct is care rather than tidying. THE PERFORMANCE IS IN HER BROWS AND HER EYES throughout, and in the gentleness of her hands with the pillow. SHE REGISTERS THE BROKEN POT AND CHOOSES HER MOTHER OVER IT, and that choice is the whole point of the scene. She is concerned and confused, never frightened, never grieving and never dramatic. SHE NEVER CRIES AND HER EYES STAY COMPLETELY DRY. She does not gasp, does not startle, does not cover her mouth, does not call out and does not clean anything up. THE MOTHER IS COMPLETELY UNCONSCIOUS AND UNAWARE — she never stirs, never wakes, never opens her eyes and never reacts, even while being moved, and her snoring is played straight and never for comedy. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT: the daughter breathes visibly, blinks at uneven intervals, and her fingers work slightly against whatever she is touching. NOBODY LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: head slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouette built from soft rounded primary solids that reads instantly in blackout. Face simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple nose, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations, never strand-by-strand, never flyaway. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: timber holds carved figure, plaster holds a tooth, painted joinery holds brush direction and soft chips, brass holds a dulled patina, clay holds thumb marks and a fractured edge. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery rather than a hard mechanical stop. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never evenly paced. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes visibly, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

Proportion pushed toward warmth: head slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouette built from soft rounded primary solids that reads instantly in blackout. Face simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple nose, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction and physical bead, timber holds carved grain, metal holds dents and oxidation, wicker holds weave. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Bodies squash on impact and stretch on reach. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic. Between actions she never freezes — she breathes, blinks, shifts weight, adjusts.

CONTACT FIRST, THEN MOTION — CRITICAL: nothing moves until a hand, a foot or a body has visibly touched it. The bike does not fall until her hands have visibly released it. She navigates the kerb and the paving with real clearance and never passes through, clips into or overlaps anything.

The paint on her forearms goes all the way up past where the sleeves were. Then she reaches UP for the brass taps — the basin rim is at her chest and the taps sit above it — and turns one on. Water starts running into the ceramic. HARD CUT.

SHOT 2 · 5–10s · WASHING · 30 degrees [65mm], camera at 100 cm, pushing in forty centimetres. Frame LEFT: the timber edge of the washstand and the frosted window above in the mid plane. Frame CENTRE: the basin, the running water and her two hands under it, large in frame. Frame RIGHT: her forearms and the bunched sleeves at her elbows.

She works at the ring of colour round each wrist. Water runs off her hands and goes pink, then brown, then muddy in the bottom of the basin before it drains.
7.5–10s — THE PAINT DOES NOT REALLY COME OFF. The surface loosens and thins and the water carries colour away, but it stays down in the creases of her palms, in the nail beds, in the fine lines of her knuckles and in a stubborn ring at each wrist. She scrubs harder, then harder again, digging one thumbnail under the edge of a patch. Her breathing is still audible but slowing. Her shoulders drop a little. She stops scrubbing. She turns her hands over once under the water and looks at them, still stained. HARD CUT.

SHOT 3 · 10–15s · THE MIRROR · 24 degrees [85mm], camera at 125 cm, pushing in twenty-five centimetres very slowly. Frame CENTRE: the small square mirror on the wall above the washstand with her face in it. Frame LEFT and RIGHT: cream plaster and the frosted window's dim glow, soft. She looks at herself — the paint still on her cardigan, the smear across the plaid, her hair, her glasses, her own face — and her breathing finally comes down to almost nothing.

Water sheets off skin and runs pink, then brown, then muddy, swirling before it drains. DRIED POSTER PAINT ON SKIN THINS AND LOOSENS UNDER WATER AND SCRUBBING BUT DOES NOT COME OFF — it stays in every crease, under every nail and in a ring at each wrist no matter how hard she works. She has been level and unreadable every time something has gone wrong in this film, and here, alone, in a dim room with nobody to hold it for, it finally shows on her face — and even then it is tiny. She never loads paint from the water jar, never loads straight from a paint jar, never rinses in paint. Show this order plainly.

PHYSICS: bedcovers lift with real weight and drag on themselves rather than flying. Bare feet compress on cold timber and the toes curl, and a board takes weight in stages rather than all at once. A lamp switch clicks and the filament comes up over about a tenth of a second, and the lamp's arm holds wherever it is set by friction. A chair lifted rather than dragged makes almost no sound. A screw lid takes two hands and a quarter turn. Poster paint tipped from a jar falls as a thick slow blob that holds a peak where it lands. Squeezed from a tube it comes out as a coiling ribbon. Wet bristles tapped on a glass rim shed droplets that run back down the inside. Water clouds pink then muddy in visible swirls that settle. Bristles wiped on a stiff rag splay and spring back. Paint on bare porous timber sinks into the grain and darkens it at the stroke edges, sits proud in the middle, and runs downward under gravity within a second or two, slowing as it thins. Two wet colours meeting bleed at the join. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand, a foot or a body has touched it.

ACTING: the first three shots are fear and the last one is release, and the gap between them is the whole point. She is a good child doing her first genuinely forbidden thing and she is bad at it — everything is segmented, everything is checked, nothing is fluid. FIVE LOOKS AT THE DOOR, each longer than the last. TWO TOTAL FREEZES at sounds that turn out to be nothing, each held a full two seconds with her eyes wide and locked on the door. Two held breaths let out shakily. A hand shaking at the lamp switch and steadied with the other. And then the instant the brush touches the timber, all of it evaporates and her face goes completely absorbed and completely unguarded — she forgets to be afraid, which is exactly what painting does to her and exactly why she will keep doing it for the next eight years. She does not look pleased with herself and does not perform delight. She works. She blinks at uneven intervals, breathes visibly, and never holds a still expression except in the two deliberate freezes. She never looks toward the lens.

5–7s — her hand is on the knob and it is ALREADY TURNED, held all the way over, the latch withdrawn and out of sight in the door edge. Her knuckles are tight and her fingers are working — this is a controlled movement with effort in it.

THEN THE KNOB ROTATES BACK UNDER HER FINGERS, slow and controlled, degree by degree, and the latch settles into the strike with a small soft click rather than a bang. A brass knob turns against real spring resistance and returns under controlled fingers. A palm and a cheek laid flat against a door leaf compress slightly against it. A thumb drawn across glass in a hanging frame makes real contact without shifting the frame on its hook. Flat shoes on herringbone timber make soft contact with the boards, and a checked stumble puts an audible extra step in. Loose wide-leg trousers move a beat behind the leg. Hair swings heavily a beat behind the head and settles with a small overshoot, and hangs forward when she leans her head to the door. A stoneware jug and its dried stems do not move when someone passes. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. NO OBJECT MOVES BEFORE A HAND OR A BODY HAS TOUCHED IT.

ACTING: she is moving through her own house early in the morning with someone asleep behind a door, and every choice she makes after the first three seconds is about not waking them. THE OPENING IS FAST AND SLIGHTLY CLUMSY AND THE SWITCH TO SILENCE IS INSTANT — that contrast is the entire joke and it is played with her body, not her face. The closing of the door is the most careful thing she does and it takes real time. The listening is genuine, all her attention gone to her ear, her eyes unfocused. THE SMILE AT THE DOOR AND THE SMIRK AT THE WALL ARE DIFFERENT EXPRESSIONS and must not be played the same way — the first is warm and symmetrical and reaches the eyes, the second is one-sided, drier and more knowing. The touch on the photograph is brief and unsentimental and she does not linger over it. THREE INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS SUSTAINED THROUGHOUT: she breathes visibly, she blinks at uneven intervals, and her fingers work slightly against whatever they are touching. SHE NEVER LOOKS AT THE LENS at any point in any shot.

GEOMETRY MAP — all left and right camera-relative. The camera stands at the near end of the room looking down its length. Frame LEFT: THE OPEN PANELLED DOOR IN THE FAR LEFT CORNER, which is the exit, with a near round table cropped in the foreground below it. Frame CENTRE-LEFT: the chalkboard and the low bench with its row of terracotta pots in the mid plane. Frame CENTRE: the open floorboards with children crossing them away from the lens toward that far door, and beyond them the back round table where she sits, small in the depth. Frame CENTRE-RIGHT: the shelving, the ceramic sink and the tall tap against the far wall. Frame RIGHT: the bank of windows, the radiator, the windowsill houseplant and a foreground round table, cropped.

FIRST FRAME: already in motion. The shot opens with three children already crossing the floor toward the far corner door, chairs already shoved back, backpacks already going onto shoulders, and the camera already drifting. Nothing is held, nothing is static, there is no establishing hold, and the frame does not begin on the exact geometry of the supplied plate.

OPTICS: 46 degrees horizontal field of view [40mm], held constant for the entire twelve seconds. No zoom, no focal change and no lens breathing at any point. Deep enough focus that both the far corner door and the back table stay legible, with neither sharpened or favoured over the room.

CAMERA: one continuous move with no cut. A slow drift to the right covering about seventy centimetres across the twelve seconds at a constant rate, with a very slight push in of about thirty centimetres. THE CAMERA NEVER SETTLES ON HER OR MOVES TOWARD HER SPECIFICALLY — its interest stays on the room and the stream of children crossing it toward the door. Gentle handheld register throughout, three to six degrees of cant, floating and drifting with small organic corrections. Never locked, never stabilized, never mechanically smooth, never gimbal-glide.

LIGHT: low warm late-afternoon sun through the tall bank of windows at frame RIGHT, raking hard across the room from the side and throwing long soft-edged parallelograms of gold across the floorboards, up the tables and along the far wall. The chalkboard catches a bright raking wedge across one corner. The children pass in and out of those light bars as they cross toward the door, lit then unlit then lit again, and the space beyond the open door is noticeably darker than the room so each child is briefly silhouetted as they pass through it. THE BACK TABLE WHERE SHE SITS GETS NO SPECIAL TREATMENT — whatever warm bounce falls on that part of the room and nothing more, no shaft, no pool, no highlight singling her out. Generous warm bounce off cream plaster fills every shadow. Shadows soft-edged, lifted and tinted warm amber, never crushed. No pure black anywhere at any depth. Exposure never shifts. Nothing electric is on.

COLOUR: warm and saturated — the warmest and most colourful register in the film. Roughly 28% warm cream and bone in the plaster and walls, 24% honey and gold in the raking sun and pale floorboards, 16% warm timber umber in tables, chairs, shelving and bench, 12% terracotta orange in the row of pots and the windowsill pot, 12% mixed bright colour across the children's clothes and BACKPACKS and the paintings pinned on the walls, plus butter yellow in her cardigan and glasses, sap green in the houseplant, and the muted jar colours on the shelves. High saturation, warm-biased, constant across the whole shot.

DEPTH AND CLARITY: the air is completely clear. No dust, no motes, no particles, no haze, no mist, no fog, no volumetric shafts, no god rays, no visible sunbeam and nothing suspended anywhere at any depth. The sunlight lands on surfaces and never becomes visible in the space it crosses. Depth is carried only by a slight softening of the far plane and the shallow softness on the near foreground tables. Macro contrast low with blacks lifted at every depth, micro contrast high on plaster tooth, chalkboard slate, timber grain, paint-marked floorboards, knitted wool, canvas and nylon bag fabric, paper and clay.

ACTION TIMING:
0–3s — the room is already emptying fast toward the far left corner door. Three children are crossing the floor away from the lens with BACKPACKS ON — one squared on both shoulders, one hanging off a single shoulder, one held by its top handle in a hand. A fourth shoves her chair back hard, SWINGS HER BACKPACK UP ONTO ONE SHOULDER mid-stride and follows them. Two of them are LAUGHING at something — mouths open, one with her head tipped back, brief and easy, over in a couple of seconds. Neither of them waves. Behind all of it in the depth, our girl is already at her table with her head down over loose sheets of paper and no bag anywhere near her.
3–6s — three more go. ONE OF THEM WAVES on the move — turning her head back over her shoulder as she walks away toward the door and throwing a short flap at shoulder height without stopping, her eyes clearly angled off past the camera's left side and slightly upward, her mouth closed. The other two just leave, heads down, backpacks on. One is STILL WORKING HER SECOND ARM THROUGH A STRAP as she walks and does not slow down to do it. Another drops a pencil case, crouches fast, scoops it and carries on. The first children reach the far door and pass through it into the darker space beyond, briefly silhouetted. At the back table our girl slides one sheet aside and pulls another closer, comparing two side by side. She does not look up.
6–9s — the last cluster funnels toward the corner. One child is jogging the final steps to catch a friend already at the door, her backpack bouncing, and the friend laughs as she arrives — a short burst, mouth open, no words. TWO MORE WAVE as they go, both turning their heads back over their shoulders briefly, both eyelines off past the camera. Another two do not. One child's backpack is hanging much too low and knocks against the back of her legs as she walks. A chair gets caught on a strap and dragged half a metre before it comes free. At the back, our girl turns one sheet over, looks at its reverse, and sets it down on the pile.
9–12s — the last two children reach the far corner door and go through it, the taller one raising a hand back over her shoulder without turning fully, her eyes forward and away. The open door swings slightly and settles. THE DOORWAY STANDS EMPTY. THE NOISE DRAINS OUT WITH THEM. The camera drifts on, still taking in the whole room, and the low gold light and the shoved-back chairs are what fill the frame. Our girl is still there at the back, still head down, still going through her papers, small and unremarked in the depth. She has not looked up once. LAST FRAME: the emptied classroom in raking afternoon sun, chairs at odd angles all over the floor, the open door standing empty in the far left corner, and one small girl in the background at a table covered in loose drawings, absorbed in them.

PHYSICS: backpacks have real weight and swing on a shoulder a beat behind the body, and one worn too low knocks against the back of the legs at each stride. A bag swung up onto a shoulder mid-stride arcs and lands with a compression through that shoulder. A half-packed bag gapes open and has to be compressed with a forearm. An arm working into a second strap while walking makes the whole upper body twist and correct. Children's chairs are light and scrape and knock on timber floorboards when shoved, some tipping onto two legs before settling and one catching on a strap and dragging. A dropped pencil case lands flat and slides a little. Loose sheets of paper are light and stiff and slide over one another with a dry rasp, their curled corners catching. An open door swings slightly on its hinges as bodies pass close and settles after the last one. Nothing floats, nothing slides on its own, nothing stops instantly. No object moves before a hand or a body has touched it.

ACTING: the leaving children are ordinary and quick and slightly chaotic — this is the end of a school day and nobody is performing anything. Their laughter is real and brief and scattered, never a group event, and only a few of them wave, casually and over a shoulder on the way out. NOT ONE OF THEM LOOKS AT THE LENS. Our girl in the background does almost nothing and is never singled out: head down, hands moving over paper, completely absorbed, entirely unbothered by the room emptying around her. She is not lonely and not left out — she is just busy with something that matters more to her than leaving does. She glances up once, very briefly, around seven seconds, not at anybody in particular, and goes straight back down. Every child blinks at uneven intervals and never simultaneously with another, breathes at a clearly different rate, and never does the same thing at the same time as anybody else.

AUDIO: diegetic sound only. A classroom emptying fast at the end of the day. Children's chairs scraping, knocking and being shoved back, several at once and at different pitches, one dragging on a strap. Small feet crossing floorboards toward the far corner, some jogging, all quick, the footsteps receding as they reach the door and going briefly hollow as they pass into the corridor beyond. Backpacks being zipped on the move, buckles snapping, straps swinging and knocking, one bag thumping against the back of a pair of legs. A pencil case dropping flat and sliding. REAL AUDIBLE LAUGHTER in two or three short scattered bursts from different children, never all together and never sustained. Hard quick breathing from hurrying. A door swinging slightly on its hinges and settling. The general soft bustle of a dozen children leaving fast — footsteps, cloth, bags, furniture — WITH NO VOICES IN IT AT ALL, no chatter, no calling out, and no laughter that shapes into words. Under it all, faint and close, the dry rasp of loose sheets of paper being slid over one another at the back table. As the children go, ALL OF THE BUSTLE THINS AND FALLS AWAY across the last three seconds until what is left is the quiet room tone of an empty classroom, one radiator ticking faintly, muffled distant sound through the window glass, and just the paper. No speech, no words, no whisper and no vocalisation that shapes a word from anybody at any point. NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.

LOCKS: one unbroken twelve-second shot with a slow rightward drift and no cut, in warm low late-afternoon sun. A classroom empties FAST at the end of the day. EVERY CHILD HAS A BACKPACK — all twelve either already wearing one or visibly putting one on as they move, all different, worn every different way. THEY ALL LEAVE THROUGH THE OPEN PANELLED DOOR IN THE FAR LEFT CORNER, crossing the floor AWAY FROM THE LENS and passing through it into the darker space beyond — NOBODY EXITS PAST THE CAMERA. Two or three laugh in short scattered bursts with their mouths open and NOBODY EVER SPEAKS A WORD. ONLY THREE OR FOUR WAVE, briefly and over a shoulder on the move — the rest just go. Those who wave are waving to their teacher, WHO IS OFF FRAME BEHIND AND BESIDE THE CAMERA AND IS NEVER SEEN, and NOT ONE CHILD EVER LOOKS AT THE LENS. MEANWHILE, IN THE BACKGROUND AND NEVER AS THE FOCUS, our girl sits at the back table with NO BACKPACK, going through LOOSE SHEETS OF DRAWINGS whose content we never see clearly. THERE IS NO ART BOX ANYWHERE IN THIS SHOT. The camera never favours her, the light never singles her out, and she never looks up. By the last frame the doorway stands empty. Nothing moves without a hand or a body touching it first. Nobody speaks, no mouth ever forms a word, and nobody looks at the lens.

SIX SHOTS — 26 seconds. Shot 1 runs 0–4s, shot 2 runs 4–8s, shot 3 runs 8–14s, shot 4 runs 14–19s, shot 5 runs 19–23s, shot 6 runs 23–26s. Hard cuts between them, instantaneous, no dissolves, no fades, no transitional frames. Real-time throughout, no slow motion, no ramping, no speed change anywhere.
NO BGM — no background music of any kind. No score, no soundtrack, no instrumental, no underscore, no ambient musical pad, no drone, no tone bed, no swell, no sting, no humming, no singing, no whistling, no lyrics. Diegetic sound effects and room tone only. Nothing musical anywhere at any point.
ABSOLUTELY NO DIALOGUE — CRITICAL: nobody in this sequence speaks, ever. No spoken words, no talking, no whispering, no shouting, no muttering, no calling out, no vocalising of any kind. NO MOUTH EVER FORMS A WORD OR MOVES AS IF SPEAKING at any point, on either of them, in the foreground or the background. The mother's entire position is communicated by her crossed arms, her stance, her tapping foot and her face, and never by her mouth — her lips stay closed and still throughout. Mouths may open for BREATH only and never for a consonant, a vowel or a word. There is no dialogue audio and no mouthed dialogue.
NO ON-SCREEN TEXT: no titles, no captions, no subtitles, no watermarks, no logos, no timecode, no interface overlay, no lower thirds. No lettering of any kind burned into the frame anywhere at any point.

SHE ONLY EVER USES THE FAR RIGHT DOOR — CRITICAL AND ABSOLUTE: the landing has two bedroom doors meeting at a corner. THE ONE ON THE RIGHT IS HERS AND IT IS THE ONLY DOOR SHE EVER TOUCHES IN THIS ENTIRE SEQUENCE. She comes out of the RIGHT door in shot 1. She goes into the RIGHT door in shot 5. She comes out of the RIGHT door in shot 6. THE LEFT DOOR IS HER MOTHER'S AND IT STAYS SHUT FOR THE WHOLE SEQUENCE — it never opens, she never touches it, she never approaches it, she never looks at it, and nobody comes out of it at any point. Do not have her use the left door, do not have her use a different door in different shots, and do not swap which door she belongs to between the morning and the evening. Every entrance and exit she makes is through the same far right door.

THE DOORS ALWAYS OPEN INWARD, AWAY FROM THE CAMERA — CRITICAL: the right-hand door opens INTO her room, which means the leaf always swings AWAY from the lens and never toward it. IT NEVER SWINGS OUT ONTO THE LANDING AND IT NEVER OPENS TOWARD CAMERA. When it opens, the leaf travels away from us into the room beyond and the opening it leaves is a gap in the wall plane. When it closes, the leaf comes back toward us and seats flush inside its architrave. Because the leaf is recessed inside its frame and swings inward, NO HINGES ARE VISIBLE ON IT AT ANY POINT.

WE BARELY SEE THE ROOM BEHIND IT — CRITICAL: at no point does the interior of her bedroom read as a room. No bed, no desk, no window, no floor, no furniture, no wall and no object from inside is ever legible. THE CAMERA IS DELIBERATELY POSITIONED AT A SHALLOW OBLIQUE ANGLE TO THAT DOOR — off to one side rather than square to it — so that when the leaf swings inward IT MASKS THE SPACE BEHIND IT, and the gap that appears reads only as a narrow band of soft undifferentiated interior shadow with nothing resolving in it. She comes out from behind that leaf and goes in behind it. Do not render a bedroom interior at any point in any shot.

HER HAIR IS COMPLETELY WRECKED — CRITICAL: in shots 1 through 5 she has just woken up and HER HAIR IS EXTREMELY FRIZZY. Not a bit messy — properly frizzed out and enormous. The whole mass has expanded and lifted well away from her head, roughly half again its normal volume, with a broad soft halo of loose fibres standing off it in every direction and catching the light around its edges. One entire section on the crown is pushed straight upright and stays there. The side she slept on is crushed flat against her skull and kinked hard at a sharp angle where it was folded under her all night. The blunt fringe is shoved sideways across her forehead in a solid slab and stuck there, one corner of it sticking out horizontally. Individual clumps have separated and gone their own way. IT SHOULD READ AS GENUINELY FUNNY AND COMPLETELY UNBRUSHED, and she never touches it or fixes it at any point.

THE MATCH — CRITICAL, THIS IS THE POINT OF THE SEQUENCE: shot 5 and shot 6 are a matched pair on THE SAME FAR RIGHT DOOR. SHOT 5 is the little girl going INTO that door and slamming it in bright morning light. SHOT 6 is that same door, from THE EXACT SAME CAMERA POSITION, THE EXACT SAME HEIGHT, THE EXACT SAME SHALLOW ANGLE AND THE EXACT SAME LENS — but the light has changed to warm low evening and the girl who comes out is EIGHT YEARS OLDER. The frame must be identical: the same distance from the door, the same amount of landing floor in shot, the same portion of the corner and the mother's shut left door visible, the same framed pictures on the plaster at the same position in frame, the same console and guard rail at the same edge. NOTHING IN THE ARCHITECTURE OR THE CAMERA CHANGES BETWEEN THE TWO SHOTS. Only the light and the person change. Generate these two to match precisely so they cut as one frame across eight years.

THE LIGHT CHANGES ONLY ONCE — shots 1 through 5 are BRIGHT MORNING: clean early daylight, the landing and the great room open and light, sun reaching the corner of the landing and daylight spilling under the doors. SHOT 6 IS WARM LOW EVENING: the same spaces lit by a low late sun from a shifted angle, warmer and more golden, longer softer shadows, the corner patch shifted and reddened. No electric light is on at any point. The change happens on the cut between shot 5 and shot 6 and nowhere else.

THE PLANT HAS BEEN CLEANED AND IT IS DEVASTATING — CRITICAL: the terracotta pot is back on the high shelf and IT IS COMPLETELY BARE. Every mark she made in the night — the sun, the clouds, the dots, the red line — IS GONE. The clay is scrubbed clean, slightly paler and rawer than the rest of it where it has been worked at, with a faint damp darkness still in the porous surface and one small pale scoured patch where the sun used to be. There is no trace of the drawing left. The ivy above it is thriving, glossy and immaculate, every leaf clean. THE PLANT HAS NEVER LOOKED BETTER AND HER DRAWING HAS BEEN ERASED, and those two facts sit in the same frame.

THE PLANT NEVER MOVES — CRITICAL: the ivy does not move, react, lean or respond at any point, to anybody or anything. It has no face and no expression. It is as still as furniture in every frame it appears in.

CONTACT FIRST, THEN MOTION — CRITICAL: nothing moves until a hand, a foot or a body has visibly touched it. The door does not move until fingers are on it. She navigates the console, the guard rail, the treads, the sofa and the coffee table with real clearance and never passes through, clips into or overlaps any of them.

STYLE: stylized 3D animated feature rendering — appealing caricature, not photoreal and not cel-shaded. NOT CLAYMATION AND NOT STOP MOTION — smooth continuous CG feature animation, no clay, no plasticine, no armature seams, no faceted hand-pressed surfaces on any body, no stop-motion stutter, no frame-stepped movement. Proportion pushed toward warmth: heads slightly oversized against the body, hands and feet slightly undersized, silhouettes built from soft rounded primary solids that read instantly in blackout. Faces simplified — large clear eyes with a visible wet iris and a single soft catchlight, small simple noses, brows and mouth carrying the entire performance. Skin completely matte and poreless with generous subsurface scattering at the ears, nose, fingertips and jaw edge. Zero pore texture, zero peach fuzz, zero blemish detail, zero skin micro-noise. Hair is a sculpted mass with groomed clumps and carved separations — and where it is frizzed, the mass expands and lifts with soft standing separations and a fine halo at its edges rather than becoming individual flyaway strands. Cloth is the highest-fidelity element in frame — real weight, real fold behaviour, visible weave and stitch, soft wear at cuffs and hems. Surfaces hand-crafted rather than scanned: paint holds brush direction, timber holds carved grain, clay holds thumb marks and hand-thrown ridges. Warm, hand-made, lived-in and slightly softened — never plastic, never glossy, never render-clean.

THE ANIMATION — CRITICAL: character motion is warm, weighted, hand-animated feature animation, not motion capture and not realistic human timing. Every movement carries visible anticipation before it — a small dip, lean or counter-motion first — then the action, then a soft settle with a slight overshoot and recovery. Bodies squash a little on impact and stretch a little on reach, held within believable anatomy. Timing is slow-in and slow-out, never linear, never robotic, never evenly paced. Between actions nobody freezes — they breathe visibly, blink, shift weight, adjust.
